20408.m: In Lehrplan 21, media literacy is learnt in the Media and Computer Science module.

20409.q: According to Swiss studies, which device do almost all young people aged 12 to 19 use every day?
20409.e: The JAMES study by the ZHAW surveys young people in Switzerland every two years. Almost all of them have their own phone and use it every day.
20409.m: The mobile phone is the most important media device for Swiss young people.

20410.q: What can you find in the legal notice (imprint) of a website?
a: Details of who is responsible for the site
20410.e: The legal notice gives the name and address of the operators. It helps you judge how trustworthy a site is.
20410.m: The legal notice says who is behind a website.

20411.q: How can you tell that a website is more likely to be trustworthy?
a: It names sources and has a legal notice
It has lots of colourful pictures
It asks for your password straight away
20411.e: Genuine sites show who is behind them and back up their statements with sources. The federal government's “Youth and Media” platform, for example, offers tips on this.
20411.m: Trustworthy sites name sources and the people responsible.

20412.q: What is a good strategy against too much screen time?
a: Charging your phone next to your pillow at night
20412.e: Phone-free times, for example at meals or before sleeping, help you control your media use consciously.
20412.m: Phone-free times help me use media consciously.

20413.q: What is the difference between a news article and a comment piece in a newspaper?
a: The comment piece gives a personal opinion
The comment piece is always longer
The comment piece has no headline
The comment piece only contains numbers
20413.e: A news article reports on events as factually as possible. A comment piece is marked as an opinion article.
20413.m: News reports, comment pieces give opinions.

20414.q: What is a phishing attack called that is specifically tailored to a particular person or company?
20414.e: In spear phishing, attackers research their victim beforehand and use real names, projects or contacts. This makes the message seem especially believable.
20414.m: The more personal a suspicious message seems, the more carefully you should check it.

20415.q: What does ransomware typically do on an infected system?
a: It encrypts data and demands a ransom.
It redirects searches to fake pages.
20415.e: Ransomware makes files unusable by encrypting them and usually demands payment in cryptocurrency for the key. Regular offline backups are the most important protection.
20415.m: Against ransomware, up-to-date backups kept off the network help most.

20416.q: What is meant by a zero-day vulnerability?
a: A weakness for which there is no patch yet
A fault that appears right after purchase
A virus that is deleted after zero days
A vulnerability that can only be exploited at weekends
20416.e: The manufacturer has had “zero days” to fix the weakness because it is still unknown to them or has only just become known. Such vulnerabilities are very valuable on black markets.
20416.m: No update yet protects against a zero-day vulnerability.

20417.q: How does a DDoS attack work?
a: Many hijacked devices flood a server with requests.
An attacker guesses the administrator password.
Malicious code is smuggled into a database query.
Data is secretly read while in transit.
20417.e: In a distributed denial of service attack, often thousands of devices in a botnet attack at the same time. The service is overloaded and can no longer be reached by real users.
20417.m: A DDoS attack paralyses services by overloading them.

20418.q: Which combination is two-factor authentication in the true sense?
a: Password and a code from an app on your phone
20418.e: Two-factor authentication requires two different types of factor, such as knowledge (password) and possession (phone). Password and security question are both knowledge.
20418.m: Real two-factor authentication combines different kinds of proof.

20419.q: What is the federal office responsible for cybersecurity in Switzerland since 2024 called?
20419.e: On 1 January 2024 the former National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) became the Federal Office for Cybersecurity BACS. It belongs to the Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport (DDPS).
20419.m: The BACS is the federal government’s central point of contact for cyberattacks.

20420.q: What has applied to operators of critical infrastructure in Switzerland since 1 April 2025?
a: They must report cyberattacks to the BACS within 24 hours.
They may no longer use cloud services.
They must mirror all data abroad.
They must hold a hacking competition every year.
20420.e: With the amendment of the Information Security Act, there is a duty to report cyberattacks on critical infrastructure such as energy, hospitals or banks. The report to the BACS must be made within 24 hours of discovery.
20420.m: Critical infrastructure in Switzerland must report cyberattacks quickly.

20421.q: Which security vulnerability did the WannaCry ransomware exploit in 2017?
a: A vulnerability in the Windows SMB protocol
A vulnerability in the Bluetooth standard
A vulnerability in Wi-Fi routers with WPA2
A vulnerability in the Outlook email program
20421.e: WannaCry spread via the “EternalBlue” exploit, which used a weakness in Windows’ SMB file-sharing protocol. Hundreds of thousands of computers worldwide that had not installed updates were affected.
20421.m: Security updates that are not installed can lead to worldwide damage.

20422.q: In asymmetric encryption, what do you use to encrypt a message to someone?
20422.e: Anyone may know the public key; but only whoever has the matching private key can decrypt. So no secret has to be exchanged beforehand.
20422.m: The public key locks, the private key unlocks.

20423.q: Which mathematical problem is the security of RSA based on?
a: The difficulty of factorising large numbers into primes
The infinity of the number pi
The difficulty of adding large numbers
20423.e: Multiplying two large primes is easy; splitting the product again is practically impossible with today’s computers. RSA was presented in 1977 by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman.
20423.m: RSA is secure as long as factorising huge numbers takes too long.

20424.q: Which symmetric method was adopted as a standard by the US standards institute NIST in 2001?
20424.e: The Advanced Encryption Standard is based on the Rijndael algorithm by the Belgian cryptologists Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen. It replaced the outdated DES and is used worldwide today.
20424.m: AES is today the most important standard for symmetric encryption.

20425.q: Which problem did the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, published in 1976, solve?
a: Agreeing on a shared key over an insecure channel
20425.e: It lets two parties create a secret key even though third parties are listening to the whole conversation. The method was a milestone of public-key cryptography.
20425.m: With Diffie-Hellman a shared secret is created without ever being transmitted.

20426.q: What does end-to-end encryption mean in a messaging app?
a: Only the sender and recipient can read the message.
The message is deleted after it is read.
Only the provider’s server can read the message.
The message is only sent at the end of the day.
20426.e: The message is encrypted on the sender’s device and only decrypted on the recipient’s device. Even the provider whose server it passes through only sees unreadable data.
20426.m: With end-to-end encryption not even the provider can read along.

20427.q: What does the word “HALLO” become with the Caesar cipher and a shift of 3 letters?
20427.e: Each letter is moved three places along the alphabet: H becomes K, A becomes D, L becomes O and O becomes R. This gives KDOOR.
20427.m: The Caesar cipher shifts every letter by the same number of places.

20428.q: Which property must a cryptographic hash function such as SHA-256 have?
a: The input practically cannot be worked out from the hash value.
The hash value is always as long as the input.
The hash value can be decrypted with a key.
The same input gives a different hash value every time.
20428.e: Hash functions are one-way functions with a fixed output length; for SHA-256 it is 256 bits. That is why passwords are stored as hash values rather than in plain text.
20428.m: A hash value is a fingerprint from which the data cannot be recovered.

20429.q: A password consists of 8 lower-case letters (26 possible characters). At most, how long does a computer making 1 billion attempts per second need to try every possibility?
20429.e: There are 26 to the power 8, about 208.8 billion combinations. Divided by 1 billion per second, that is about 209 seconds, roughly 3.5 minutes.
20429.m: Short passwords made of only one type of character are cracked in minutes.

20430.q: Which protocol encrypts the connection in HTTPS?
20430.e: Transport Layer Security (formerly SSL) encrypts the data between browser and web server and uses certificates to check the server’s identity. The padlock symbol in the browser shows such a connection.
20430.m: HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS.

20431.q: What do the three classic Vs of big data stand for?
20431.e: Big data describes amounts of data that are very large (volume), created quickly (velocity) and varied in form (variety). Further Vs such as veracity were often added later.
20431.m: Big data is large, fast and varied.

20432.q: In a town, ice cream sales correlate with sunburn. What is the best explanation?
a: A third cause, sunny weather, affects both.
Sunburn makes people want ice cream.
The correlation proves a direct link.
20432.e: A correlation only shows that two quantities vary together. Here a confounding variable is behind it: when the sun shines, both values rise.

20433.q: The daily screen times of five people are 10, 20, 30, 40 and 200 minutes. What is the median?
20433.e: The median is the middle value of the ordered list, here the third of five values, so 30. The mean would be 300 divided by 5, so 60, because the outlier 200 pushes it up a lot.
20433.m: The median is more robust to outliers than the mean.

20434.q: What is an A/B test in online marketing?
a: Two versions are shown at random to different user groups and compared.
A test of whether a website is accessible.
A check of whether advertising complies with the law.
A speed comparison of two servers.
20434.e: Users are randomly assigned version A or B, for example two colours of a button. Then statistics are used to check which version more often leads to the desired behaviour.
20434.m: A/B tests are used to optimise websites with real user data.

20435.q: An online shop has 2000 visitors in one day, and 50 of them buy something. What is the conversion rate?
20435.e: The conversion rate is the share of visitors who carry out a desired action. 50 divided by 2000 gives 0.025, so 2.5 per cent.
20435.m: The conversion rate measures how many visitors become customers.

20436.q: What are the metadata of a mobile phone call?
a: Who phoned whom, when and for how long
20436.e: Metadata are data about data, meaning the circumstances of communication rather than its content. Even from these you can work out relationships, habits and whereabouts.
20436.m: Even without content, metadata reveal a lot about a person.

20437.q: How does pseudonymisation differ from anonymisation?
a: Pseudonymised data can be linked back to a person with extra knowledge.
Anonymised data still contain the name.
There is no difference between the terms.
20437.e: With pseudonymisation, for example, the name is replaced by an ID number, but the table linking them still exists. With true anonymisation it is no longer possible to identify the person.
20437.m: Pseudonymised data still count as personal data.

a: Cookies from other providers that track users across many websites
Cookies that only the browser itself can read
Cookies that expire after three days
Cookies that store passwords in encrypted form
20438.e: They are not set by the site you visit, but for example by embedded advertising networks. This builds a cross-site profile of your browsing behaviour.
20438.m: Third-party cookies are mainly used for cross-site tracking.

20439.q: What principle does collaborative filtering work on?
a: It recommends what similar users liked.
It only recommends content with the same keywords.
It recommends the newest content first.
20439.e: Collaborative filtering looks for users with similar behaviour and suggests what they liked. A typical example is the note “Customers who bought this also bought”.
20439.m: Collaborative filtering uses the behaviour of similar people.

20440.q: What characterises content-based filtering for recommendations?
a: It compares features of content with what you already liked.
It only evaluates other users’ ratings.
20440.e: If someone often listens to calm jazz pieces, the system suggests more pieces with similar features such as tempo or genre. Other users play no part in this.
20440.m: Content-based filtering looks for things similar to what you already know.

20441.q: What does the cold start problem describe in recommender systems?
a: For new users or content there is not yet enough data for good recommendations.
Servers start more slowly in winter.
Old content is never recommended again.
Recommendations only work after a restart.
20441.e: Without previous clicks, purchases or ratings, an algorithm can hardly recognise preferences. That is why platforms often ask about your interests at the start.
20441.m: Recommender systems need data before they can recommend well.

20442.q: Who coined the term “filter bubble” with a book in 2011?
20442.e: The internet activist Eli Pariser described how personalised algorithms mainly show users content that fits their existing views. How strong this effect really is, is debated in research.
20442.m: Personalisation can narrow your view of the internet.

20443.q: How does an echo chamber differ from a filter bubble?
a: In an echo chamber like-minded people reinforce each other themselves.
An echo chamber is created only by algorithms.
Echo chambers only exist on music services.
An echo chamber filters out advertising.
20443.e: The filter bubble arises mainly from algorithmic selection. The echo chamber arises from social groups in which opinions are constantly repeated and thereby reinforced.
20443.m: In an echo chamber you mainly hear the echo of your own opinion.

20444.q: What do many recommendation algorithms on social networks mainly optimise for?
20444.e: The longer users stay and the more they like, comment or share, the more adverts can be shown. Emotional and polarising content often gets a particularly large amount of interaction.
20444.m: Whatever generates a lot of interaction is often shown more.

20445.q: What did a team have to achieve in the “Netflix Prize” to win the 1 million US dollars in 2009?
a: Improve prediction accuracy by 10 per cent
20445.e: Netflix was looking for a better algorithm to predict film ratings. The team “BellKor’s Pragmatic Chaos” beat the in-house system by just over 10 per cent.
20445.m: The Netflix Prize showed how valuable good recommendation algorithms are.

20446.q: What does the EU’s Digital Services Act require of very large platforms regarding recommender systems?
a: At least one option that is not based on profiling
A fee for each recommended post
20446.e: Very large online platforms must offer users a recommendation option that is not based on their personal profile data, such as a chronological feed. They must also disclose the main parameters of their systems.
20446.m: In the EU you can choose a non-personalised feed on large platforms.

20447.q: Who proposed a test in 1950 of whether a machine can hold a conversation like a human?
20447.e: In his paper “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, Alan Turing described the “imitation game”. If a person in a text conversation cannot tell machine from human, the test is passed.
20447.m: The Turing test checks whether a machine seems human.

20448.q: For which 1956 conference was the term “artificial intelligence” coined?
20448.e: John McCarthy chose the term in 1955 in the funding proposal for a summer project at Dartmouth College in the USA, which took place in 1956. This meeting is regarded as the birth of AI as a field of research.
20448.m: AI research as a subject began at Dartmouth in 1956.

20449.q: What characterises supervised learning in machine learning?
a: The model learns from examples with known correct answers.
A person supervises every calculation step.
The model learns without any data.
The model learns only through reward and punishment.
20449.e: In supervised learning the training data are labelled, for example pictures marked “cat” or “dog”. The model learns to infer these labels from the inputs.
20449.m: Supervised learning needs labelled training data.

20450.q: At its core, what does a large language model (LLM) do when it generates text?
a: It predicts the likely next piece of text step by step.
It copies whole answers from a database.
It understands language exactly like a human.
It searches the whole internet for every answer.
20450.e: Language models are trained on huge amounts of text and calculate probabilities for the next token. Many such steps produce whole texts.
20450.m: A language model produces text word by word from probabilities.

20451.q: What is called a “hallucination” in AI chatbots?
a: A convincingly worded but false statement
A deliberate lie by the developers
20451.e: Because language models produce plausible texts, they can supply invented facts, quotations or sources that sound real. So you should always check important information.
20451.m: Just because an AI says something confidently does not make it true.

20452.q: Which architecture, presented in 2017, forms the basis of today’s language models?
20452.e: In the paper “Attention Is All You Need”, researchers from Google presented the Transformer. Its attention mechanism captures relationships between all the words of a text at once.
20452.m: Modern language models are based on the Transformer architecture.

20453.q: How is the EU’s AI Act basically structured?
a: It sorts AI systems into levels according to their risk.
It bans every form of AI.
It only applies to robots in factories.
It only regulates the prices of AI products.
20453.e: The AI Act came into force on 1 August 2024. The higher the risk to people, the stricter the obligations; some uses, such as social scoring by authorities, are banned completely.
20453.m: The AI Act regulates AI more strictly the riskier it is.

20454.q: Which program defeated the Go professional Lee Sedol in a five-game match in 2016?
20454.e: DeepMind’s AlphaGo won 4 to 1. Because of its enormous number of possible positions, Go was long considered too difficult for computers.
20454.m: With AlphaGo, an AI beat a world-class Go player for the first time.

20455.q: Why can an AI used to select job applicants discriminate, even though nobody programmed it to?
a: It takes on biases from the training data.
It has developed its own prejudices.
It works only with random numbers.
20455.e: If certain groups were disadvantaged in earlier decisions, the model learns this pattern as “success”. This is called algorithmic bias.
20455.m: An AI is only as fair as the data it learns from.

20456.q: How does disinformation differ from misinformation?
a: Disinformation is spread deliberately to deceive.
20456.e: With misinformation, the person often believes the information is true. Disinformation, on the other hand, is deliberately invented or falsified, for example for political or financial aims.

a: Automated accounts that behave like humans on social networks
20457.e: Social bots automatically post, like and share and can give the impression that many people share an opinion. They are also used to spread disinformation.
20457.m: Behind many likes there may be a program rather than people.

20458.q: What is the Russian organisation in St Petersburg that became known as a troll factory called?
20458.e: The Internet Research Agency ran thousands of fake accounts and tried, among other things, to influence the 2016 US presidential election. This was documented in US investigations.
20458.m: Troll factories control many fake accounts to influence opinions.

20459.q: What does “lateral reading” mean when checking an unfamiliar website?
a: You open other sources to find out who is behind the site.
You read the page from right to left.
You read the page several times in a row.
20459.e: Fact-checkers do not stay on the site in question, but search in new tabs for information about where it comes from. This helps you see more quickly whether a source is trustworthy.
20459.m: To check a source, you should also search outside that source.

20460.q: What is the idea of “prebunking” against disinformation?
a: Preparing people in advance against typical tricks of deception
20460.e: Prebunking is based on inoculation theory: anyone who gets to know a weakened form of manipulation becomes more resistant. So it works preventively rather than disproving false claims afterwards.
20460.m: If you know manipulation tricks, you are less likely to fall for them.

20461.q: What did an MIT study published in “Science” in 2018 find about news on Twitter?
a: False reports spread faster and further than true ones.
True reports were shared ten times more often.
Bots spread almost all false reports on their own.
20461.e: The researchers analysed about 126,000 news cascades. False reports often seemed more novel and triggered stronger emotions, and it was mainly people, not bots, who spread them.
20461.m: False news often spreads faster than true news.

20462.q: What is the effect called whereby a statement seems more believable if you have heard it often?
20462.e: Repeated statements feel familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for truth. Disinformation campaigns exploit this by spreading claims again and again.
20462.m: Repetition does not make a statement truer, only more familiar.

20463.q: What do you call the tendency to believe mainly information that supports your own opinion?
20463.e: With confirmation bias, people look for and judge information in a way that confirms their expectations. This makes them vulnerable to false reports that fit.
20463.m: You should check especially carefully any report that fits neatly into your view of the world.

20464.q: Where does the term “deepfake” come from?
20464.e: A Reddit user called “deepfakes” published videos manipulated with AI in 2017. The word combines “deep learning” and “fake”.
20464.m: A deepfake is a forgery created with deep learning.

20465.q: How does a generative adversarial network (GAN) work?
a: A generator creates fakes, a discriminator tries to detect them.
Two people edit a video together.
A program copies pictures from the internet.
A camera films from two angles.
20465.e: The two networks train against each other until the fakes can hardly be told apart from the real thing. GANs were presented in 2014 by Ian Goodfellow and colleagues.
20465.m: In a GAN, forger and checker push each other to top performance.

20466.q: How are cloned voices typically used in scam calls?
a: Scammers imitate bosses or relatives and urgently ask for money.
They are only used for audiobooks.
They automatically read out weather reports.
They replace passwords when logging in.
20466.e: A few seconds of recorded speech are now enough to copy a voice deceptively well. If someone unexpectedly asks for money, it helps to call back on a known number or use an agreed code word.
20466.m: If someone urgently asks for money on the phone, always call back.

a: A deception made with simple methods such as slowing down or cropping
20467.e: Even a slowed-down video can make a person seem drunk, or a quotation is taken out of context. No AI is needed for this.
20467.m: Even simple edits can seriously distort videos.

20468.q: What is the C2PA standard (Content Credentials) for images and videos meant to make possible?
a: Making the origin and editing of media traceable
20468.e: C2PA attaches cryptographically secured origin information to media files, for example which camera or software was involved. This lets you check whether and how content has been changed.
20468.m: Proof of origin helps tell real media from manipulated media.

20469.q: What does the EU’s AI Act require for deepfakes?
a: They must be labelled as artificially created or altered.
They are banned in every case.
They must have a minimum length.
20469.e: Anyone creating AI content that deceptively resembles real people or events must disclose that it is artificial. Simpler rules apply to obviously artistic or satirical works.
20469.m: In the EU, deepfakes must be made recognisable as such.

20470.q: What does the “liar’s dividend” mean in connection with deepfakes?
a: Real recordings can be denied as supposed fakes.
Lies are rewarded on social networks.
Deepfake software is given away free.
20470.e: Because everyone knows fakes are possible, people who are caught can claim a real video is a deepfake. This damages trust in evidence as a whole.
20470.m: Deepfakes also threaten trust in real recordings.

20471.q: Since when has Switzerland’s fully revised Data Protection Act (FADP) been in force?
20471.e: The new FADP replaced the law of 1992 and adapted Swiss data protection to digital developments and to the EU’s GDPR. There was no transition period.
20471.m: The new Swiss Data Protection Act has applied since September 2023.

20472.q: Whose data does the revised Swiss FADP protect?
a: Only the data of natural persons
The data of people and companies equally
20472.e: With the revision, legal entities such as companies and associations were removed from its scope. This brings the FADP into line with the GDPR.
20472.m: The FADP protects people, not companies.

20473.q: Who supervises compliance with data protection by federal bodies and private parties in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA)
20473.e: The FDPIC can open investigations and issue rulings, for example ordering data to be deleted. However, it does not impose fines itself.
20473.m: The FDPIC is the federal data protection authority.

20474.q: What is the maximum fine under the Swiss FADP, and who is it aimed at?
a: Up to 250,000 francs, mainly the responsible individuals
Up to 20 million francs, only companies
Up to 4 per cent of turnover, only corporations
20474.e: Unlike the GDPR, the FADP’s penalties are basically aimed at the responsible natural persons. The fines are imposed by the cantonal criminal authorities.
20474.m: Under Swiss data protection law, individuals can be fined personally.

20475.q: Which data count as particularly sensitive personal data under the FADP?
a: Data about health or religious views
20475.e: Particularly sensitive data include health, religion, political views, genetic and biometric data. Stricter rules apply to processing them.

20476.q: What does “privacy by default” mean in the Swiss FADP?
a: Default settings must be as privacy-friendly as possible.
Data may be published by default.
Every user must use a pseudonym.
Data protection only applies on explicit request.
20476.e: Without users doing anything, only as much data as is needed for the purpose should be processed. In addition, “privacy by design” requires data protection right from development.
20476.m: Privacy-friendly settings should apply from the start.

20477.q: What can a person demand under the right of access in the FADP?
a: To find out whether and which data a company processes about them
The release of a company’s business figures
The deletion of all data on the internet
Compensation for every piece of stored data
20477.e: Access is usually free of charge and must be given within 30 days. It covers, for example, the data themselves, the purpose and the recipients.
20477.m: Everyone may find out what data are stored about them.

20478.q: Since when has the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applied?
20478.e: The GDPR was adopted in 2016 and, after a two-year transition period, has applied directly in all EU states since May 2018. It standardises data protection across the EU.
20478.m: A uniform data protection law has applied in the EU since 2018.

20479.q: What is the maximum fine under the GDPR?
a: 20 million euros or 4 per cent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
1 per cent of profit in the EU
20479.e: For large corporations the upper limit depends on worldwide turnover. This is meant to make the penalties noticeable even for very large companies.
20479.m: The GDPR threatens large corporations with fines based on turnover.

20480.q: Why must a Swiss company also comply with the GDPR if it sells goods online to customers in the EU?
a: Because of the market location principle
Because Switzerland is an EU member
Because all servers are in the EU
Because the FADP does not apply to online shops
20480.e: The GDPR also applies to companies outside the EU if they offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour. What matters is where the people concerned are.
20480.m: Anyone serving customers in the EU must comply with the GDPR.

20481.q: What does the GDPR require of a company if customer data have been hacked and the people affected are at risk of harm?
a: It must report the breach to the data protection authority quickly.
It only has to inform the police.
It need do nothing if it closes the gap.
It must delete all customer data at once.
20481.e: The GDPR requires a report to the supervisory authority, usually within 72 hours. If the risk is high, the people affected must also be informed. The Swiss FADP requires a report “as soon as possible”.
20481.m: In the EU, data breaches must be reported quickly.

20482.q: After a 2014 ruling by the European Court of Justice, what can you sometimes demand from search engines?
a: That they no longer show links to old reports about you
That they immediately delete all data about you worldwide
That they pay you for every search for your name
That they never again allow your name as a search term
20482.e: A Spaniard demanded that Google no longer show links to an old newspaper report about him. The Court ruled in his favour; this is called the “right to be forgotten”. The report itself, however, remains.
20482.m: In some cases you can demand that search engines remove old links.

20483.q: Against which company did the Irish data protection authority impose the highest GDPR fine so far, 1.2 billion euros, in 2023?
20483.e: The reason was the transfer of Facebook user data from the EU to the USA without adequate protection. The fine is the highest since the GDPR was introduced (as of 2026).
20483.m: Even big tech companies have to pay for breaches of data protection.

20484.q: What does the right to data portability in the GDPR allow?
a: Receiving your own data in a common format and taking them with you
Viewing other people’s profiles without permission
Selling other people’s data to companies
Using the internet free of charge everywhere
20484.e: The right to data portability is meant to make it easier to switch to another provider. The data must be handed over in a structured, machine-readable form.
20484.m: You may take your data with you to another provider.

a: Basic features are free, extra features cost money.
You only pay once at the start.
20485.e: The word combines “free” and “premium”. Many apps first win a large user base this way and then earn money from a small share of paying customers.
20485.m: With freemium, a few pay for extras so that many can use it free.

20486.q: On many ad-funded free platforms, what do users “pay” with?
20486.e: Platforms sell advertising space and use behavioural data to target adverts. Hence the saying “If you are not paying for the product, you are the product”.
20486.m: Free services are often funded by data and advertising.

20487.q: An advertiser books 2 million impressions at a cost per thousand (CPM) of 5 francs. How much does the campaign cost?
20487.e: The CPM is the price for 1000 impressions. 2,000,000 divided by 1000 gives 2000 packages, times 5 francs makes 10,000 francs.
20487.m: The cost per thousand gives the cost of a thousand ad impressions.

20488.q: What does the theory of the “long tail”, popularised by Chris Anderson in 2004, describe?
a: Online, it also pays to sell many niche products in small quantities.
Only bestsellers make a profit online.
Customers stay online longer and longer.
20488.e: Because digital storage costs hardly any space, online retailers can offer huge ranges. Many rarely bought products together add up to large sales.
20488.m: Online, the sum of many niches can pay off.

20489.q: What happens in real-time bidding in online advertising?
a: Ad spaces are auctioned in milliseconds as a page loads.
Adverts are only shown live on television.
Users bid money to switch off adverts.
Adverts are only billed after a month.
20489.e: When a web page is opened, data about the user are sent to ad exchanges, and advertisers automatically bid for the ad slot. A lot of personal data is often passed on in the process.
20489.m: In real-time bidding, every ad impression is auctioned in a flash.

20490.q: A streaming service has 10,000 subscribers and loses 500 of them in one month. What is the monthly churn rate?
20490.e: The churn rate is the share of customers who cancel in a given period. 500 divided by 10,000 gives 0.05, so 5 per cent.
20490.m: A low churn rate is crucial for subscription models.

20491.q: How do you earn money with affiliate marketing?
a: Through commission on sales made via your own referral link
By selling your own data to banks
Through a fixed wage from a platform
20491.e: Influencers or websites use special links through which purchases are tracked. They receive a share of each purchase they bring in; such links must be recognisable as advertising.
20491.m: Many product links have a commission behind them.

20492.q: What is a direct network effect?
a: A service becomes more valuable for everyone the more people use it.
A network gets faster the fewer people use it.
A service gets cheaper over time.
20492.e: A messaging app is only useful if your friends use it too. With every new user, the benefit rises for all existing users.
20492.m: Network effects make large platforms ever more attractive.

20493.q: In a network with 10 participants, everyone is to be directly connected to everyone else. How many connections are there?
20493.e: The number of connections is n times (n minus 1) divided by 2, so 10 times 9 divided by 2 equals 45. This is the basis of Metcalfe’s law, according to which the value of a network grows roughly with the square of the number of participants.
20493.m: The possible connections grow much faster than the number of participants.

20494.q: What characterises a two-sided platform such as a ride-hailing service?
a: It brings together two different user groups that need each other.
It has two websites with the same content.
It belongs to two companies at once.
20494.e: Passengers come because there are many drivers, and drivers come because there are many passengers. These are called indirect network effects.
20494.m: Two-sided platforms depend on bringing two groups together.

20495.q: What does the lock-in effect mean on digital platforms?
a: High switching costs keep users tied to one provider.
Accounts are locked after a wrong password.
Platforms close their services at night.
Users can only use one device.
20495.e: Anyone with lots of photos, contacts or purchased apps with one provider is reluctant to switch. This strengthens the market power of large platforms.
20495.m: The more you have invested in a platform, the harder it is to switch.

20496.q: Which EU law obliges so-called gatekeepers such as large app stores and search engines to compete fairly?
20496.e: The DMA has applied since 2023, and the obligations for designated gatekeepers since March 2024. For example, it prohibits unfairly favouring one’s own offers in search results.
20496.m: The DMA is meant to limit the power of large gatekeeper platforms.

20497.q: Why do “winner takes all” markets often arise in the platform economy?
a: Network effects make the largest provider ever more attractive.
Small providers are not allowed to advertise.
By law, customers must choose the market leader.
20497.e: Whoever has the most users offers the greatest benefit and so attracts even more users. In this way a few companies can dominate a market almost completely.
20497.m: Network effects can lead to monopolies.

20498.q: What is a core problem of the gig economy on courier platforms?
a: Workers are often treated as self-employed and have less social security.
Customers are not allowed to leave ratings.
Platforms are not allowed to charge fees.
Jobs are only given to companies.
20498.e: Platforms pass small jobs to people who are often not employees. Whether this is bogus self-employment occupies the courts in many countries, including Switzerland.
20498.m: In the gig economy, social security is often disputed.

20499.q: What did the case of an AI recruiting tool at Amazon, reported in 2018, show?
a: The tool rated applications from women worse.
The tool only read English CVs.
20499.e: The system had learned from applications over the previous ten years, which came mostly from men. Amazon therefore dropped the project.
20499.m: Historical inequality in data can make an AI unfair.

20500.q: Which MIT online experiment collected millions of judgements on how self-driving cars should decide in unavoidable accidents?
20500.e: The Moral Machine presented variations of the trolley problem. The answers from many countries showed clear cultural differences in moral decisions.
20500.m: Moral decisions for machines are not the same all over the world.

20501.q: Why is “explainable AI” called for in digital ethics?
a: People should be able to understand how an AI decision was reached.
AI should explain its programming language.
AI should only answer in English.
20501.e: Many models are a black box whose decisions even experts can hardly understand. But for loans or diagnoses, being able to follow the reasoning is important for oversight and fairness.
20501.m: Important decisions by an AI should be understandable.

20502.q: What does “dual use” mean for digital technologies?
a: They can be used for useful as well as harmful purposes.
They work on two devices at once.
20502.e: Facial recognition, for example, can find missing people but can also enable mass surveillance. That is why export controls and rules of use are debated.
20502.m: The same technology can help or harm.

20503.q: Who coined the term “surveillance capitalism” with her book?
20503.e: The emeritus Harvard professor describes how companies use human behaviour as a raw material in order to sell predictions. Her book appeared in German in 2018 and in English in 2019.
20503.m: Behavioural data are a valuable raw material in the digital economy.

20504.q: What does the term “digital divide” refer to?
a: Unequal access to digital technologies and skills
20504.e: The divide exists, for example, between countries, age groups or income groups. Those without access or knowledge are at a disadvantage in education, work and dealings with authorities.
20504.m: Digital participation cannot be taken for granted by everyone.

a: People trust automatic systems too much, even when they are wrong.
Robots work more slowly than people.
20505.e: When a system gives a recommendation, people often accept it without checking. That is why it is not enough just to formally involve a human in the decision.
20505.m: You should also check automatic suggestions critically.

20506.q: What are design tricks called that lead users into decisions against their own interests?
20506.e: The term was coined in 2010 by the British UX designer Harry Brignull. Examples are hidden costs or pre-ticked consent boxes.

a: A decline button with shaming text such as “No thanks, I don’t want to save money”
A confirmation email after a purchase
A test of whether users are real people
20507.e: The user is meant to feel bad about turning down an offer. This builds up pressure to agree after all.
20507.m: You don’t need to feel ashamed for saying no.

20508.q: What does the dark pattern “roach motel” stand for?
a: Easy to get in, but hard to get out again, for example with a subscription
A virus that hides in the system
20508.e: A subscription can be taken out with one click, but cancelling is hidden or only possible by letter. The EU’s DSA bans such misleading designs on online platforms.
20508.m: Cancelling should be as easy as signing up.

20509.q: Which psychological principle do features like “pull to refresh” use, much like slot machines?
a: Rewards only at the end of the month
20509.e: Because you never know whether exciting new content will appear, you repeat the action again and again. This variable reinforcement strongly encourages habitual behaviour.
20509.m: Unpredictable rewards keep people hooked for especially long.

a: Faking a spontaneous grassroots movement by organised players
20510.e: The name refers to the artificial turf brand AstroTurf: instead of real grass roots there are only artificial ones. Companies or groups hide the fact that they are behind the posts.
20510.m: Not every apparent popular movement is genuine.

20511.q: What came to light in 2018 in the Cambridge Analytica scandal?
a: Data of up to 87 million Facebook users were used for political microtargeting.
A hacker stole all of Google’s passwords.
A messaging app was run without encryption.
An online shop sold fake books.
20511.e: Through a personality test app, data were also collected from the participants’ friends. The company used profiles for targeted political advertising.
20511.m: Personal data can be misused for targeted political influence.

20512.q: Which tactic does a booking site use with the note “Only 1 room left, 12 people are looking at it right now”?
20512.e: Such notes create time pressure and the fear of missing out. If they are false or misleading, they breach fair trading law.
20512.m: Time pressure when shopping online is often a sales trick.

20513.q: What is a “sock puppet” on the internet?
a: A fake second account someone uses to support themselves
A children’s programme on video platforms
20513.e: With sock puppets someone pretends that several independent people share their opinion. In this way discussions and ratings are manipulated.
20513.m: Several voices online may come from the same person.

20812.q: What is the German word ‘Hallo’ in English?
20812.e: In English you say ‘Hello’ when you greet someone.

20813.q: What is the German greeting ‘Guten Morgen’ in English?
20813.e: ‘Morgen’ means morning, so in the morning you say ‘Good morning’.
20813.m: In the morning you say ‘Guten Morgen’, or ‘Good morning’.

20814.q: What is the German ‘Gute Nacht’ in English?
20814.e: Before going to sleep, you say ‘Good night’ in English and ‘Gute Nacht’ in German.
20814.m: Before sleeping you wish someone ‘Good night’.

20815.q: What is the German ‘Auf Wiedersehen’ in English?
20815.e: When you leave, you say ‘Goodbye’ or just ‘Bye’ in English.

20816.q: What is the German word ‘Danke’ in English?
20816.e: When you thank someone, you say ‘Thank you’ or just ‘Thanks’ in English.

20817.q: What is the German word ‘Bitte’ in English when you ask for something?
20817.e: When you politely ask for something, you say ‘please’ in English.
20817.m: Polite children say ‘bitte’ in German and ‘please’ in English.

20819.q: What is the German sentence ‘Ich heisse Anna’ in English?
20819.e: When you introduce yourself in English, you say ‘My name is ...’.
20819.m: With ‘My name is’ you tell someone your name in English.

20820.q: What is the German number ‘eins’ in English?
20820.e: The number 1 is ‘eins’ in German and ‘one’ in English.

20821.q: What is the German number ‘drei’ in English?
20821.e: The number 3 is ‘drei’ in German and ‘three’ in English. A ‘tree’ is something quite different.

20822.q: What is the German number ‘fünf’ in English?
20822.e: The number 5 is ‘fünf’ in German and ‘five’ in English.

20823.e: ‘Seven’ is the English word for the number 7. It sounds similar to the German ‘sieben’.

20824.q: What is the German number ‘zehn’ in English?
20824.e: The number 10 is ‘zehn’ in German and ‘ten’ in English.

20825.e: ‘Eight’ is the English word for the number 8. In German it is ‘acht’.

20826.q: What is the German number ‘zwölf’ in English?
20826.e: The number 12 is ‘twelve’ in English. It sounds a little like the German ‘zwölf’.

20827.e: ‘Twenty’ is the English word for the number 20. In German it is ‘zwanzig’.

20828.q: What is ‘two plus two’ in English words?
20828.e: Two plus two makes four, and in English you write it as ‘four’.

20829.q: What is the German colour ‘rot’ in English?
20829.e: The colour ‘rot’ in German is ‘red’ in English.

20830.q: What is the German colour ‘blau’ in English?
20830.e: The colour ‘blau’ in German is ‘blue’ in English.

20831.q: What is the German colour ‘grün’ in English?
20831.e: The colour ‘grün’ in German is ‘green’ in English. Grass is green.

20832.q: What is the German colour ‘gelb’ in English?
20832.e: The colour ‘gelb’ in German is ‘yellow’ in English. People often paint the sun yellow.

20833.e: ‘Black’ is ‘schwarz’ in German. The night is often black.

20834.q: What is the German colour ‘weiss’ in English?
20834.e: The colour ‘weiss’ in German is ‘white’ in English. Snow is white.

20835.e: ‘Brown’ is ‘braun’ in German. Chocolate is usually brown.

20836.q: What is the German colour ‘violett’ in English?
20836.e: The colour ‘violett’ in German is usually ‘purple’ in English.

20837.e: ‘Grey’ is ‘grau’ in German. An elephant is grey.

20838.q: What is the German word ‘Hund’ in English?
20838.e: The German word ‘Hund’ means ‘dog’ in English.

20839.q: What is the German word ‘Katze’ in English?
20839.e: The German word ‘Katze’ means ‘cat’ in English.

20841.q: What is the German word ‘Kuh’ in English?
20841.e: The German word ‘Kuh’ means ‘cow’. In Switzerland you see lots of cows in the meadows.

20842.e: ‘Bird’ is ‘Vogel’ in German. Most birds can fly.

20843.q: What is the German word ‘Maus’ in English?
20843.e: The German word ‘Maus’ means ‘mouse’ in English.

20844.e: ‘Fish’ is ‘Fisch’ in German. Fish live in water.

20845.q: What is the German word ‘Schwein’ in English?
20845.e: The German word ‘Schwein’ means ‘pig’ in English.

20846.e: ‘Rabbit’ is ‘Kaninchen’ in German. A hare, on the other hand, is ‘Hase’.

20847.q: What is the German word ‘Mutter’ in English?
20847.e: The German word ‘Mutter’ means ‘mother’; people often say ‘mum’.

20848.q: What is the German word ‘Vater’ in English?
20848.e: The German word ‘Vater’ means ‘father’; people often say ‘dad’.

20849.q: How do you say ‘my sister’ in German?
20849.e: ‘Sister’ is ‘Schwester’ in German. She is a girl with the same parents.

20850.q: What is the German word ‘Bruder’ in English?
20850.e: The German word ‘Bruder’ means ‘brother’ in English.

20851.q: What is the German word ‘Grossmutter’ in English?
20851.e: The German word ‘Grossmutter’ means ‘grandmother’, or ‘granny’ for short.

20852.q: How do you say ‘my grandfather’ in German?
20852.e: A grandfather is the father of your mum or dad. In German he is the ‘Grossvater’.

20853.q: What is the German word ‘Tante’ in English?
20853.e: The German word ‘Tante’ means ‘aunt’. An ‘ant’ is an insect.

20854.q: What is the German word ‘Familie’ in English?
20854.e: The German word ‘Familie’ means ‘family’ in English.

20855.q: What is the German word ‘Kopf’ in English?
20855.e: The German word ‘Kopf’ means ‘head’ in English.

20856.q: What is the German word ‘Bein’ in English?
20856.e: The German word ‘Bein’ means ‘leg’. We walk and run with our legs.

20857.e: ‘Nose’ is ‘Nase’ in German. We smell with it.

20858.q: What is the German word ‘Auge’ in English?
20858.e: The German word ‘Auge’ means ‘eye’. We see with our eyes.

20859.e: ‘Mouth’ is ‘Mund’ in German. We eat and speak with our mouth.

20860.q: What is the German word ‘Fuss’ in English?
20860.e: The German word ‘Fuss’ means ‘foot’. More than one foot are ‘feet’.

20861.e: ‘Ear’ is ‘Ohr’ in German. We hear with our ears.

20862.q: What is the German word ‘Haare’ in English?
20862.e: The German word ‘Haare’ means ‘hair’ in English.

20863.q: What is the German word ‘Apfel’ in English?
20863.e: The German word ‘Apfel’ means ‘apple’ in English.

20864.q: What is the German word ‘Brot’ in English?
20864.e: The German word ‘Brot’ means ‘bread’ in English.

20865.e: ‘Milk’ is ‘Milch’ in German. Swiss cows give a lot of milk.

20866.q: What is the German word ‘Käse’ in English?
20866.e: The German word ‘Käse’ means ‘cheese’. Switzerland is famous for its cheese.

20868.q: What is the German word ‘Ei’ in English?
20868.e: The German word ‘Ei’ means ‘egg’ in English.

20869.e: ‘Banana’ is ‘Banane’ in German. The word looks almost the same in both languages.

20870.q: What is the German word ‘Kuchen’ in English?
20870.e: The German word ‘Kuchen’ means ‘cake’. On birthdays there is often a birthday cake.

20871.q: What is the German word ‘Schuhe’ in English?
20871.e: The German word ‘Schuhe’ means ‘shoes’ in English.

20873.q: What is the German word ‘Socken’ in English?
20873.e: The German word ‘Socken’ means ‘socks’ in English.

20875.q: What is the German word ‘Kleid’ in English?
20875.e: The German word ‘Kleid’ means ‘dress’ in English.

20876.e: ‘Trousers’ is ‘Hose’ in German. In America people also say ‘pants’.

20877.q: What is the German word ‘Rock’ in English?
20877.e: The German word ‘Rock’ means ‘skirt’. A dress is ‘Kleid’ and a shirt is ‘Hemd’.

20878.e: ‘Gloves’ is ‘Handschuhe’ in German, literally ‘hand shoes’. In winter they keep your hands warm.

20879.q: What is the German word ‘Schule’ in English?
20879.e: The German word ‘Schule’ means ‘school’ in English.

20880.q: What is the German word ‘Buch’ in English?
20880.e: The German word ‘Buch’ means ‘book’ in English.

20882.q: What is the German word ‘Lehrerin’ in English?
20882.e: In German a female teacher is ‘Lehrerin’ and a male teacher ‘Lehrer’. In English both are ‘teacher’.

20883.q: Which German word means a ‘rubber’ at school?
20883.e: In Britain an eraser is called a ‘rubber’; in America it is an ‘eraser’. In German it is ‘Radiergummi’.

20884.q: What is the German word ‘Schultasche’ in English?
20884.e: The German word ‘Schultasche’ means ‘schoolbag’ in English.

20885.e: ‘Ruler’ is ‘Lineal’ in German. You use it to draw straight lines.

20886.q: What is the German word ‘Tisch’ in English?
20886.e: The German word ‘Tisch’ means ‘table’ in English.

20887.q: What is the German day ‘Montag’ in English?
20887.e: ‘Montag’ is ‘Monday’. In English the days of the week always start with a capital letter.

20888.e: ‘Friday’ is ‘Freitag’ in German. The two words sound similar.

20889.q: What is the German day ‘Sonntag’ in English?
20889.e: ‘Sonntag’ is ‘Sunday’. In both languages the word contains the sun: ‘Sonne’ and ‘sun’.

20891.q: What is the German day ‘Samstag’ in English?
20891.e: The German day ‘Samstag’ is ‘Saturday’ in English.

20892.e: ‘Tuesday’ is ‘Dienstag’ in German. It comes after Monday.

20893.q: What is the German day ‘Donnerstag’ in English?
20893.e: The German day ‘Donnerstag’ is ‘Thursday’ in English.

20894.q: What is the German word ‘Wochenende’ in English?
20894.e: Saturday and Sunday together make the weekend, in German ‘Wochenende’.

20895.q: What is the German month ‘Januar’ in English?
20895.e: ‘Januar’ is ‘January’. In English, months start with a capital letter.

20896.e: ‘May’ is ‘Mai’ in German. It is the fifth month of the year.

20897.q: What is the German month ‘Dezember’ in English?
20897.e: ‘Dezember’ is ‘December’. Many people celebrate Christmas in December.

20898.e: ‘March’ is ‘März’ in German. It is the third month of the year.

20899.q: What is the German month ‘Juni’ in English?
20899.e: ‘Juni’ is ‘June’. It is the sixth month of the year.

20900.e: ‘July’ is ‘Juli’ in German. It is the seventh month of the year.

20901.q: What is the German month ‘Oktober’ in English?
20901.e: ‘Oktober’ is ‘October’ in English, with a c instead of a k.

20902.q: What is the German word ‘Monat’ in English?
20902.e: The German word ‘Monat’ means ‘month’. The moon is ‘Mond’ in German.

20903.q: How do you say ‘Hello’ (good day) in French?
20903.e: To greet someone in French you say ‘Bonjour’. You hear it everywhere in French-speaking Switzerland.
20903.m: In French you greet someone with ‘Bonjour’.

20904.q: How do you say ‘Thank you’ in French?
20904.e: When you thank someone in French, you say ‘merci’. People in German-speaking Switzerland often say ‘merci’ too.
20904.m: In French you say thank you with ‘merci’.

20905.q: How do you say ‘yes’ in French?
20905.e: ‘Yes’ in French is ‘oui’. You pronounce it roughly like ‘wee’.
20905.m: The French word for yes is ‘oui’.

20906.q: How do you say ‘Goodbye’ in French?
20906.e: When you leave, you say ‘Au revoir’ in French.
20906.m: In French you say goodbye with ‘Au revoir’.

20907.e: The cat is ‘le chat’ in French.
20907.m: The cat is ‘le chat’ in French.

20908.q: How do you say ‘one, two, three’ in French?
20908.e: In French you count ‘un, deux, trois’. ‘Uno, dos, tres’ is Spanish and ‘uno, due, tre’ is Italian.
20908.m: In French you count ‘un, deux, trois’.

20909.e: ‘Rouge’ is the French word for red.
20909.m: The French ‘rouge’ is the colour red.

20910.e: Mother in French is ‘la mère’, with an accent on the first e (è). ‘La mer’ without an accent is the sea.
20910.m: The mother is ‘la mère’ in French.

20911.e: Bread is ‘le pain’ in French. At the bakery you might order ‘un pain’.

20912.q: What is the Swiss word ‘Velo’ in English?
20912.e: In Switzerland a bike is called a ‘Velo’. In English it is a ‘bicycle’ or ‘bike’; a ‘motorbike’ has an engine.
20912.m: A ‘Velo’ is a ‘bicycle’ or ‘bike’ in English.

20913.e: The kitchen is the room where you cook. In German it is ‘Küche’, and to cook is ‘kochen’.

20914.q: What is the German word ‘Schmetterling’ in English?
20914.e: A ‘Schmetterling’ is a butterfly. A dragonfly is ‘Libelle’ and a ladybird is ‘Marienkäfer’.

20915.e: The order is Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, in German Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag. So ‘Wednesday’ is ‘Mittwoch’.

20916.q: Which English word is the opposite of ‘expensive’?
20916.e: ‘Cheap’ means costing little money and is the opposite of ‘expensive’.
20916.m: What is not expensive is cheap.

20917.q: What is the German word ‘Wolke’ in English?
20917.e: A ‘Wolke’ is a cloud. A crowd is a large group of people and a clock tells the time.

20918.e: After August comes September, just as in German.

20919.e: ‘Gross’ plus ‘Mutter’ makes ‘Grossmutter’, the grandmother. The grandfather is ‘Grossvater’.

20920.q: What is the Swiss word ‘Rüebli’ in English?
20920.e: In Switzerland a carrot is called a ‘Rüebli’. A cucumber and a cabbage are different vegetables.

20921.q: What does the French word ‘la gare’ mean?
20921.e: ‘La gare’ is the railway station, for example ‘la gare de Lausanne’.
20921.m: Trains leave from the station, the ‘gare’.

20922.q: What word do people in French-speaking Switzerland use for the number 90?
20922.e: In French-speaking Switzerland people say ‘nonante’ for 90. In France they say ‘quatre-vingt-dix’.
20922.m: In French-speaking Switzerland 70 is ‘septante’ and 90 is ‘nonante’.

20923.q: How do you say ‘Friday’ in French?
20923.e: The week goes lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche. Friday is ‘vendredi’.

20924.q: What does the French word ‘la fenêtre’ mean?
20924.e: ‘La fenêtre’ is the window. The door is ‘la porte’.

20925.q: How do you say ‘red’ in French?
20925.e: Red is ‘rouge’. ‘Jaune’ is yellow, ‘vert’ green and ‘bleu’ blue.
20925.m: The colour red is ‘rouge’ in French.

20926.q: What does the French word ‘le frère’ mean?
20926.e: ‘Le frère’ is the brother and ‘la sœur’ the sister.
20926.m: My brother is ‘mon frère’ in French.

20928.q: What does ‘la pomme de terre’ mean?
20928.e: Literally it means ‘apple of the earth’, and it is the potato. The apple on its own is ‘la pomme’.
20928.m: A potato is ‘la pomme de terre’ in French.

20929.q: Which English sentence has the correct word order?
20929.e: English usually follows subject, verb, object. Time phrases like ‘every day’ go at the end or the start of the sentence.
20929.m: In an English sentence the subject is followed by the verb and then the object.

20930.e: In French, colour adjectives come after the noun, so ‘une voiture rouge’.
20930.m: In French the colour comes after the noun.

20931.q: Which word is missing in the sentence ‘She ___ a sister.’?
20931.e: With he, she and it, the present tense form of ‘to have’ is ‘has’.

20932.q: Which verb form fits the sentence ‘Nous ___ à Berne.’?
20932.e: ‘Nous’ goes with the ending -ons, so ‘nous habitons’.
20932.m: Verbs with ‘nous’ usually end in -ons in the present tense.

a: There are three cats in the garden.
There is three cats in the garden.
It are three cats in the garden.
There be three cats in the garden.
20933.e: For several things you say ‘there are’, for one thing ‘there is’.
20933.m: For the plural you use ‘there are’.

20934.q: What does the sentence ‘Il fait beau aujourd'hui.’ mean?
20934.e: ‘Il fait beau’ describes nice weather, and ‘aujourd'hui’ means today.
20934.m: When the weather is nice, you say ‘il fait beau’ in French.

20935.q: Which indefinite article goes before ‘orange’ in English?
20935.e: Before words that start with a vowel sound you use ‘an’. ‘The’ is the definite article.

20936.q: Which article goes with the French word ‘maison’ (house)?
20936.e: ‘Maison’ is feminine and starts with a consonant, so it is ‘la maison’.
20936.m: The house is feminine in French: ‘la maison’.

20937.q: Which English question word asks about a place?
20937.e: ‘Where’ asks about a place. ‘When’ asks about time, ‘why’ about a reason and ‘who’ about a person.
20937.m: With ‘where’ you ask about a place.

20938.q: How do you ask ‘What's your name?’ in French?
20938.e: ‘S'appeler’ means to be called. With ‘Comment tu t'appelles ?’ you ask someone's name.
20938.m: You ask someone's name with ‘Comment tu t'appelles ?’.

20939.q: Which English question is formed correctly?
20939.e: In the present tense, questions are formed with ‘do’ or ‘does’. With ‘you’ it is ‘do’.
20939.m: English questions in the present tense are formed with ‘do’ or ‘does’.

20940.q: Which word is missing in the question ‘___ she play tennis?’?
20940.e: With he, she and it, a present tense question needs ‘does’. The main verb then stays in its base form.

20941.q: What does the French question word ‘pourquoi’ mean?
20941.e: ‘Pourquoi’ means why. The answer often starts with ‘parce que’ (because).
20941.m: The answer to ‘pourquoi’ often starts with ‘parce que’.

20942.q: How do you ask someone's age in French?
20942.e: In French you ‘have’ an age, so you ask ‘Quel âge as-tu ?’. The answer might be ‘J'ai douze ans’.
20942.m: In French you ask someone's age with ‘Quel âge as-tu ?’.

20943.q: Which word is missing in the question ‘___ much is this T-shirt?’?
20943.e: ‘How much’ asks about a price or an amount you cannot count.
20943.m: In English you ask about the price with ‘How much?’.

20944.q: Which words can start a yes/no question in French?
20944.e: ‘Est-ce que’ turns a statement into a yes/no question, for example ‘Est-ce que tu viens ?’.
20944.m: With ‘est-ce que’ a statement becomes a yes/no question.

20945.q: What is the negative of ‘I like fish.’?
20945.e: In the present tense you make negatives with ‘don't’ or ‘doesn't’. With ‘I’ it is ‘don't’.
20945.m: With ‘I’, ‘you’, ‘we’ and ‘they’ you use ‘don't’ for the negative.

20946.q: Which word is missing in the sentence ‘He ___ speak French.’?
20946.e: With he, she and it you make the present tense negative with ‘doesn't’. The verb stays in its base form.
20946.m: With ‘he’ you use ‘doesn't’ and the base form of the verb.

20947.q: What is the negative of ‘Je mange.’?
20947.e: In French, ‘ne’ and ‘pas’ go around the verb.
20947.m: In a French negative the verb sits between ‘ne’ and ‘pas’.

20948.q: What does ‘Je ne sais pas.’ mean?
20948.e: ‘Savoir’ means to know and ‘je sais’ means I know. With ‘ne ... pas’ it becomes ‘I don't know’.
20948.m: If you don't know something, you say ‘Je ne sais pas’ in French.

20949.q: What does the French negative ‘ne ... jamais’ mean?
20949.e: ‘Jamais’ means never. ‘Rien’ means nothing and ‘personne’ nobody.
20949.m: With ‘ne ... jamais’ you say ‘never’ in French.

20950.q: Which word is missing in the sentence ‘They ___ at home yesterday.’?
20950.e: ‘Yesterday’ needs the past tense of ‘to be’. With ‘they’ it is ‘were’, and the negative is ‘weren't’.
20950.m: With ‘they’ the negative past of ‘to be’ is ‘weren't’.

20951.q: What is the negative of ‘J'ai un chat.’?
a: Je ne pas ai un chat.
20951.e: Before a vowel ‘ne’ becomes ‘n'’. After the negative, ‘un’ usually becomes ‘de’.

20952.q: Which English sentence is a correct negative?
20952.e: With ‘I’ you use ‘don't’. A double negative like ‘haven't got no’ is wrong in standard English.
20952.m: In English you only use one negative per sentence.

20953.e: A sister is a female person, so you replace her with ‘she’.
20953.m: For a female person you use ‘she’ in English.

20954.q: Which English pronoun replaces ‘Tom and I’ as the subject?
20954.e: ‘Tom and I’ together are ‘we’ when they are the subject. ‘Us’ is the object form.
20954.m: I and another person together are ‘we’.

20955.q: Which French pronoun is often used instead of ‘nous’ in everyday speech?
20955.e: In everyday speech people often say ‘on’ for we, for example ‘On va au cinéma ?’. The verb is then in the third person singular.
20955.m: In everyday French many people say ‘on’ instead of ‘nous’.

20956.e: For a group made up only of females you use ‘elles’.
20956.m: In French you replace several girls or women with ‘elles’.

20957.q: What is the polite form of ‘you’ in French?
20957.e: ‘Vous’ is the polite form and also the plural of ‘tu’.
20957.m: In French you address adults you don't know well with ‘vous’.

20958.q: Which word is missing in the question ‘Can you help ___?’ when you mean yourself?
20958.e: After a verb you use the object form. The object form of ‘I’ is ‘me’.
20958.m: After a verb you use ‘me’ instead of ‘I’.

20959.q: Which French pronoun replaces ‘Marc et Julie’?
20959.e: As soon as a group includes a male person, you use ‘ils’.
20959.m: In French a mixed group is replaced with ‘ils’.

20960.q: What do you normally use the English pronoun ‘it’ for?
a: for a thing or an animal
20960.e: ‘It’ stands for things and usually also for animals. For people you use ‘he’ or ‘she’.
20960.m: In English you replace things with ‘it’.

20961.e: ‘To buy’ is ‘kaufen’ in German. ‘Verkaufen’ means to sell and ‘bezahlen’ to pay.

20962.q: What does the French verb ‘aller’ mean?
20962.e: ‘Aller’ means to go. It is irregular, for example ‘je vais’.
20962.m: The verb ‘aller’ means to go and is irregular.

20963.q: What does the French verb ‘faire’ mean?
20963.e: ‘Faire’ means to make or to do, for example ‘faire du sport’.
20963.m: If you do sport, you say ‘je fais du sport’ in French.

20964.e: ‘To forget’ is ‘vergessen’ in German. ‘Verlieren’ means to lose and ‘vermissen’ to miss.

20965.q: What does the French verb ‘prendre’ mean?
20965.e: ‘Prendre’ means to take, for example ‘prendre le train’. To give is ‘donner’.
20965.m: In French you take the train with ‘prendre le train’.

20966.e: ‘To understand’ is ‘verstehen’ in German. In English the past form is ‘understood’.

20967.q: What does the French verb ‘vouloir’ mean?
20967.e: ‘Vouloir’ means to want. The polite form ‘je voudrais’ means ‘I would like’.
20967.m: With ‘je voudrais’ you politely say what you would like in French.

20968.q: What does the French verb ‘venir’ mean?
20968.e: ‘Venir’ means to come, for example ‘Tu viens avec moi ?’ (Are you coming with me?). To stay is ‘rester’ and to wait ‘attendre’.
20968.m: The French verb ‘venir’ means to come.

20969.q: Which verb form fits the sentence ‘He ___ to school every day.’?
20969.e: With he, she and it the verb gets an -s in the simple present; with ‘go’ it is ‘goes’.
20969.m: With ‘he’, ‘she’ and ‘it’ the verb gets an -s in the present tense.

20970.q: Which verb form fits the sentence ‘Je ___ français.’?
20970.e: For verbs ending in -er, the form with ‘je’ ends in -e, so ‘je parle’.
20970.m: For -er verbs the form with ‘je’ ends in -e.

20971.q: Which verb form fits the question ‘Tu ___ un frère ?’?
20971.e: In the present tense ‘avoir’ goes j'ai, tu as, il a. So ‘tu’ needs ‘as’.

20972.q: Which verb form fits the question ‘Vous ___ suisses ?’?
20972.e: With ‘vous’ the verb ‘être’ is ‘êtes’. ‘Sommes’ goes with ‘nous’.

20973.q: Which verb form fits the sentence ‘I ___ hungry.’?
20973.e: With ‘I’ the verb ‘to be’ is always ‘am’.

20974.q: Which verb form fits the sentence ‘Ils ___ au cinéma.’?
20974.e: With ‘ils’ the verb ‘aller’ is ‘vont’. ‘Je vais’, ‘il va’ and ‘vous allez’ are other persons.

20975.q: Which word is missing in the sentence ‘Look! It ___ raining.’?
20975.e: For something happening right now you use the present progressive, with ‘is’ for ‘it’.
20975.m: What is happening right now goes in the present progressive in English.

20976.q: Which verb form fits the sentence ‘Nous ___ nos devoirs.’?

20977.q: What is the simple past of ‘go’?
20977.e: ‘Go’ is irregular; its simple past is ‘went’. ‘Gone’ is the past participle.

20978.q: What is the simple past of ‘buy’?
20978.e: ‘Buy’ is irregular and its simple past is ‘bought’. ‘Brought’ belongs to ‘bring’.

20979.q: Which verb form fits the sentence ‘Yesterday I ___ a film.’?
20979.e: ‘Yesterday’ needs the simple past. With regular verbs you add -ed.
20979.m: Regular verbs form the simple past with -ed.

20980.q: Which auxiliary verb fits the sentence ‘J'___ mangé une pomme.’?
20980.e: Most verbs form the passé composé with ‘avoir’. With ‘je’ it is ‘j'ai’.
20980.m: Most verbs form the passé composé with ‘avoir’.

20981.q: Which auxiliary verb fits the sentence ‘Elle ___ allée à Genève.’?
20981.e: ‘Aller’ forms the passé composé with ‘être’. That is why it is ‘elle est allée’.
20981.m: The verb ‘aller’ forms the passé composé with ‘être’.

20982.q: Which signal word typically shows the simple past in English?
20982.e: ‘Yesterday’ points to a finished action in the past.
20982.m: With ‘yesterday’ or ‘last week’ English usually uses the simple past.

20983.q: Which short answer fits ‘Did you see the match?’?
20983.e: The question starts with ‘did’, so the short answer uses ‘did’.
20983.m: In a short answer you repeat the auxiliary verb of the question.

20984.q: What is the past participle of ‘faire’?
20984.e: ‘Faire’ is irregular; the participle is ‘fait’, as in ‘j'ai fait’.

20985.q: What is the past participle of ‘voir’?
20985.e: ‘Voir’ is irregular; the participle is ‘vu’, for example ‘j'ai vu’.

20986.q: What time is ‘It's half past seven’?
20986.e: ‘Half past seven’ means half an hour after seven, so 7.30. In German you say ‘halb acht’, half an hour before eight.
20986.m: With ‘half past’ you add half an hour to the hour.

20987.q: What time is ‘Il est huit heures et quart’?
20987.e: ‘Et quart’ means and a quarter, so a quarter of an hour after eight.
20987.m: With ‘et quart’ you add a quarter of an hour in French.

20988.e: ‘To’ means before. A quarter to nine is 8.45.
20988.m: With ‘quarter to’ there is still a quarter of an hour until the full hour.

20989.e: ‘Midi’ is midday, so 12 o'clock. Midnight is ‘minuit’.
20989.m: At 12 o'clock in the day it is ‘midi’ in French.

20990.q: What time is ‘Il est trois heures moins le quart’?
20990.e: ‘Moins le quart’ means minus a quarter. Three o'clock minus 15 minutes makes 2.45.
20990.m: With ‘moins le quart’ you take away a quarter of an hour.

20991.q: How do you say 10.20 in English?
20991.e: Up to the half hour you say how many minutes ‘past’ the hour it is. 20 minutes after ten is ‘twenty past ten’.
20991.m: Up to the half hour you use ‘past’ in English.

20992.q: What does the English abbreviation ‘a.m.’ mean with a time?
20992.e: ‘A.m.’ comes from the Latin ‘ante meridiem’ and means before noon. After noon is ‘p.m.’.
20992.m: In English, times in the morning are marked ‘a.m.’.

20993.q: What time is ‘Il est dix heures et demie’?
20993.e: ‘Et demie’ means and a half, so half an hour after ten.
20993.m: With ‘et demie’ you add half an hour in French.

20994.e: ‘Abbiegen’ means to turn and ‘links’ means left. Right is ‘rechts’.

20995.e: ‘Tout droit’ means straight on. ‘Allez’ here is the polite command with ‘vous’.
20995.m: If you go ‘tout droit’, you go straight on.

20996.e: ‘À droite’ means to the right. ‘Droite’ here means the right-hand side.
20996.m: If you go ‘à droite’, you turn right.

20997.e: ‘Next to’ is ‘neben’ in German. ‘Hinter’ means behind and ‘gegenüber’ opposite.

20998.q: What does the French phrase ‘en face de’ mean?
20998.e: ‘En face de’ means opposite. Next to is ‘à côté de’.
20998.m: What is ‘en face de’ something is opposite it.

20999.q: Which is the correct way to ask the way to the station in English?
a: How do I get to the station?
Where do I get the station?
What is the way at station?
20999.e: The correct question is ‘How do I get to the station?’. ‘To get to’ means to reach a place.
20999.m: You ask the way in English with ‘How do I get to ...?’.

21000.q: What does ‘la deuxième rue à gauche’ mean?
a: the second street on the left
the second street on the right
the first street on the left
the second crossroads on the right
21000.e: ‘Deuxième’ means second, ‘rue’ street and ‘à gauche’ on the left.

21001.e: ‘Traffic lights’ are the light signals on the road, in German ‘Ampel’. A crossroads is ‘Kreuzung’.

21002.q: What does ‘Je voudrais un croissant, s'il vous plaît.’ mean?
a: Do you have any croissants left?
21002.e: ‘Je voudrais’ means I would like, and ‘s'il vous plaît’ means please. In Switzerland a croissant is often called a ‘Gipfeli’.
21002.m: At the bakery you order politely with ‘Je voudrais ..., s'il vous plaît’.

21004.q: What does ‘L'addition, s'il vous plaît.’ mean in a restaurant?
21004.e: In a restaurant ‘l'addition’ is the bill. The menu is ‘la carte’.
21004.m: To pay, you ask for ‘l'addition’ in French.

21005.q: What is the polite reply to ‘Thank you!’ in English?
21005.e: ‘You're welcome’ is the polite reply. You use ‘Excuse me’ to get someone's attention.

21006.q: When do you say ‘Enchanté’ in French?
21006.e: ‘Enchanté’ means pleased to meet you and is said when you meet someone for the first time. Women write ‘enchantée’.
21006.m: When you meet someone, you say ‘Enchanté’ in French.

21007.q: What do you say in English when someone sneezes?
21007.e: After a sneeze you say ‘Bless you!’, like ‘Gesundheit!’ in German.
21007.m: When someone sneezes, you say ‘Bless you!’ in English.

21008.e: ‘Bientôt’ means soon. You say it to someone you will see again soon.
21008.m: With ‘À bientôt’ you say ‘see you soon’ in French.

21010.m: To apologise in French, you say ‘Je suis désolé’.

21011.q: Which form correctly completes the sentence ‘If I had known, I ___ come.’?
21011.e: This is a type 3 conditional (third conditional) about the past. The main clause has ‘would have’ plus the past participle.
21011.m: In the third conditional, ‘if’ is followed by the past perfect and the main clause has ‘would have’.

21012.q: Which English sentence uses inversion after ‘Hardly’ correctly?
a: Hardly had she arrived when the phone rang.
Hardly she had arrived when the phone rang.
Hardly did she arrived when the phone rang.
Hardly she arrived when the phone had rang.
21012.e: When a limiting adverb such as ‘hardly’ comes at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary verb and the subject swap places. That is why it is ‘had she arrived’.
21012.m: After a negative adverb at the start of a sentence, English uses inversion.

21013.q: Which form does the formal English subjunctive require in ‘It is essential that he ___ on time.’?
21013.e: After expressions such as ‘essential’, ‘insist’ or ‘demand’, formal English uses the mandative subjunctive. It is the base form of the verb without an ending.
21013.m: The English subjunctive after ‘essential that’ uses the base form of the verb.

21014.q: Which form fits in ‘He stopped ___ last year.’ if it means that he gave up smoking?
21014.e: ‘Stop’ plus the gerund means to end an activity. ‘Stop’ plus the infinitive, by contrast, means to pause in order to do something.
21014.m: After ‘stop’, the gerund names the activity that is ended.

21015.q: What is ‘She said: “I am tired.”’ correctly in reported speech?
a: She said that she was tired.
She said that she is being tired.
She said that I was tired.
She said that she had be tired.
21015.e: When the reporting verb is in the past, the present simple usually shifts back to the past simple in reported speech. The pronoun is also adjusted.
21015.m: In reported speech, the tense usually shifts back one step after a reporting verb in the past.

21016.q: What is ‘They are building a new bridge.’ in the passive?
a: A new bridge is being built.
A new bridge has been built.
A new bridge was being built.
21016.e: The passive of the present continuous is formed with ‘is/are being’ plus the past participle. The tense of the active sentence stays the same.
21016.m: The passive of the present continuous is formed with ‘being’ and the past participle.

21017.q: Which English relative pronoun may NOT introduce a non-defining relative clause?
21017.e: Non-defining relative clauses stand between commas and give extra information. They must not be introduced with ‘that’.
21017.m: In English relative clauses between commas, you never use ‘that’.

21018.q: Which form completes the mixed conditional ‘If I had studied medicine, I ___ a doctor now.’?
21018.e: The condition lies in the past, the result concerns the present (‘now’). That is why the main clause has ‘would’ plus the base form.
21018.m: A mixed conditional links a past condition with a result in the present.

21019.q: Which form correctly completes ‘I am used to ___ early.’?
21019.e: In ‘be used to’, ‘to’ is a preposition, so a gerund follows. The expression means to be accustomed to something.
21019.m: After ‘be used to’, English always uses a gerund or a noun.

21020.q: Which question tag correctly completes ‘Nobody called, ___?’
21020.e: ‘Nobody’ is already negative, so the tag is positive. In English, the pronoun used for ‘nobody’ and ‘somebody’ is ‘they’.
21020.m: After a negative sentence, English uses a positive question tag.

21021.q: Which verb form correctly completes ‘Il faut que tu ___ (venir) demain.’?
21021.e: After ‘il faut que’, French uses the subjunctive. The present subjunctive of ‘venir’ in the 2nd person singular is ‘que tu viennes’.
21021.m: After ‘il faut que’, French requires the subjunctive.

21022.q: Which form correctly completes ‘Les lettres que j’ai ___ (écrire)’?
21022.e: With the auxiliary verb ‘avoir’, the participle agrees with the direct object if it comes before it. Here ‘que’ stands for ‘les lettres’, which is feminine plural.
21022.m: With ‘avoir’, the participle agrees when the direct object comes before the verb.

21023.q: Which verb form correctly completes ‘Bien qu’il ___ malade, il travaille.’?
21023.e: The conjunction ‘bien que’ (although) requires the subjunctive. The present subjunctive of ‘être’ is ‘qu’il soit’.
21023.m: After ‘bien que’, French always uses the subjunctive.

21024.q: How do you replace both objects in ‘Je donne le livre à Marie.’ with pronouns?
21024.e: The direct object ‘le livre’ becomes ‘le’, the indirect object ‘à Marie’ becomes ‘lui’. In the third person, ‘le’ comes before ‘lui’.
21024.m: When ‘le’ and ‘lui’ meet, the direct object pronoun comes first.

21025.q: Which form correctly completes ‘Si j’avais de l’argent, j’___ une voiture.’?
21025.e: After ‘si’ with the imperfect, the main clause has the present conditional. It expresses a hypothetical result in the present.
21025.m: After ‘si’ with the imperfect, the main clause has the present conditional.

21026.q: Which form correctly completes ‘Elle s’est ___ les mains.’ (laver)?
21026.e: The direct object ‘les mains’ comes after the verb, and the reflexive pronoun is the indirect object here. That is why the participle does not agree.
21026.m: With reflexive verbs, the participle stays unchanged if the direct object follows.

21028.q: According to French standard usage, which mood follows the conjunction ‘après que’?
21028.e: ‘Après que’ refers to an action that is already completed, so real, and according to the standard requires the indicative. In everyday speech you often hear the subjunctive, but it is considered non-standard.
21028.m: After ‘après que’, standard French uses the indicative; after ‘avant que’, the subjunctive.

21029.q: What is the plural of the French noun ‘le cheval’?
21029.e: Most nouns ending in ‘-al’ form their plural with ‘-aux’. Exceptions include ‘bals’, ‘festivals’ and ‘carnavals’.
21029.m: Nouns ending in ‘-al’ usually end in ‘-aux’ in the plural.

21030.q: What does ‘Je n’ai que dix francs.’ mean?
a: I do not have ten francs.
I have at least ten francs.
I no longer have ten francs.
21030.e: The construction ‘ne ... que’ is not a negation but a restriction. It corresponds to the English ‘only’.
21030.m: The phrase ‘ne ... que’ means ‘only’ in English.

21031.q: Which form correctly completes ‘By next June, she ___ her degree.’?
21031.e: ‘By next June’ refers to a point in the future by which the action will be completed. For this you use the future perfect.
21031.m: The future perfect describes what will be completed by a point in the future.

21032.q: Which form correctly completes ‘When I arrived, they ___ for two hours.’?
21032.e: The action had already been going on for a while before a point in the past. For this you use the past perfect continuous.
21032.m: The past perfect continuous stresses the duration of an action before a point in the past.

21033.q: Which form correctly completes the literary sentence ‘Quand il ___ fini, il partit.’?
21033.e: In the narrative tense passé simple, an action immediately before another is expressed with the passé antérieur. It is formed with the passé simple of ‘avoir’ or ‘être’.
21033.m: The passé antérieur is used mainly in literary texts alongside the passé simple.

21034.q: Which tense is the French verb form ‘j’aurai fini’?
21034.e: The futur antérieur is formed with the futur simple of ‘avoir’ or ‘être’ and the participle. It describes an action that will be completed before another future action.
21034.m: The futur antérieur is formed with the future of the auxiliary and the past participle.

21035.q: How do you form the French plus-que-parfait?
21035.e: The plus-que-parfait expresses something earlier in the past, such as ‘j’avais mangé’. The auxiliary verb is in the imperfect.
21035.m: The plus-que-parfait is made up of the imperfect of the auxiliary and the participle.

21036.q: Which form correctly completes ‘This time tomorrow I ___ on the beach.’?
21036.e: For an action that will be in progress at a particular point in the future, you use the future continuous. It is formed with ‘will be’ plus ‘-ing’.
21036.m: The future continuous describes an action in progress at a future point in time.

21037.q: What is the passé simple of ‘être’ in the 3rd person singular?
