21318.e: The method, named after the Basel physicist Eduard Hagenbach-Bischoff, is set out in the Federal Act on Political Rights. Mathematically it is the same as the D’Hondt method and tends to favour large lists.
21318.m: In National Council elections seats are distributed using the Hagenbach-Bischoff method.

21319.q: How are the 200 National Council seats distributed among the cantons?
a: By the area of the cantons
21319.e: The seats are redistributed before each general election, and every canton gets at least one seat. The basis is the permanent resident population, so people without a Swiss passport count too.
21319.m: Cantons with more people get more National Council seats.

21320.q: What does the ban on instructions in Article 161 of the Federal Constitution mean?
a: Members of parliament vote without instructions
Parties may not advertise in elections
The Federal Council may not submit proposals
Cantons may not give their opinion
21320.e: Members of the Federal Assembly are not bound by instructions from parties, cantons or associations. This free mandate is a key feature of representative democracy.
21320.m: Members of parliament decide according to their own conscience and without instructions.

21321.q: What is it called when you write candidates from different lists on one ballot paper in National Council elections?
21321.e: With panachage you add names from other party lists to your ballot paper. With cumulation, on the other hand, you write the same name twice.
21321.m: Panachage means mixing candidates from different lists.

21322.q: Which body elects the members of the Federal Council?
21322.e: For this the National Council and the Council of States meet together as the United Federal Assembly. The election takes place after each general election of the National Council.
21322.m: The National Council and the Council of States elect the Federal Council together.

21323.q: Which thinker argued that the general will (volonté générale) cannot be represented by elected deputies?
21323.e: In “The Social Contract” (1762) Rousseau wrote that the sovereignty of the people cannot be handed over. That is why he is seen as an important early thinker of direct democracy.
21323.m: Rousseau saw the people themselves as the bearers of the general will.

21324.q: In which year was the National Council first elected by proportional representation?
21324.e: On 13 October 1918 the people and the cantons accepted the popular initiative for electing the National Council by proportional representation. In the first proportional elections in October 1919, the Free Democrats lost 43 seats and with them their absolute majority.
21324.m: Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by proportional representation.

21325.q: Which theory of international relations sees states as actors that mainly strive for power and security in an anarchic system?
21325.e: Realism, for example in Hans Morgenthau’s work, assumes that there is no world government above the states. So states must ensure their own security.
21325.m: Realism stresses the power and self-interest of states.

21326.q: According to the realist theory of international relations, what does not exist, which is why states must ensure their own security?
a: A world government above the states
21326.e: Realists such as Hans Morgenthau or Kenneth Waltz speak of an anarchic system. Because no higher authority guarantees protection, states strive for power and security.
21326.m: Without a world government, every state ensures its own security.

21327.q: According to the theory of constructivism, what mainly shapes international politics?
21327.e: Constructivism stresses that the interests of states arise from ideas and interaction. A well-known sentence is Alexander Wendt’s: “Anarchy is what states make of it”.
21327.m: For constructivism, ideas and norms shape international politics.

21328.q: What is the situation called in which one state’s arming is seen by others as a threat and triggers counter-arming?
21328.e: Even arms meant for defence can create distrust, because other states cannot be sure of the intentions. This can lead to an arms spiral even though nobody wants war.
21328.m: The security dilemma can lead to an arms race despite peaceful intentions.

21329.q: What is the term coined by Joseph Nye for influence through the attraction of culture, values and policies?
21329.e: Nye distinguished power through force and payment (hard power) from power through persuasion and attractiveness. Soft power works, for example, through culture, education and credible values.
21329.m: Soft power is based on attraction instead of force.

21330.q: Which peace settlement is seen as the starting point of the modern system of sovereign states and freed the Swiss Confederation from the Holy Roman Empire?
21330.e: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years’ War and strengthened the sovereignty of individual states. The mayor of Basel, Johann Rudolf Wettstein, obtained the formal exemption of the Confederation from the Empire.
21330.m: Since 1648 the sovereignty of states has been a basic principle of the world of states.

21331.q: Which thesis says that democratic states hardly ever go to war with each other?
21331.e: The thesis goes back to Immanuel Kant’s essay “Perpetual Peace” (1795). The reasons given are shared values, separation of powers and economic ties.
21331.m: According to democratic peace theory, democracies hardly ever fight each other.

21332.q: What is the world order during the Cold War, with two dominant superpowers, called?
21332.e: From about 1947 to 1991 the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other with their alliance systems. After the collapse of the Soviet Union people spoke of a unipolar order.
21332.m: In the Cold War the world was divided into two power blocs.

21333.q: In which city were the 1907 conventions signed on which Switzerland’s law of neutrality is based?
21333.e: The 1907 Hague Conventions forbid warring parties, for example, to move troops through neutral territory. The neutral state, for its part, may not support any warring party militarily.
21333.m: Switzerland’s law of neutrality is based on the 1907 Hague Conventions.

21334.q: How many Geneva Conventions were signed in 1949?
21334.e: The four conventions protect wounded soldiers on land, shipwrecked people at sea, prisoners of war and civilians. They form the core of international humanitarian law, and Switzerland is the depositary state.
21334.m: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 are the heart of international humanitarian law.

21335.q: According to the UN Charter, when may a state use force against another state?
a: In self-defence or with permission from the Security Council
When the other state does not pay its debts
21335.e: The Charter generally bans force between states. Exceptions are self-defence against an attack and measures decided by the Security Council.
21335.m: The UN Charter generally bans states from using force.

21336.q: In which city is the International Criminal Court based?
21336.e: The International Criminal Court is based on the Rome Statute of 1998 and began its work in 2002. It prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression.
21336.m: The International Criminal Court in The Hague tries individuals for the most serious crimes.

21337.q: Which court is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations?
21337.e: The International Court of Justice decides disputes between states and gives legal opinions. Its 15 judges are elected by the General Assembly and the Security Council.
21337.m: Disputes between states go before the International Court of Justice.

21338.q: Which ban is considered peremptory in international law, so that no treaty may depart from it?
21338.e: Peremptory norms (ius cogens) include the bans on genocide, torture and slavery. A treaty that breaks them is void.
21338.m: No state can set aside peremptory rules like the ban on torture by treaty.

21339.q: Which principle says that treaties that have been concluded must be kept?
21339.e: The principle is laid down in Article 26 of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. Treaties must be carried out in good faith.
21339.m: Under the principle “pacta sunt servanda”, treaties must be kept.

21340.q: What is international law called that arises from a general practice of states accepted as law?
21340.e: Besides treaties, Article 38 of the ICJ Statute names custom as a source of law. It requires consistent state practice and the belief that one is legally bound.
21340.m: Customary law arises from state practice and legal conviction.

21341.q: Since which year has Switzerland been a party to the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)?
21341.e: Switzerland ratified the ECHR in November 1974. Since then people in Switzerland can turn to the Court in Strasbourg once they have used up all domestic legal remedies.
21341.m: The ECHR has applied to Switzerland since 1974.

21342.q: In which year were the USA and the Soviet Union on the brink of nuclear war during the Cuban Missile Crisis?
21342.e: The Soviet Union had stationed nuclear missiles in Cuba, and the USA imposed a naval blockade. After thirteen days the missiles were withdrawn, and the USA later withdrew missiles from Turkey.
21342.m: The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is seen as the most dangerous moment of the Cold War.

21343.q: Which task has Switzerland carried out on the inter-Korean border since 1953?
a: Protecting power for the USA in North Korea
Seat of a peace court for Korea
21343.e: After the 1953 ceasefire the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission was formed, and Switzerland still belongs to it today (as of 2026). A peace treaty between the warring parties was never signed.
21343.m: Since 1953 Switzerland has helped monitor the ceasefire in Korea.

21344.q: Which two states have been in dispute over the Kashmir region since 1947?
21344.e: After the partition of British India in 1947, both new states claimed the territory. Part of the region is also controlled by China.
21344.m: The Kashmir conflict goes back to the partition of British India.

21345.q: Since which year has the island of Cyprus been divided in practice?
21345.e: After a coup and Turkey’s subsequent intervention, the island was divided in 1974. A UN peacekeeping force monitors the buffer zone between the two parts.

21346.q: Which parties signed the first Oslo Accord in 1993?
21346.e: In the accord Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization recognised each other. It provided for Palestinian self-government in parts of the West Bank and in the Gaza Strip.
21346.m: The 1993 Oslo Accord brought mutual recognition between Israel and the PLO.

21347.q: Which war was ended in 1995 with the Dayton Agreement?
21347.e: The agreement, negotiated in Dayton (USA) and signed in Paris, divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities. It still contains the country’s constitution today.
21347.m: The Dayton Agreement ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995.

21348.q: Which UN mission has been meant to prepare a referendum on the status of Western Sahara since 1991?
21348.e: The Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara was created in 1991 after a ceasefire between Morocco and the Polisario Front. The referendum still has not taken place.
21348.m: The status of Western Sahara has been unresolved for decades.

21349.q: What assumption is known as the domino theory, set out by US President Eisenhower in 1954?
a: If one state falls to communism, its neighbours follow
Democracies do not go to war with each other
Nuclear weapons prevent any major war
Trade makes wars between states impossible
21349.e: The theory was applied mainly to Southeast Asia. It served as a justification for US involvement in Vietnam.
21349.m: The domino theory shaped US foreign policy in Southeast Asia.

a: How geography influences the power and politics of states
How rocks and mountains are formed
How elections are run in a country
21350.e: Geopolitics asks, for example, why straits, raw materials or borders matter to states. Classic theories come from the Briton Halford Mackinder or the American Alfred Mahan.
21350.m: Geopolitics links geography with power politics.

21351.q: Which 1961 agreement sets out the privileges and immunities of diplomats?
21351.e: The Vienna Convention sets down the rules of diplomatic relations. For example, it protects the inviolability of embassies and of diplomats themselves.
21351.m: The 1961 Vienna Convention is the basis of diplomatic law.

21352.q: What is a diplomat called whom the host state declares unwelcome?
21352.e: The host state can make this declaration at any time and without giving reasons. The sending state must then recall the person.
21352.m: A persona non grata has to leave the host state.

21353.q: What is the host state’s consent to the appointment of a new ambassador called?
21353.e: Before an ambassador is appointed, the sending state asks the host state for its consent. The exequatur, on the other hand, is the approval of a consul.
21353.m: Without agrément no ambassador can take up office.

21354.q: Whose interests has Switzerland represented in Iran as protecting power since 1980?
21354.e: After diplomatic relations between the USA and Iran were broken off, Switzerland took on this protecting power mandate in 1980, and it still exists today (as of 2026). It is one of Switzerland’s best-known good offices.
21354.m: As a protecting power, Switzerland mediates between states without direct relations.

21355.q: Which two leaders met at a summit in Geneva in 1985?
a: John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev
21355.e: At the Geneva summit in November 1985 the leaders of the USA and the Soviet Union met in person for the first time. The meeting is seen as the beginning of détente at the end of the Cold War.
21355.m: In 1985 Geneva hosted an important Cold War summit.

21356.q: What is the form of mediation called in which a mediator travels back and forth between the parties to a conflict, as Henry Kissinger did in the 1970s?
21356.e: After the 1973 Yom Kippur War, Kissinger travelled back and forth between Israel, Egypt and Syria. This meant the parties did not have to talk to each other directly.
21356.m: In shuttle diplomacy a mediator carries messages between the parties.

21357.q: Between which states did so-called ping-pong diplomacy begin a rapprochement in 1971?
21357.e: A US table tennis team was invited to China in 1971. This paved the way for President Nixon’s visit to Beijing in 1972.
21357.m: In 1971 a table tennis tournament opened the door between the USA and China.

21358.q: Which war was ended in 1962 by the Évian Accords, whose negotiations Switzerland supported with its good offices?
21358.e: Switzerland made secret contacts possible between France and the Algerian liberation front FLN. The accords led to Algeria’s independence in 1962.
21358.m: The Évian Accords brought Algeria independence in 1962.

21359.q: What is the longest-serving ambassador called who represents a country’s diplomatic corps?
21359.e: The doyen speaks on behalf of all the ambassadors in a country at official events. In many countries with a Catholic tradition, this role is traditionally taken by the papal nuncio.
21359.m: The doyen is the spokesperson of the diplomatic corps.

21360.q: Which state is not a permanent member of the UN Security Council?
21360.e: The permanent members are China, France, Great Britain, Russia and the USA. Ten further members are each elected for two years.
21360.m: The Security Council has five permanent members with a veto.

21361.q: How many votes does a substantive decision in the UN Security Council need?
21361.e: Under Article 27 of the Charter, nine yes votes are needed, and none of the five permanent members may vote against. In practice, an abstention does not count as a veto.
21361.m: A permanent member can block any substantive Security Council decision.

21362.q: How many member states does NATO have (as of 2026)?
21362.e: Finland joined in 2023, and Sweden followed in 2024 as the 32nd member. Switzerland is not a member but works with NATO in the Partnership for Peace.

21363.q: Which country holds the chairmanship of the OSCE in 2026?
21363.e: Switzerland took over the chairmanship of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, with 57 participating states, for the third time after 1996 and 2014. The chairmanship changes every year.

21364.q: Since which year has Switzerland been a member of the Council of Europe?
21364.e: The Council of Europe, based in Strasbourg, was founded in 1949 and works for human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Switzerland joined it in 1963.
21364.m: Switzerland has belonged to the Council of Europe since 1963.

21365.q: In which year did women in Switzerland get the right to vote and stand for election at federal level?
21365.e: On 7 February 1971 the men voted in favour, after a first proposal had been rejected in 1959. In autumn 1971 the first women were elected to the National Council.
21365.m: Since 1971 Swiss women have been able to vote and stand for election at federal level.

21366.q: How did women in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden get the cantonal right to vote in 1990?
a: Through a ruling of the Federal Supreme Court
Through a decision of the Landsgemeinde
Through a decision of the Federal Council
21366.e: The men had still rejected women’s suffrage in April 1990. In November 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that this breached equal rights in the Federal Constitution.
21366.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden introduced women’s suffrage in 1990 on the orders of the Federal Supreme Court.

21367.q: Roughly what was the turnout in the 2023 National Council elections?
21367.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, turnout in 2023 was 46.6 per cent. For decades fewer than half of voters have taken part in National Council elections.
21367.m: In National Council elections usually fewer than half of voters take part.

21368.q: Which action is seen in political science as an unconventional form of political participation?
a: Being a member of a party
21368.e: Conventional forms are tied to elections, parties and institutions. Unconventional forms such as demonstrations or boycotts take place outside these procedures and became more common from the 1960s.
21368.m: Demonstrations are one of the unconventional forms of participation.

21369.q: What is the procedure called in which cantons, parties and associations can comment on draft federal laws?
21369.e: The consultation procedure takes place before the debate in parliament. It is meant to test whether a proposal will be accepted and help avoid later referendums.
21369.m: In the consultation procedure, those affected can comment early on new laws.

21370.q: Which political right in Switzerland also belongs to people without the right to vote, such as children or foreigners?
21370.e: Under Article 33 of the Federal Constitution, every person has the right to address requests and concerns to the authorities. The authorities must take note of the petition but do not have to grant it.
21370.m: In Switzerland anyone may submit a petition.

21371.q: From what age have Swiss citizens been able to vote and stand for election at federal level since 1991?
21371.e: In 1991 the people and the cantons lowered the voting age from 20 to 18. At federal level this limit still applies today (as of 2026).
21371.m: At federal level you can vote and stand for election from 18.

21372.q: What does political science call the feeling of being able to make a difference politically through your own actions?
21372.e: The technical term is “political efficacy”. People with a strong sense of efficacy have been shown to take part in elections and votes more often.
21372.m: People who believe in their own political efficacy are more likely to take part.

21373.q: Which term describes the role of the media as a watchdog over government, parliament and the courts?
21373.e: The media are meant to uncover wrongdoing and keep a critical eye on the powerful. Unlike the three powers of the state, however, they have no legitimacy from the state.
21373.m: The media are seen as the fourth estate.

21374.q: What is the approach by McCombs and Shaw (1972) called, according to which the media decide what topics the public thinks about?
21374.e: In the 1968 US election campaign the researchers showed that the topics stressed by the media were also seen as important by voters. So the media tell people less what to think than what to think about.
21374.m: Through agenda-setting the media influence how important topics seem.

21375.q: What is it called when the media put a topic into a frame of interpretation by selecting and stressing certain aspects?
21375.e: Depending on the frame, the same event can appear, for example, as a question of security or of the economy. This affects how the public judges causes and solutions.
21375.m: Framing decides in what light a topic appears.

21376.q: Which theory by Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann (1974) says that people tend to keep quiet about their opinion if they believe they are in the minority?
21376.e: Out of fear of isolation, supposed minorities speak up less often. This makes the majority opinion seem ever stronger than it really is.
21376.m: The spiral of silence explains why supposed minorities fall silent.

21377.q: Who coined the term “filter bubble” in 2011 with a book of the same name?
21377.e: Pariser described how algorithms mainly show users content that fits their existing preferences. As a result, other points of view are seen less often.
21377.m: Algorithms can shut people into a filter bubble.

21378.q: What share of voters said no to the 2018 No Billag initiative to abolish the radio and television licence fee?
21378.e: On 4 March 2018, 71.6 per cent of voters and all the cantons rejected the initiative. This meant the funding of the SRG through a fee remained.
21378.m: The No Billag initiative was clearly rejected in 2018.

21379.q: Which body in Switzerland judges complaints about breaches of the journalists’ code?
21379.e: The Press Council is a self-regulatory body of the industry and is based on the “Declaration of the Duties and Rights of Journalists”. Its opinions are not legally binding.
21379.m: The Press Council watches over journalistic ethics.

21380.q: What does the editorial secrecy guaranteed in the Federal Constitution protect?
21380.e: Media freedom in the Federal Constitution bans censorship and protects editorial secrecy. Without protection of sources, many informants would no longer come forward.
21380.m: Editorial secrecy protects the media’s sources.

21381.q: Which colour do you get when you mix blue and yellow?
21381.e: Blue and yellow together make green. You can easily try this out with your paint box.

21382.q: Which colour do you get when you mix red and yellow?
21382.e: Red and yellow together make orange. Orange is the colour of oranges and carrots.

21383.q: Which colour do you get when you mix red and blue?
21383.e: Red and blue together make purple. It is also called violet or lilac.

21384.q: Which colour do you get when you mix a lot of white into red?
21384.e: White makes a colour lighter. With white, red becomes pink.

21385.q: Which three colours in the paint box are called the primary colours?
21385.e: From red, yellow and blue you can mix many other colours. That is why they are called primary colours.
21385.m: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours.

21386.q: Apart from white, which colour is on the Swiss flag?
21386.e: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background.
21386.m: The Swiss flag is red with a white cross.

21387.q: Which colour is considered a warm colour?
21387.e: Orange reminds us of fire and the sun. That is why orange, red and yellow count as warm colours.
21387.m: Red, orange and yellow look warm.

21388.q: Which tool do you use to paint with watercolours?
21388.e: With the paintbrush you pick up water and paint and use it to paint on the paper.
21388.m: You use a paintbrush to put watercolours on paper.

21389.q: Which colour is exactly opposite red on the colour wheel?
21389.e: On the colour wheel, green is opposite red. Such opposite colours look especially bright next to each other.
21389.m: Red and green are opposite colours.

21390.q: What is the stand that a picture rests on while it is being painted called?
21390.e: An easel holds the picture at a slant or upright so that you can paint comfortably standing up.
21390.m: When you paint, the picture stands on an easel.

21391.q: What do many painters paint their oil pictures on?
21391.e: A canvas is a strong fabric stretched over a wooden frame. Oil paint sticks to it well.
21391.m: Many oil paintings are painted on canvas.

21392.q: What is a painted picture of a person called?
21392.e: A portrait shows a person, often mainly their face.

21393.q: What is a picture showing fruit, flowers or objects on a table called?
21393.e: A still life shows things that do not move, for example a bowl of fruit.
21393.m: A still life shows quiet things such as fruit or flowers.

21394.q: What is the board that painters mix their colours on called?
21394.e: The painter mixes the colours on the palette before painting them onto the picture.
21394.m: You mix the colours on the palette.

21395.q: What is a picture in which painters have painted themselves called?
21395.e: For a self-portrait, painters often look in a mirror and paint themselves.
21395.m: In a self-portrait, the artist paints themselves.

21396.q: What is a picture that shows mountains, meadows and lakes called?
21396.e: A landscape painting shows nature, for example mountains, forests or lakes.

21397.q: Which Swiss painter is known for pictures of mountains and a woodcutter?
21397.e: Ferdinand Hodler painted many Swiss mountains and lakes. His painting “The Woodcutter” is very well known.
21397.m: Ferdinand Hodler painted mountains, lakes and the Woodcutter.

21398.q: What do you usually draw a sketch with at school?
21398.e: With a pencil you can draw fine lines and rub out mistakes.
21398.m: For a sketch you usually use a pencil.

21399.q: What can you use to remove pencil lines?
21399.e: The rubber rubs the pencil lines off the paper.
21399.m: You remove pencil lines with a rubber.

21400.q: Which tool do you use to draw a nice round circle?
21400.e: With compasses, one point is stuck firmly in the paper. The pencil turns around it and draws a circle.
21400.m: You draw circles with a pair of compasses.

21401.q: What do you use to draw perfectly straight lines?
21401.e: You put the ruler on the paper and run the pencil along its edge.
21401.m: You draw straight lines with a ruler.

21402.q: What is a quick, simple drawing done as a first draft called?
21402.e: A sketch is drawn quickly. It only shows the most important things.
21402.m: A sketch is a quick first drawing.

21403.q: What are stories told in drawn pictures with speech bubbles called?
21403.e: In a comic, many pictures one after another tell a story. What the characters say is written in speech bubbles.
21403.m: A comic tells a story in pictures.

21404.q: What do people often use to draw on the blackboard?
21404.e: Chalk leaves light lines on the blackboard. You can wipe them off with a wet sponge.
21404.m: You write on the blackboard with chalk.

21405.q: What is a picture made of pieces of paper glued on called?
21405.e: For a collage you cut out paper, photos or fabric and glue them together to make a picture.
21405.m: A collage is made of pieces glued on.

21406.q: What is a figure made of stone, wood or metal called?
21406.e: A sculpture is a work of art that you can look at from all sides.
21406.m: A sculpture is a figure made of stone, wood or metal.

21407.q: What is an artist who carves figures out of stone called?
21407.e: A sculptor uses a hammer and tools to carve figures out of stone or wood.
21407.m: A sculptor makes figures out of stone or wood.

21408.q: Which tool does a sculptor use together with the hammer?
21408.e: The sculptor strikes the chisel with the hammer. This breaks small pieces off the stone.
21408.m: You work stone with a hammer and chisel.

21409.q: What do you shape figures from that are then fired in a kiln?
21409.e: Clay is soft and easy to shape. In the hot kiln it becomes hard.
21409.m: Clay becomes hard in the kiln.

21410.q: Which Swiss artist made very thin, tall figures out of bronze?
21410.e: Alberto Giacometti came from the Bregaglia valley in the Grisons. His walking figures are very thin and tall.
21410.m: Alberto Giacometti made very thin figures.

21411.q: Which Swiss artist built funny machines that move and make noise?
21411.e: Jean Tinguely built machines from wheels and scrap metal. There is a museum with his works in Basel.
21411.m: Jean Tinguely built art machines that move.

21412.q: What is the famous statue in New York that holds up a torch called?
21412.e: The Statue of Liberty stands on an island off New York. It was a gift from France.
21412.m: The Statue of Liberty in New York holds a torch.

21413.q: Which artist created the sculpture “The Thinker”?
21413.e: The French sculptor Auguste Rodin made “The Thinker”. The figure sits resting its chin on its hand.
21413.m: Auguste Rodin's Thinker rests his chin on his hand.

21414.q: What is a building where works of art and old things are displayed called?
21414.e: In a museum you can look at art, old objects or animals and learn a lot.
21414.m: Works of art and old things are shown in a museum.

21415.q: What are you usually not allowed to do in an art museum?
21415.e: Skin has grease and dirt on it. If lots of people touch the paintings, they get damaged over time.
21415.m: In a museum you look with your eyes, not with your hands.

21416.q: In which city is the big Louvre art museum?
21416.e: The Louvre is one of the largest museums in the world. In front of the entrance there is a glass pyramid.
21416.m: The Louvre is a big museum in Paris.

21417.q: In which city is the Swiss Museum of Transport?
21417.e: The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne shows trains, cars, ships and aeroplanes.
21417.m: The Swiss Museum of Transport is in Lucerne.

21418.q: In which city is the National Museum with the largest collection on Swiss history?
21418.e: The National Museum stands by Zurich main station. It looks like a castle.
21418.m: The National Museum is in Zurich.

21419.q: What is a place where pictures are displayed and often sold called?
21419.e: In a gallery, pictures by artists hang on the walls. If you want, you can often buy a picture there too.
21419.m: In a gallery, pictures are shown and sold.

21420.q: In which city is the Zentrum Paul Klee?
21420.e: The Zentrum Paul Klee in Bern shows many pictures by the painter Paul Klee. The building looks like three waves.
21420.m: The Zentrum Paul Klee is in Bern.

21421.q: Near which city is the Fondation Beyeler art museum?
21421.e: The Fondation Beyeler is in Riehen, very close to Basel. Pictures by famous painters hang there.
21421.m: The Fondation Beyeler is near Basel.

21422.q: What did Giuseppe Arcimboldo paint funny faces out of?
21422.e: Arcimboldo was a painter from Italy who lived more than 400 years ago. In his paintings, a pear becomes a nose, for example.
21422.m: Arcimboldo painted faces made of fruit and vegetables.

21423.q: Who painted the famous picture “The Scream”?
21423.e: Edvard Munch was a painter from Norway. In the picture, a figure holds its hands to its head.
21423.m: The Scream is by Edvard Munch from Norway.

21424.q: Which flowers on a pond did Claude Monet paint very often?
21424.e: Claude Monet had a garden with a pond in France. He painted the water lilies there again and again.
21424.m: Claude Monet often painted the water lilies in his pond.

21425.q: Which Swiss painter often painted children and village life?
21425.e: Albert Anker lived in Ins in the canton of Bern. He painted children at school, playing and with their grandparents.
21425.m: Albert Anker painted children and village life.

21426.q: What is the girl in Jan Vermeer's famous painting wearing on her ear?
21426.e: The painting is called “Girl with a Pearl Earring”. Jan Vermeer painted it in Holland.
21426.m: Vermeer's girl wears a pearl earring.

21427.q: Which country does the famous picture “The Great Wave off Kanagawa” come from?
21427.e: The Japanese artist Hokusai made this picture. It shows a huge wave with a mountain in the background.
21427.m: The Great Wave comes from Japan.

21428.q: Which painter painted the large picture “The Night Watch”?
21428.e: Rembrandt was a painter from Holland. “The Night Watch” shows a group of men with weapons and a flag.
21428.m: The Night Watch is a painting by Rembrandt.

21429.q: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican?
21429.e: Michelangelo spent years painting this ceiling on high scaffolding. He was also a great sculptor.
21429.m: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

21430.q: Which country did Leonardo da Vinci come from?
21430.e: Leonardo was born in Italy. He worked in Florence, Milan and, at the end of his life, in France.
21430.m: Leonardo da Vinci came from Italy.

21431.q: Which mural by Leonardo shows Jesus eating with his disciples?
21431.e: Leonardo painted “The Last Supper” on the wall of a monastery in Milan.
21431.m: Leonardo's Last Supper is in Milan.

21432.q: How did Leonardo da Vinci often write in his notebooks?
21432.e: Leonardo often wrote from right to left. His notes are easiest to read with a mirror.
21432.m: Leonardo often wrote in mirror writing.

21433.q: What did Leonardo da Vinci draw long before they really existed?
21433.e: Leonardo watched birds and drew machines for flying. Real aeroplanes were only built much later.

21434.q: Apart from being a painter, what else was Leonardo da Vinci?
21434.e: Leonardo invented many machines and studied nature and the human body.
21434.m: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter and an inventor.

21435.q: Roughly when did Leonardo da Vinci live?
21435.e: Leonardo lived from 1452 to 1519. That is about 500 years ago.
21435.m: Leonardo da Vinci lived about 500 years ago.

21436.q: The name “da Vinci” means “from Vinci”. What is Vinci?
21436.e: Leonardo was born near the small town of Vinci. That is where his name comes from.
21436.m: Leonardo is named after the town of Vinci.

21437.q: Which yellow flowers did Vincent van Gogh paint in a vase?
21437.e: Van Gogh painted several pictures of sunflowers in a vase. He loved the colour yellow.

21438.q: Which country did Vincent van Gogh come from?
21438.e: Van Gogh was born in the Netherlands. It is also called Holland.
21438.m: Vincent van Gogh came from the Netherlands.

21439.q: What is the name of van Gogh's painting of a night sky full of swirling stars?
21439.e: In “The Starry Night”, stars and the moon shine over a village. The sky seems to be spinning.
21439.m: The Starry Night shows a swirling sky.

21440.q: Which room did van Gogh paint several times?
21440.e: Van Gogh painted his bedroom in Arles with a bed, chairs and pictures on the wall. There are three versions of it.
21440.m: Van Gogh painted his bedroom several times.

21441.q: How many of his paintings was van Gogh able to sell during his lifetime?
21441.e: Van Gogh was poor and hardly known. He sold only very few paintings, and his brother Theo helped him with money. He only became famous after his death.
21441.m: Van Gogh only became famous after his death.

21442.q: In which city is the Van Gogh Museum?
21442.e: The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam has the largest collection of his paintings.
21442.m: The Van Gogh Museum is in Amsterdam.

21443.q: How can you recognise many of van Gogh's paintings?
21443.e: Van Gogh put the paint on thickly. You can see his brushstrokes clearly; they look like waves.
21443.m: Van Gogh painted with strong brushstrokes.

21444.q: In which country did van Gogh paint many colourful pictures, for example in Arles?
21444.e: Van Gogh moved to the south of France. He liked the bright light and the colours there.
21444.m: Van Gogh painted many pictures in the south of France.

21445.q: Which country did Pablo Picasso come from?
21445.e: Picasso was born in Málaga in Spain. Later he lived in France for a long time.

21446.q: What is the name of Picasso's art style in which faces are made of angular shapes?
21446.e: In Cubism, things are broken up into corners and flat surfaces. This way you can see a face from the front and the side at the same time.
21446.m: In Cubism, pictures are made of angular shapes.

21447.q: In which colour did Picasso paint almost all his pictures for a while?
21447.e: This time is called his “Blue Period”. The pictures seem sad and quiet.

21448.q: Which animal did Picasso draw as a symbol of peace?
21448.e: Picasso drew a white dove. The dove of peace became famous all over the world.
21448.m: The dove is a symbol of peace.

21449.q: What is the name of Picasso's big painting about war?
21449.e: Guernica is a town in Spain that was bombed in 1937. Picasso painted a huge picture about it in black, white and grey.
21449.m: Guernica shows the suffering of war.

21450.e: Pablo Picasso was a painter from Spain. He painted a great many pictures and became famous all over the world.
21450.m: Pablo Picasso was a famous painter.

21451.q: How did Picasso paint faces in many of his well-known pictures?
a: From the front and the side at the same time
21451.e: Picasso often showed a face from several sides at once. So you see the nose from the side and both eyes from the front, for example.
21451.m: Picasso showed faces from several sides at once.

21452.q: Apart from pictures, what else did Picasso make?
21452.e: Picasso also made figures out of metal and painted plates and pots made of clay.
21452.m: Picasso also made sculptures and pottery.

21453.q: What is the Eiffel Tower built from?
21453.e: The Eiffel Tower is made of many iron parts joined with rivets. It was finished in 1889.
21453.m: The Eiffel Tower is built of iron.

21454.q: What are the huge tombs of the pharaohs in Egypt called?
21454.e: The pyramids are tombs for kings of ancient Egypt. They are over 4,000 years old.
21454.m: The pyramids are the tombs of the pharaohs.

21455.q: Which very long structure was built in China for protection?
21455.e: The Great Wall of China is thousands of kilometres long. It was meant to protect the country from attackers.
21455.m: The Great Wall of China is very long.

21456.q: In which city is the wooden Chapel Bridge?
21456.e: The Chapel Bridge crosses the Reuss. It is one of the oldest wooden bridges in Europe and has a water tower.
21456.m: The Chapel Bridge is in Lucerne.

21457.q: In which city is the Colosseum?
21457.e: The Colosseum is a huge arena from Roman times. Gladiators used to fight there.

21458.q: What is special about the tower of Pisa in Italy?
21458.e: The ground under the tower is soft. That is why the tower started leaning to one side while it was still being built.

21459.q: In which city is the clock tower that people call “Big Ben”?
21459.e: Big Ben is actually the name of the great bell in the tower. The tower stands by the Parliament in London.

21460.q: Which famous architect came from La Chaux-de-Fonds?
21460.e: Le Corbusier built houses all over the world. His picture was on the Swiss ten-franc note.
21460.m: Le Corbusier was a famous architect from Switzerland.

21461.q: What is the famous tower with a clock in Bern's old town called?
21461.e: At the Zytglogge, figures move shortly before every full hour. Lots of people watch.
21461.m: The Zytglogge is Bern's clock tower.

21462.q: What are the names of the two brothers who collected and wrote down many fairy tales?
21462.e: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected fairy tales in Germany. Their book is known all over the world.
21462.m: The Brothers Grimm wrote down many fairy tales.

21463.q: Who does Little Red Riding Hood meet in the forest?
21463.e: Little Red Riding Hood wants to visit her grandmother. In the forest she meets the big bad wolf.
21463.m: Little Red Riding Hood meets the wolf in the forest.

21464.q: With how many dwarfs does Snow White live?
21464.e: Snow White flees into the forest and finds the house of the seven dwarfs.
21464.m: Snow White lives with the seven dwarfs.

21465.q: What is the witch's house in “Hansel and Gretel” made of?
21465.e: In the Brothers Grimm's fairy tale, the house is made of bread, the roof of cake and the windows of sugar. Today people often call it a gingerbread house.
21465.m: You can eat the witch's house in Hansel and Gretel.

21466.q: What does Cinderella lose on the castle stairs?
21466.e: Cinderella runs away and loses a golden shoe. The prince uses it to look for her.

21467.q: How long does Sleeping Beauty sleep?
21467.e: Sleeping Beauty pricks herself on a spindle and sleeps for a hundred years. A thorny hedge grows around the castle.
21467.m: Sleeping Beauty sleeps for a hundred years.

21468.q: In the fairy tale “The Frog Prince”, what does the princess drop into the well?
21468.e: The princess is playing with her golden ball. A frog fetches it out of the well.
21468.m: The frog fetches the golden ball out of the well.

21469.q: Which country did the fairy tale writer Hans Christian Andersen come from?
21469.e: Hans Christian Andersen wrote “The Little Mermaid”, for example. There is a statue of her in Copenhagen.
21469.m: Hans Christian Andersen came from Denmark.

21470.q: Which words do many fairy tales begin with?
a: “And they all lived happily ever after”
21470.e: With “Once upon a time” you know straight away that a fairy tale is being told. “And they all lived happily ever after” often comes at the end.
21470.m: Many fairy tales begin with “Once upon a time”.

21471.q: What is the start of the Basel Carnival at 4 o'clock in the morning called?
21471.e: At the Morgenstreich, all the lights in Basel go out. Then groups with lanterns, piccolos and drums parade through the city.
21471.m: The Basel Carnival begins with the Morgenstreich.

21472.q: What is burned at the Sechseläuten in Zurich?
21472.e: The Böögg is a snowman full of firecrackers. It stands for winter, which is being driven away.
21472.m: The Böögg burns at the Sechseläuten.

21473.q: What are “Räbeliechtli” lanterns carved from in autumn?
21473.e: Räben are white turnips. You hollow them out, carve patterns into them and put a candle inside.

21474.q: At Chinese New Year, each year has a sign. What is it?
21474.e: In the Chinese calendar there are twelve animals, for example the dragon, the rabbit or the horse. Each year has its own animal.
21474.m: In the Chinese calendar, each year has an animal.

21475.q: Which festival do many people from India celebrate as a festival of lights?
21475.e: At Diwali, people light lots of small lights and lamps. They stand for good winning.
21475.m: Diwali is the festival of lights in India.

21476.q: At which festival do people often paint eggs?
21476.e: At Easter, people dye and paint eggs. They are often hidden for the children.

21477.q: What do the children in the Engadine do at Chalandamarz, on 1 March?
21477.e: The children march through the village with bells. With the noise they want to chase winter away.
21477.m: At Chalandamarz, children drive winter away with bells.

21478.q: What is smashed at the Escalade in Geneva?
21478.e: The Escalade commemorates an attack on Geneva in 1602. The youngest and the oldest family members smash the chocolate pot together.
21478.m: At the Escalade, people smash a chocolate pot.

21479.q: In which country is the famous Lascaux cave with Stone Age paintings of animals?
21479.e: The Lascaux cave is in south-west France. Its paintings of horses, deer and wild cattle are about 17,000 to 19,000 years old.
21479.m: The Lascaux cave paintings are in France.

21480.q: What is the roughly 30,000-year-old “Venus of Willendorf”?
a: A small female figure from the Stone Age
21480.e: The small limestone figure was found in Austria in 1908. It is one of the oldest works of art made by humans.
21480.m: The Venus of Willendorf is a figure from the Stone Age.

21481.q: Which architectural style followed the Romanesque style in the Middle Ages?
21481.e: From about 1140, the Gothic style developed out of the Romanesque in France. It then spread throughout Europe.

21482.q: What makes a Romanesque church especially easy to recognise?
21482.e: Romanesque churches have massive walls, small windows and round arches. This makes them look heavy and castle-like.
21482.m: Romanesque churches have thick walls and round arches.

a: A picture made of many small stones
A picture on damp lime plaster
21483.e: A mosaic is put together from small pieces of stone, glass or ceramic. The Romans already decorated floors and walls with them.
21483.m: A mosaic is made of many small stones.

21484.q: What is the wall painting in which you paint onto lime plaster that is still damp called?
21484.e: In a fresco, the paint bonds firmly with the plaster as it dries. That is why frescoes often last for many centuries.
21484.m: A fresco is painted onto damp plaster.

21485.q: Which Pop Art artist became famous for pictures of soup tins?
21485.e: Andy Warhol exhibited his “Campbell's Soup Cans” in 1962. Pop Art made everyday objects and advertising a subject of art.
21485.m: Andy Warhol painted famous soup tins.

21486.q: Which Spanish Surrealist painted the “melting clocks” in the painting “The Persistence of Memory”?
21486.e: Salvador Dalí painted the picture in 1931. Surrealism shows dreamlike and illogical scenes.
21486.m: Salvador Dalí painted the melting clocks.

21487.q: Which era did Neoclassicism around 1800 take as its model?
21487.e: Neoclassicism took the art of the ancient Greeks and Romans as its model. Columns, gables and clear, calm shapes are typical.
21487.m: Neoclassicism imitates the art of antiquity.

21488.q: What does the French word “Renaissance” mean?
21488.e: “Rebirth” refers to the new interest in the art and knowledge of antiquity. The era lasted from about 1400 to 1600.

21489.q: Who painted the mural “The Last Supper” in Milan?
21489.e: Leonardo painted the picture between about 1495 and 1498 in the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. It shows Jesus with his twelve disciples.
21489.m: The Last Supper in Milan is by Leonardo da Vinci.

21490.q: Which artist created the marble statue “David” in Florence, which is more than five metres tall?
21490.e: Michelangelo carved David from a single block of marble between 1501 and 1504. The original is now in the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence.
21490.m: Michelangelo created the David in Florence.

21491.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican between 1508 and 1512?
21491.e: Pope Julius II gave Michelangelo the commission. The ceiling paintings show scenes from the story of the Creation.
21491.m: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

21492.q: Who painted “The Birth of Venus”, in which the goddess stands on a shell?
21492.e: Sandro Botticelli painted the picture around 1485 in Florence. Today it hangs in the Uffizi.
21492.m: The Birth of Venus is by Sandro Botticelli.

21493.q: Which way of drawing with a vanishing point creates depth on a flat picture?
21493.e: In linear perspective, all the lines that lead into the distance meet at one vanishing point. It was developed in the early Renaissance in Florence.
21493.m: Linear perspective creates depth with a vanishing point.

21494.q: Which German Renaissance artist painted the famous watercolour “Young Hare” in 1502?
21494.e: Albrecht Dürer from Nuremberg was a painter and printmaker. His “Young Hare” is painted so precisely that you can see almost every hair.
21494.m: Albrecht Dürer painted the Young Hare.

21495.q: Which rich banking family supported many Renaissance artists in Florence?
21495.e: The Medici ruled Florence for a long time and gave commissions to artists such as Botticelli and Michelangelo. Supporters like this are called patrons.
21495.m: The Medici supported the arts in Florence.

21496.q: Who painted the large fresco “The School of Athens” in the Vatican?
21496.e: Raphael painted the fresco between 1509 and 1511. It shows famous thinkers of antiquity such as Plato and Aristotle.
21496.m: The School of Athens is a work by Raphael.

21497.q: Roughly in which period was the Baroque era?
21497.e: The Baroque followed the Renaissance and lasted from about 1600 to 1750. After it came Rococo and Neoclassicism.
21497.m: The Baroque lasted from about 1600 to 1750.

21498.q: Which Italian painter became famous for very strong contrasts of light and dark?
21498.e: Caravaggio made his figures light up brightly against an almost black background. This effect influenced many Baroque painters.
21498.m: Caravaggio painted with strong contrasts of light and dark.

21499.q: Which Dutch painter created the large group portrait “The Night Watch” in 1642?
21499.e: Rembrandt van Rijn painted Amsterdam's company of civic guards. The painting now hangs in the Rijksmuseum.
21499.m: The Night Watch is by Rembrandt.

21500.q: Which Flemish Baroque painter from Antwerp is known for strong, lively figures?
21500.e: Peter Paul Rubens ran a large workshop in Antwerp. His paintings are full of movement, colour and light.
21500.m: Peter Paul Rubens was a Flemish Baroque painter.

21501.q: Which French king had the magnificent Baroque palace of Versailles extended?
21501.e: Louis XIV, the “Sun King”, made Versailles his seat of government. The palace became a model for many royal courts in Europe.

21502.q: Which monastery in the canton of Schwyz has one of the best-known Baroque churches in Switzerland?
21502.e: The abbey church of Einsiedeln was magnificently built in the Baroque style in the 18th century. It is also an important place of pilgrimage.
21502.m: The abbey church of Einsiedeln is a Baroque masterpiece.

21503.q: The Baroque artist Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed many fountains and the colonnades in St Peter's Square. In which city did he mainly work?
21503.e: Gian Lorenzo Bernini shaped Baroque Rome. His colonnades surround St Peter's Square like two open arms.

21504.q: Which composer is considered one of the most important musicians of the Baroque?
21504.e: Johann Sebastian Bach lived from 1685 to 1750. The year of his death is often given as the end of Baroque music.
21504.m: Johann Sebastian Bach was a great Baroque composer.

21505.q: The painter Diego Velázquez was court painter to a king. Which country did he come from?
21505.e: Diego Velázquez was court painter to King Philip IV of Spain. His best-known painting is called “Las Meninas”.
21505.m: Velázquez was a Spanish court painter.

21506.q: Which painting gave Impressionism its name?
21506.e: A critic mocked Claude Monet's painting “Impression, soleil levant”, which was shown at the group's first joint exhibition. The artists then adopted the name themselves.
21506.m: Impressionism is named after a painting by Monet.

21507.q: In which country did Impressionism begin?
21507.e: Impressionism began around 1870 in France, mainly in Paris. From there it spread to many countries.

21508.q: Which water plants from his garden pond did Claude Monet paint in a great many pictures?
21508.e: Monet created a garden with a water lily pond in Giverny in France. He painted the water lilies again and again at different times of day.
21508.m: Claude Monet often painted water lilies.

21509.q: Which Impressionist painted ballet dancers especially often?
21509.e: Edgar Degas watched dancers practising and on stage. He painted and drew them in hundreds of works.
21509.m: Edgar Degas liked to paint ballet dancers.

21510.q: What is painting outdoors in nature instead of in the studio called?
21510.e: The Impressionists often painted outdoors, in French “en plein air”. New paints in tubes, which were easy to carry, helped them.
21510.m: Open-air painting takes place outdoors in nature.

21511.q: What did the Impressionists mainly want to capture in their paintings?
21511.e: The Impressionists painted with quick, visible brushstrokes. In this way they wanted to show the effect of light at a particular moment.
21511.m: Impressionists paint the light of the moment.

21512.q: How did many critics first react to the Impressionists' paintings?
a: They bought all the paintings straight away
They did not notice them at all
21512.e: At the first exhibition in Paris in 1874, many critics thought the quickly painted pictures were unfinished. Today they are among the most popular paintings in the world.
21512.m: The Impressionists were mocked at first.

21513.q: What are the pictures in Pointillism made of?
21513.e: In Pointillism, pure dots of colour are placed close together. Only in the eye of the viewer do they blend into areas of colour. Georges Seurat is famous for it.
21513.m: In Pointillism, you paint with dots of colour.

21514.q: How can you often recognise an Impressionist painting?
a: By pictures entirely in black and white
By pieces of newspaper glued on
21514.e: The Impressionists painted quickly, often outdoors. The individual brushstrokes remain visible and look blurry close up.

21515.q: What is most important in Expressionist paintings?
a: Being as true to nature as possible
21515.e: Expressionism comes from the Latin word for “expression”. The artists wanted to show what they felt, not exactly what something looks like.

21516.q: Which Norwegian painter created the picture “The Scream”?
21516.e: Edvard Munch created “The Scream” in 1893 in several versions. The picture is seen as a forerunner of Expressionism.
21516.m: The Scream is by Edvard Munch.

21517.q: Which colours did Expressionist painters often use?
a: Only browns like in old photos
21517.e: The Expressionists painted blue horses or green faces, for example. The colours were meant to show feelings, not reality.
21517.m: Expressionists painted with strong, unnatural colours.

21518.q: What was the Munich artists' group around Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc called?
21518.e: Kandinsky and Franz Marc founded the Blue Rider in Munich in 1911. Both loved the colour blue, and Marc liked painting horses.
21518.m: Kandinsky and Franz Marc belonged to the Blue Rider.

21519.q: Which animals did Franz Marc paint especially often, often in blue or yellow?
21519.e: Franz Marc painted “The Tower of Blue Horses”, for example. For him, colours had their own meaning; blue stood for the spiritual.
21519.m: Franz Marc liked to paint colourful horses.

21520.q: In which place in the Grisons did the painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner live from 1917?
21520.e: Kirchner moved to Davos to recover and stayed until his death in 1938. There he painted mountains and farmers; today there is a Kirchner Museum.
21520.m: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner lived in Davos.

21521.q: In which city is the Zentrum Paul Klee, with around 4,000 of his works?
21521.e: Paul Klee grew up in Bern. The Zentrum Paul Klee opened in 2005 and was built by the architect Renzo Piano.
21521.m: The Zentrum Paul Klee is in Bern.

21522.q: What does the name of the French painters' group “Les Fauves” around Henri Matisse mean?
21522.e: In 1905 a critic called the painters “wild beasts” because of their glaring, unmixed colours. Fauvism was closely related to Expressionism.
21522.m: Les Fauves means the wild beasts.

21523.q: Which country did the Expressionist painter Egon Schiele come from?
21523.e: Egon Schiele lived in Vienna and died in 1918 aged only 28. He painted expressive, often twisted bodies.
21523.m: Egon Schiele was a painter from Austria.

21524.q: Which two artists are considered the founders of Cubism?
21524.e: Picasso and Braque worked closely together in Paris from about 1907. Together they developed the new way of painting.

21525.q: Which French word does the name “Cubism” come from?
21525.e: A critic said that Braque's landscapes were made of little cubes. That is how the name Cubism came about.
21525.m: Cubism is named after the cube.

21526.q: Which shapes are typical of Cubist paintings?
a: Fine lines as exact as a photo
21526.e: The Cubists broke people and things up into angular surfaces. Picasso's work of 1907 with five angular female figures is considered the first Cubist painting.
21526.m: In Cubism, pictures are made of angular surfaces.

21527.q: How do Cubist paintings show an object?
a: From several viewpoints at the same time
21527.e: The Cubists broke things up into surfaces and showed different views side by side. This way you can see a face from the front and the side at the same time.
21527.m: Cubism shows things from several sides at once.

21528.q: What is the technique in which pieces of paper or fabric are glued onto a picture called?
21528.e: The word collage comes from the French “coller”, meaning to glue. Picasso and Braque used this technique from 1912.
21528.m: In a collage, materials are glued on.

21529.q: Which colours did Picasso and Braque mostly use in their early Cubist paintings?
21529.e: In the early phase of Cubism, shapes were what mattered most. That is why the artists painted with muted colours; later the pictures became more colourful.
21529.m: Early Cubist paintings have muted colours.

21530.q: In which city did Cubism begin?
21530.e: Picasso and Braque lived and worked in Paris at the beginning of the 20th century. At that time the city was the centre of modern art.

21531.q: Which country did Pablo Picasso, one of the founders of Cubism, come from?
21531.e: Picasso was born in Málaga in Spain in 1881. Later he lived in France for a long time and helped to develop Cubism there.

21532.q: Which country did the painter Vincent van Gogh come from?
21532.e: Vincent van Gogh was born in the Netherlands in 1853. Later he lived in France, where many of his best-known paintings were made.
21532.m: Vincent van Gogh came from the Netherlands.

21533.q: Which Mexican painter became famous above all for her colourful self-portraits?
21533.e: Frida Kahlo painted herself in many pictures, often with flowers and animals. After a serious accident, she worked through her pain in her art.

21534.q: Which sculptor from the Grisons is known for his very slender, elongated figures?
21534.e: Alberto Giacometti came from the Bregaglia valley in the Grisons. His “Walking Man” sculptures are among the most expensive sculptures in the world.
21534.m: Alberto Giacometti created very slender figures.

21535.q: Which Swiss painter painted “The Woodcutter” and mountains such as the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau?
21535.e: Ferdinand Hodler lived from 1853 to 1918 and is considered one of the most important Swiss painters. Clear shapes and repeated, similar figures are typical of him.

21536.q: Which Swiss artist built moving machine sculptures such as the Carnival Fountain in Basel?
21536.e: Jean Tinguely built sculptures from scrap and motors that move and make noises. There is a Museum Tinguely of his own in Basel.
21536.m: Jean Tinguely built moving machine sculptures.

21537.q: Which Bernese painter from Ins often painted children and village life?
21537.e: Albert Anker lived from 1831 to 1910. His detailed pictures of schoolchildren and farmhouse rooms are very popular in Switzerland.
21537.m: Albert Anker painted Swiss village life.

21538.q: What are the large, colourful female figures by the artist Niki de Saint Phalle called?
21538.e: Niki de Saint Phalle created her cheerful Nanas from 1965. One of her large figures, the “Guardian Angel”, hangs in the hall of Zurich main station.
21538.m: Niki de Saint Phalle's female figures are called Nanas.

21539.q: Which Swiss artist covered a cup, saucer and spoon with fur in 1936?
21539.e: Meret Oppenheim's work “Breakfast in Fur” belongs to Surrealism. Today it is in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
21539.m: Meret Oppenheim created the fur teacup.

21540.q: Which Austrian painter is known for pictures with lots of gold leaf, such as “The Kiss”?
21540.e: Gustav Klimt painted “The Kiss” around 1908 in Vienna. He was an important Art Nouveau artist.
21540.m: Gustav Klimt painted with lots of gold leaf.

21541.q: What is the name of the anonymous British street artist who sprays pictures onto walls using stencils?
21541.e: Officially, nobody knows who Banksy is. His stencil pictures appear on walls by surprise and are often critical or funny.
21541.m: Banksy is an anonymous street artist.

21542.q: In which museum does the “Mona Lisa” hang?
21542.e: The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre in Paris behind bulletproof glass. Millions of visitors come to see it every year.
21542.m: The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

21543.e: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa at the beginning of the 16th century in oil paint on a wooden panel. He was a painter, inventor and scientist all in one.
21543.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.

21544.q: Who painted “The Starry Night”, with its swirling sky, in 1889?
21544.e: Van Gogh painted the picture from memory in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. Today it hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
21544.m: The Starry Night is by Vincent van Gogh.

21545.q: Which event does Picasso's 1937 painting “Guernica” recall?
a: The bombing of a Spanish town
21545.e: In the Spanish Civil War, the Basque town of Guernica was bombed from the air. Picasso painted the huge picture in black, white and grey as an accusation against war.
21545.m: Guernica shows the suffering after a bombing raid.

21546.q: Who painted “Girl with a Pearl Earring”?
21546.e: Jan Vermeer from Delft painted the picture around 1665. Today it hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.
21546.m: Jan Vermeer painted Girl with a Pearl Earring.

21547.q: Which country does the colour woodblock print “The Great Wave off Kanagawa” come from?
21547.e: The Japanese artist Katsushika Hokusai created the picture around 1831. You can see Mount Fuji in the background.
21547.m: The Great Wave comes from Japan.

21548.q: Who painted the “Wanderer above the Sea of Fog”?
21548.e: Caspar David Friedrich was a painter of German Romanticism. The picture was made around 1818 and shows a man from behind standing on a rock.
21548.m: Caspar David Friedrich painted the Wanderer above the Sea of Fog.

21549.q: Which painter is known for his pictures of sunflowers in a vase?
21549.e: Vincent van Gogh painted several pictures of sunflowers in 1888 and 1889. The bright yellows are typical of him.

21550.q: Which painter is known for pictures with black lines and areas of red, yellow and blue?
21550.e: The Dutchman Piet Mondrian limited himself to primary colours, black, white and straight lines. His pictures are often called “Composition”.
21550.m: Piet Mondrian painted with primary colours and straight lines.

21551.q: The ancient Greeks built different kinds of columns. How do you recognise a Corinthian column?
a: By its capital with many leaves
By two scrolls on its capital
By a female figure instead of a column
21551.e: The Corinthian column is the most decorated of the Greek columns. Its capital is decorated with curling leaves.
21551.m: Corinthian columns have leaves on their capitals.

21552.q: To which goddess was the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens dedicated?
21552.e: The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC for Athena Parthenos. She was the protector goddess of the city of Athens.
21552.m: The Parthenon was dedicated to the goddess Athena.

21553.q: Which country did the famous architect Le Corbusier come from?
21553.e: Le Corbusier's real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, and he was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1887. He became one of the most important architects of modernism.
21553.m: Le Corbusier came from La Chaux-de-Fonds in Switzerland.

21554.q: In which architectural style is Cologne Cathedral built?
21554.e: Construction of Cologne Cathedral began in 1248 and was only completed in 1880. It shows typical Gothic features such as pointed arches and tall towers.
21554.m: Cologne Cathedral is a Gothic cathedral.

21555.q: Which architect designed the Sagrada Família church in Barcelona?
21555.e: Antoni Gaudí worked on the church from 1883 until his death in 1926. It is still being built today.
21555.m: The Sagrada Família is by Antoni Gaudí.

21556.q: Which famous school of art and architecture was founded in Weimar in 1919?
21556.e: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar. Simple, useful shapes are typical of the Bauhaus.
21556.m: The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar in 1919.

21557.q: The Basel architects Herzog & de Meuron built the Olympic Stadium in Beijing. What nickname does it have because of its shape?
21557.e: The stadium for the 2008 Olympic Games is surrounded by a mesh of steel beams. That is why it is called the “Bird's Nest”.
21557.m: The Olympic Stadium in Beijing is called the Bird's Nest.

21558.q: What is the large round window with stone tracery in Gothic churches called?
21558.e: The rose window is often above the main entrance. Its coloured glass looks like a huge flower.
21558.m: A round Gothic church window is called a rose window.

21559.q: What is Florence Cathedral in Italy especially famous for?
21559.e: Filippo Brunelleschi built the dome from 1420. With a diameter of about 45 metres, it was a technical masterpiece of the Renaissance. The leaning tower is in Pisa.
21559.m: Florence Cathedral has a huge dome.

21560.q: Which United Nations organisation names World Heritage Sites?
21560.e: UNESCO deals with education, science and culture. The World Heritage Convention has existed since 1972.

21561.q: Which Swiss old town with long arcades has been a World Heritage Site since 1983?
21561.e: Bern's old town has about six kilometres of arcades, more than almost any other city in Europe. It was added to the World Heritage List in 1983.
21561.m: The old town of Bern is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

21562.q: What is the Abbey District in St Gallen especially famous for?
a: Its Baroque library with old manuscripts
21562.e: The Abbey Library of St Gallen owns valuable manuscripts from the early Middle Ages. Its Baroque hall is considered one of the most beautiful in the world.
21562.m: The Abbey Library of St Gallen is a World Heritage Site.

21563.q: In which canton is the World Heritage Site of the Convent of St John in Müstair?
21563.e: The convent lies in the Val Müstair near the border with Italy. It is famous for wall paintings from around the year 800.
21563.m: The Müstair convent is in the Grisons.

21564.q: In which canton are the three castles that are a World Heritage Site and once protected a town?
21564.e: The castles Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro stand in Bellinzona. They have been a World Heritage Site since 2000.
21564.m: The castles of Bellinzona are in Ticino.

21565.q: What is the Lavaux World Heritage Site on Lake Geneva?
21565.e: The steep vineyard terraces in the canton of Vaud were built from the Middle Ages onwards. Lavaux has been a World Heritage Site since 2007.
21565.m: Lavaux is a landscape of vineyard terraces.

21566.q: Because of which industry did La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle become World Heritage Sites?
21566.e: The two towns in the Jura were planned and built for watchmaking, with bright homes and workshop buildings. They have been World Heritage Sites since 2009.
21566.m: La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are towns of the watch industry.

21567.q: What is the Taj Mahal in India?
21567.e: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built in the 17th century for his late wife. The white marble building stands in Agra.
21567.m: The Taj Mahal is a tomb.

21568.q: In which country is the Inca city of Machu Picchu?
21568.e: Machu Picchu lies high in the Andes at about 2,400 metres above sea level. The Incas built the city in the 15th century.

21569.q: What is the start of the Basel Carnival at 4 o'clock in the morning called?
21569.e: On the Monday after Ash Wednesday, all the lights are switched off at 4 o'clock. Then the cliques parade through the city with lanterns, drums and piccolos.
21569.m: The Basel Carnival begins with the Morgestraich.

21570.q: What is burned on a bonfire at the Zurich Sechseläuten?
21570.e: The Böögg is a snowman made of wood wool and fabric, with its head filled with firecrackers. The faster the head explodes, the nicer the summer is supposed to be.
21570.m: The Böögg is burned at the Sechseläuten.

21571.q: Which custom do children in the Engadine celebrate on 1 March with bells?
21571.e: At Chalandamarz, children march through the village with bells to drive winter away. The custom also became famous through the book “A Bell for Ursli”.
21571.m: At Chalandamarz, children ring winter out.

21572.q: Which event of 1602 does the Geneva festival “Escalade” commemorate?
a: A Savoyard attack that was fought off
The founding of the Red Cross
A great fire in the city
21572.e: On the night of 11 to 12 December 1602, the people of Geneva fought off a surprise attack by the Savoyards. Today a chocolate pot is smashed in memory of it.
21572.m: The Escalade commemorates fighting off the Savoyards in 1602.

21573.q: In which town does the big winegrowers' festival “Fête des Vignerons” take place?
21573.e: The Fête des Vignerons is celebrated only about every 20 to 25 years, most recently in 2019. It is part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
21573.m: The Fête des Vignerons takes place in Vevey.

21574.q: What is the Indian festival of lights, at which many little oil lamps are lit, called?
21574.e: Diwali is celebrated by Hindus, and also by Sikhs and Jains. The lights stand for the victory of light over darkness.
21574.m: Diwali is the Indian festival of lights.

21575.q: In which country is the “Día de los Muertos”, the Day of the Dead, celebrated with colourful skulls?
21575.e: On 1 and 2 November, families in Mexico cheerfully remember their loved ones who have died. They decorate altars with flowers, candles and sugar skulls.
21575.m: The Día de los Muertos is celebrated in Mexico.

21576.q: Which calendar decides the date of Chinese New Year?
21576.e: The Chinese calendar follows the moon and is matched up with the solar year. That is why New Year falls on a different day each year, between 21 January and 21 February.
21576.m: Chinese New Year follows the moon.

21577.q: What do the athletes at the Unspunnen Festival in Interlaken do with the Unspunnen Stone, which weighs about 83 kilograms?
a: They throw it as far as possible
They carry it up a mountain
They roll it into the lake
They carve a figure out of it
21577.e: In stone throwing, you throw the heavy stone as far as possible from a standing position. The Unspunnen Festival only takes place every few years and also features Swiss wrestling, yodelling and traditional costumes.
21577.m: At the Unspunnen Festival, the Unspunnen Stone is thrown.

21578.q: What is the transitional style between the High Renaissance and the Baroque (about 1520 to 1600), with elongated figures and artificial poses, called?
21578.e: Mannerism follows the High Renaissance and deliberately loosens its harmony through distorted proportions and cool colours. Well-known representatives are Parmigianino and Pontormo.
21578.m: Mannerism links the Renaissance with the Baroque.

21579.q: What is the extreme light-and-dark painting with almost black backgrounds, especially associated with Caravaggio, called?
21579.e: In tenebrism, brightly lit figures stand out from deep darkness. With it, Caravaggio shaped Baroque painting all over Europe around 1600.
21579.m: Caravaggio made his figures step out of the dark into the light.

21580.q: Which painting technique with soft, smoky transitions and no hard outlines is especially associated with Leonardo da Vinci?
21580.e: Sfumato comes from the Italian “fumo”, meaning smoke. Leonardo used the technique, for example in the “Mona Lisa”, to make facial features blur softly.
21580.m: In sfumato Leonardo let outlines blur like smoke.

21581.q: Which 18th-century style is seen as a playful late form of the Baroque, with a shell-like ornament called rocaille?
21581.e: Rococo (about 1730 to 1770) is named after the rocaille, an asymmetrical shell ornament. Light pastel colours and light, elegant shapes are typical.
21581.m: Rococo takes its name from the rocaille.

21582.q: Which art movement (about 1770 to 1840) deliberately looked back to Greek and Roman antiquity?
21582.e: Neoclassicism sought clarity, order and moderation on the model of antiquity. Excavations in Pompeii and Herculaneum fuelled this enthusiasm.
21582.m: Neoclassicism took antiquity as its model.

21583.q: Which painter of German Romanticism created the painting “Wanderer above the Sea of Fog”?
21583.e: Caspar David Friedrich's picture (about 1817) shows a figure seen from behind in front of a wide, misty landscape. The figure seen from behind invites viewers to put themselves into the scene.
21583.m: Caspar David Friedrich painted figures from behind in front of sublime nature.

21584.q: Which painting by Claude Monet gave Impressionism its name?
21584.e: In 1874 a critic mocked Monet's harbour painting “Impression, soleil levant” (Impression, Sunrise) and called the whole group “Impressionists”. The mocking name became the name of the style.
21584.m: A mocking name became the name of Impressionism.

21585.q: Which art style followed the Romanesque in France from about 1140?
21585.e: Gothic began in the Île-de-France when Abbot Suger had the choir of Saint-Denis rebuilt. It then spread all over Europe.
21585.m: Gothic began in France in the 12th century.

21586.q: Which style around 1900 is called “Art nouveau” in France and “Secession style” in Austria?
21586.e: The German name comes from the Munich magazine “Jugend”. Floral ornaments, curving lines and the combination of art and craft are typical.
21586.m: Art Nouveau has a different name in every country.

21587.q: Which Post-Impressionist painter wanted to break nature down into cylinders, spheres and cones and is seen as a forerunner of Cubism?
21587.e: Paul Cézanne built his pictures from areas of colour and basic geometric shapes, for example in his views of Mont Sainte-Victoire. Later artists saw him as the “father of modern art”.
21587.m: Paul Cézanne is seen as the father of modern painting.

21588.q: Which artist and author is regarded as the founder of art history writing with his artists' biographies “Le Vite” (1550)?
21588.e: Giorgio Vasari described the lives and works of Italian artists from Cimabue to Michelangelo. He also coined the term “rinascita” for the rebirth of the arts.
21588.m: Giorgio Vasari wrote the first great artists' biographies.

21589.q: Which method of representation did Leon Battista Alberti first describe as a set of rules for painters in 1435?
21589.e: In his treatise “De pictura”, Alberti put Brunelleschi's experiments into rules. He described the picture as an “open window” through which you look at the world.
21589.m: Alberti made linear perspective a rule for painters.

21590.q: Which art did Johann Joachim Winckelmann praise in 1755 with the phrase “noble simplicity and quiet grandeur”?
21590.e: Winckelmann saw in Greek statues an ideal of calm and dignity. His enthusiasm shaped Neoclassicism, which wanted to imitate antiquity.
21590.m: Winckelmann admired the noble simplicity of Greek art.

21591.q: Which two stylistic periods did the Winterthur art historian Heinrich Wölfflin compare in 1915 using pairs of opposites such as “linear and painterly”?
21591.e: In his “Principles of Art History”, Heinrich Wölfflin contrasted the clear Renaissance with the dynamic Baroque. His method of comparing pictures still shapes teaching today.
21591.m: Heinrich Wölfflin taught the careful comparison of styles.

21592.q: Which work by Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1766) examines the boundaries between painting and poetry?
21592.e: In “Laocoon”, Lessing argues that painting depicts bodies in space and poetry depicts actions in time. His starting point is the ancient Laocoon group.
21592.m: In Laocoon, Lessing separated the art of space from the art of time.

21593.q: What is the ratio of about 1 to 1.618, which has been considered especially harmonious since the Renaissance, called?
21593.e: In the golden ratio, the whole line relates to the larger part as the larger part relates to the smaller part. The ratio is (1 + √5) / 2, or about 1.618.
21593.m: The golden ratio divides a line in a ratio of about 1 to 1.618.

21594.q: Which philosopher defined beauty in the “Critique of Judgement” (1790) as “disinterested pleasure”?
21594.e: For Immanuel Kant, the beautiful pleases us without our wanting to own or use it. This idea had a lasting influence on philosophical aesthetics.
21594.m: Kant called beauty a disinterested pleasure.

21595.q: According to Walter Benjamin, what does a work of art lose when it is mass-reproduced through photography and film?
a: Its aura, the uniqueness of the original
21595.e: In 1935/36 Walter Benjamin argued that technical reproduction dissolves the uniqueness of the original, its “aura”. The text is a key work of media theory.
21595.m: Walter Benjamin described the loss of the aura through reproduction.

21596.q: Which artist published the essay “Concerning the Spiritual in Art” in 1911?
21596.e: In it, Wassily Kandinsky explained why colours and shapes without any object can have an inner effect. He compared colours with sounds in music.
21596.m: Kandinsky compared the effect of colours with music.

21597.q: In which city was the “Symbolist Manifesto”, which gave the art movement its name, published in 1886?
21597.e: The poet Jean Moréas published the manifesto in September 1886 in the Paris newspaper “Le Figaro”. Symbolism wanted to hint at ideas in images rather than name them directly.
21597.m: Symbolism got its name from a manifesto in Paris in 1886.

21598.q: Which Basel painter created the painting “Isle of the Dead” in several versions from 1880?
21598.e: Arnold Böcklin painted five versions of the gloomy rocky island with cypresses and a boat with a white figure. Around 1900 the picture was hugely popular as a reproduction.
21598.m: Arnold Böcklin painted the Isle of the Dead in five versions.

21599.q: Which Bernese painter developed the principle of “parallelism” and painted the picture “Night” in 1889/90?
21599.e: Ferdinand Hodler arranged similar figures and shapes in rhythmic repetition to make a timeless order visible. “Night” made him internationally known.
21599.m: Ferdinand Hodler arranged his figures in parallelism.

21600.q: Which subjects did the French Symbolist Gustave Moreau particularly like to paint?
21600.e: Gustave Moreau depicted subjects such as Salome or Oedipus in splendid, jewel-like pictures. His studio house in Paris is now a museum.
21600.m: Gustave Moreau painted biblical and mythological subjects like precious jewels.

21601.q: Which painter, born in Arco, created the “Alpine Triptych” with the parts “Life, Nature, Death” in the Alps of the Grisons?
21601.e: Giovanni Segantini combined a bright, divisionist style of painting with symbolic content in his Alpine pictures. He died in 1899 on the Schafberg above Pontresina; there is a Segantini Museum in St. Moritz.
21601.m: Segantini painted the coming into being and passing away of life in the Alps of the Grisons.

21602.q: Which group of artists around Paul Sérusier and Maurice Denis named themselves after the Hebrew word for “prophets”?
21602.e: The Nabis (from 1888) emphasised flat colours and a symbolic, decorative pictorial language. Félix Vallotton from Lausanne was also one of them.
21602.m: The Nabis saw themselves as prophets of a new kind of painting.
