21603.q: Which Norwegian painter is counted among the Symbolists with “The Scream” and is seen as a forerunner of Expressionism?
21603.e: In “The Scream” (1893), Edvard Munch expressed fear and inner states through distorted shapes and garish colours. He made several versions in different techniques.
21603.m: Edvard Munch made inner fear visible in a picture.

21604.q: Which Viennese painter created the gold-ground painting “The Kiss” around 1908/09?
21604.e: In his “golden period”, Gustav Klimt combined gold leaf with flat ornaments and symbolic motifs. The picture now hangs in the Belvedere in Vienna.
21604.m: Gustav Klimt painted The Kiss with real gold leaf.

21605.q: Which basic aim distinguishes Symbolism from Naturalism?
a: Hinting at ideas and states of mind through symbols
Reproducing visible reality as exactly as possible
Denouncing social injustice in a documentary way
Capturing the light and colour of the moment
21605.e: Symbolism turned against the mere depiction of reality. It sought the invisible, the dreamlike and the spiritual, which can only be hinted at in images.
21605.m: Symbolism hints at the invisible through symbols.

21606.q: Who published the first “Surrealist Manifesto” in 1924?
21606.e: André Breton defined Surrealism as “pure psychic automatism” without any control by reason. For a long time he was regarded as the spokesman of the movement in Paris.
21606.m: André Breton was the spokesman of Surrealism.

21607.q: What is the 1931 painting by Salvador Dalí with the soft, melting pocket watches called?
21607.e: The small picture hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. The soft watches are often interpreted as a symbol of the relativity of time in dreams.
21607.m: In Dalí's work, time melts like soft cheese.

21608.q: Which Belgian Surrealist painted a pipe with the inscription “Ceci n'est pas une pipe”?
21608.e: With the picture “La trahison des images” (The Treachery of Images, 1929), René Magritte showed that a painted object is only an image. The work plays with the relationship between picture, word and reality.
21608.m: Magritte reminds us that a picture is never the object itself.

21609.q: What is the technique developed by Max Ernst in 1925, in which textures such as wood grain are rubbed onto paper with a pencil, called?
21609.e: Frottage comes from the French “frotter”, meaning to rub. Max Ernst used the random textures as inspiration for fantastic imaginary worlds.
21609.m: In frottage you rub textures through onto paper.

21610.q: What is writing without any control by reason, which the Surrealists used as a path to the unconscious, called?
21610.e: In automatic writing you write so fast that your mind cannot interfere. Breton and Soupault wrote “Les Champs magnétiques” this way in 1919.
21610.m: Automatic writing is meant to let the unconscious speak.

21611.q: What is the Surrealist game in which several people take turns adding parts of a sentence or figure without seeing what came before?
21611.e: The name comes from the first sentence created this way: “Le cadavre exquis boira le vin nouveau” (The exquisite corpse will drink the new wine). The game uses chance as a creative force.
21611.m: In cadavre exquis a work emerges from chance and teamwork.

21612.q: Which Swiss artist created the object “Breakfast in Fur”, a fur-covered cup, in 1936?
21612.e: Meret Oppenheim covered a cup, saucer and spoon with animal fur. Alfred Barr bought the object for the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1936, and it became an icon of Surrealism.
21612.m: Meret Oppenheim turned a fur cup into an icon of Surrealism.

21613.q: Which psychoanalyst strongly influenced the Surrealists with his “Interpretation of Dreams”?
21613.e: Sigmund Freud's “Interpretation of Dreams” (1899/1900) described dreams as a path to the unconscious. The Surrealists wanted to open up this hidden world through art.
21613.m: Like Freud, the Surrealists looked for a way into the unconscious.

21614.q: Which Swiss sculptor belonged to the Paris Surrealists from about 1930 to 1935 and created “Le Palais à 4 heures du matin”?
21614.e: In his Surrealist phase, Alberto Giacometti from the Bregaglia created mysterious cage and stage objects. Later he became world-famous for his extremely slender figures.
21614.m: Before his slender figures, Giacometti was a Surrealist.

21615.q: Which artist exhibited the “Black Square” in 1915 and founded Suprematism?
21615.e: Kazimir Malevich showed the picture in 1915 in Petrograd in the corner of the room, where icons traditionally hang. Suprematism wanted to express the “supremacy of pure feeling”.
21615.m: Malevich made a black square an icon of modern art.

21616.q: Which Dutch group of artists was founded in 1917 around Piet Mondrian and Theo van Doesburg?
21616.e: De Stijl was also the name of the group's magazine. The group limited itself to right angles and a few colours and influenced painting, architecture and design.
21616.m: De Stijl limited itself to right angles and pure colours.

21617.q: Which colours did Piet Mondrian use in his Neoplasticist pictures besides black, white and grey?
21617.e: Mondrian limited himself to the three primary colours and the non-colours. In this way he wanted to make a universal, harmonious order visible.
21617.m: Mondrian painted only with primary colours and non-colours.

21618.q: What is the group of artists around Max Bill, Richard Paul Lohse and Camille Graeser, who worked with mathematically ordered forms, called?
21618.e: The Zurich Concretists built their pictures according to rational, verifiable rules. From the 1930s they also shaped Swiss graphic design internationally.
21618.m: The Zurich Concretists built pictures according to mathematical rules.

21619.q: What characterises a work of concrete art?
a: It depicts nothing but consists only of shapes and colours
It shows objects as true to life as possible
It consists of newspaper cuttings stuck on
It shows dreams and unreal scenes
21619.e: Theo van Doesburg coined the term “concrete art” in 1930. Such pictures represent nothing but consist only of lines, surfaces and colours. In Zurich, Max Bill and others took up the idea.
21619.m: Concrete art depicts nothing and is only itself.

21620.q: What is the branch of Abstract Expressionism associated with Jackson Pollock's drip and pour paintings called?
21620.e: Pollock laid the canvas on the floor and dripped paint onto it, known as drip painting. In Action Painting, the process of painting as a physical act is the focus.
21620.m: In Action Painting, painting itself becomes the action.

21621.q: Which Colour Field painter created large pictures with floating rectangles of colour and designed a chapel in Houston?
21621.e: Mark Rothko wanted his large areas of colour to trigger deep feelings. The Rothko Chapel in Houston opened in 1971.
21621.m: Mark Rothko wanted to awaken deep feelings with areas of colour.

21622.q: Which art movement of the 1960s works with optical illusions and flickering effects, for example in Victor Vasarely and Bridget Riley?
21622.e: Op Art stands for “Optical Art”. Thanks to precisely calculated patterns, the pictures seem to move or bulge.
21622.m: Op Art tricks the eye with flickering patterns.

21623.q: Which artist, born in Davos in 1889, is one of the pioneers of geometric abstraction and appeared on the former 50-franc note?
21623.e: Sophie Taeuber-Arp worked as a painter, textile designer, dancer and interior designer. Her portrait was on the 50-franc note of the 8th banknote series.
21623.m: Sophie Taeuber-Arp was a pioneer of abstract art.

21624.q: Which group of artists did Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Erich Heckel and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff found in Dresden in 1905?
21624.e: Die Brücke (The Bridge) is seen as the beginning of German Expressionism. Angular shapes, strong colours and woodcuts are typical. Kirchner later lived in Davos for a long time.
21624.m: Die Brücke stood at the beginning of German Expressionism.

21625.q: Which two artists published the almanac “Der Blaue Reiter” in Munich in 1912?
a: Gabriele Münter and Alexej von Jawlensky
Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Emil Nolde
21625.e: Kandinsky and Marc also organised the exhibitions of the editorial team “Der Blaue Reiter” (The Blue Rider). Both loved the colour blue, and Marc also loved horses.
21625.m: Kandinsky and Marc gave the Blue Rider its name.

21626.q: In which city was Dadaism founded in 1916 at the Cabaret Voltaire?
21626.e: Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings opened the Cabaret Voltaire in the Spiegelgasse. Artists from many countries who had fled to Switzerland because of the First World War performed sound poems and actions there.
21626.m: Dadaism was born in neutral Switzerland in the middle of the First World War.

21627.q: Which two artists developed Cubism together from about 1907/08?
21627.e: Picasso and Braque broke objects down into facets and showed them from several angles at once. A distinction is made between Analytical and Synthetic Cubism.
21627.m: Cubism shows an object from several angles at once.

21628.q: Which painting by Pablo Picasso from 1907 is considered a key work on the way to Cubism?
21628.e: The picture shows five female nudes with angular, partly mask-like faces. It broke radically with linear perspective and shocked even Picasso's friends.
21628.m: In 1907 Picasso broke radically with traditional perspective.

21629.q: Which artists around Henri Matisse were called “wild beasts” at the Paris Salon d'Automne in 1905?
21629.e: Because of their bright, unnatural colours, a critic called them “fauves”, meaning wild beasts. In their work, colour was freed from the object.
21629.m: The Fauves freed colour from the object.

21630.q: Which Italian movement celebrated speed, technology and machines in Marinetti's manifesto of 1909?
21630.e: Filippo Tommaso Marinetti published the manifesto in “Le Figaro”. The Futurists wanted to depict the movement and dynamism of the modern city.
21630.m: The Futurists glorified speed and technology.

21631.q: What did Marcel Duchamp call the industrially made everyday objects that he declared to be works of art, such as the urinal “Fountain” (1917)?
21631.e: Duchamp showed that the artist's decision and the place of exhibition can make something art. He signed “Fountain” with “R. Mutt”.
21631.m: Duchamp declared ordinary objects to be art.

21632.q: Which painter was born in Münchenbuchsee near Bern in 1879, taught at the Bauhaus and created his own poetic pictorial language?
21632.e: Paul Klee grew up in Bern, where the Zentrum Paul Klee now holds about 4000 of his works. His saying “Art does not reproduce the visible but makes visible” is famous.
21632.m: Paul Klee wanted to use art to make the invisible visible.

21633.q: Which anonymous artist had his picture “Girl with Balloon” partly shredded at Sotheby's right after it was sold in 2018?
21633.e: A shredder hidden in the frame cut the picture halfway. The work was given the new title “Love is in the Bin” and fetched an even higher price in 2021.
21633.m: Banksy turned destruction itself into a work of art.

21634.q: Which artist created the 1991 work “The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living”, a tiger shark preserved in formaldehyde?
21634.e: Damien Hirst was one of the “Young British Artists”; the work was first shown at the Saatchi Gallery in London in 1992. The shark in the glass case deals with death and transience.
21634.m: Damien Hirst confronts viewers with death.

21635.q: What is Art Basel, founded in 1970 by Basel gallery owners including Ernst Beyeler?
a: One of the most important art fairs in the world
The art museum of the city of Basel
21635.e: At Art Basel, galleries from all over the world sell modern and contemporary art. The fair has offshoots in Miami Beach, Hong Kong and Paris, among other places.
21635.m: Art Basel has been a meeting place of the art world since 1970.

21636.q: In which German city does documenta, one of the most important exhibitions of contemporary art, take place every five years?
21636.e: documenta was founded in Kassel in 1955 by Arnold Bode. It always lasts 100 days and is therefore also called the “museum of 100 days”.
21636.m: documenta in Kassel always lasts 100 days.

21637.q: Which Swiss artist duo made the 1987 film “The Way Things Go”, showing a long chain reaction of everyday objects?
21637.e: Fischli/Weiss had tyres, bottles and ladders interact in a chain reaction lasting about half an hour. The film was shown at documenta 8 and became world-famous.
21637.m: Fischli and Weiss turned a chain reaction into a work of art.

21638.q: Which Swiss video artist filled the atrium of the Museum of Modern Art in New York with “Pour Your Body Out” in 2008?
21638.e: Pipilotti Rist comes from the Rhine valley of St Gallen and is known for colourful, room-filling video installations. Visitors could lie down on a round sofa in the work.
21638.m: Pipilotti Rist bathes whole rooms in moving images.

21639.q: Which Chinese artist covered the floor of the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern in 2010 with about 100 million hand-painted porcelain sunflower seeds?
21639.e: The seeds were painted one by one by hundreds of craftspeople in Jingdezhen. The work deals with mass production and the relationship between the individual and the masses.
21639.m: With porcelain seeds, Ai Weiwei showed the masses made of individuals.

21640.q: Which performance artist sat silently facing visitors for over 700 hours in “The Artist Is Present” at the Museum of Modern Art in 2010?
21640.e: During the retrospective, Marina Abramović sat on a chair every day the museum was open. Anyone who wanted could sit opposite her and look into her eyes without a word.
21640.m: Marina Abramović makes her own body the material of art.

21641.q: Which artist couple wrapped the Reichstag in Berlin in 1995?
a: Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen
21641.e: Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the Reichstag in over 100,000 square metres of fabric. In Switzerland, in 1998, they wrapped trees in the park of the Fondation Beyeler in Riehen.
21641.m: Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped buildings to make them visible in a new way.

21642.q: In Erwin Panofsky's model for interpreting a work of art, what is the first step?
a: Describe exactly what can be seen
Estimate the market value of the picture
Interpret its meaning in the cultural context
21642.e: Panofsky starts with a pure description of the forms. Next you identify the motifs, and only at the end do you interpret the work in its cultural context.
21642.m: Panofsky interprets pictures in three stages.

21643.q: What is the method that identifies the content and motifs of pictures, for example recognising a saint by his attribute?
21643.e: Iconography literally means “image description”. It clarifies what is depicted, drawing on texts such as the Bible or ancient myths.
21643.m: Iconography identifies what is shown in a picture.

21644.q: Which attribute identifies the apostle Peter in Christian art?
21644.e: Peter carries the keys of the kingdom of heaven, according to Matthew 16:19. The sword belongs to Paul, the gridiron to Lawrence and the wheel to Catherine.
21644.m: You recognise Peter in pictures by his keys.

21645.q: What is the kind of still life that reminds us of transience with a skull, a snuffed-out candle or an hourglass called?
21645.e: Vanitas is Latin and means emptiness or vanity. In the Dutch Baroque in particular, such pictures warned that earthly riches pass away.
21645.m: The vanitas still life reminds us that life is fleeting.

21646.q: Which work by Jan van Eyck from 1434 is interpreted as a double portrait with many symbolic details such as a convex mirror and a dog?
21646.e: In the mirror on the back wall, two more people can be seen, and above it is written “Johannes de eyck fuit hic”. The dog is often interpreted as a sign of loyalty.
21646.m: In van Eyck's work even small objects carry meaning.

21647.q: What is a distorted image that only looks correct from a certain angle called, for example the skull in Holbein's “The Ambassadors” (1533)?
21647.e: Hans Holbein the Younger, who worked in Basel for a long time, painted the skull diagonally distorted across the floor. Only when viewed from the side can you recognise it as a vanitas symbol.
21647.m: An anamorphosis only reveals its subject from the right angle.

21648.q: What is a three-part work of art, often an altarpiece with a central panel and two wings, called?
21648.e: The Greek “tri” means three, “ptyche” a fold or panel. The wings could be opened differently on working days and feast days.
21648.m: A triptych consists of three panels.

21650.q: Which perspective makes distant objects appear further away through bluer and paler colours?
21650.e: The air scatters light, so distant mountains look paler and bluer. Painters such as Leonardo used this effect deliberately to create depth.
21650.m: Aerial perspective makes distant things look pale and bluish.

21651.q: Which order of columns from Greek antiquity can be recognised by capitals with spiral volutes?
21651.e: The Ionic order originated in eastern Greece and looks slimmer than the Doric. The Corinthian order, on the other hand, has acanthus leaves.
21651.m: You recognise Ionic capitals by their spirals.

21652.q: Which architect solved the construction of the huge dome of Florence Cathedral, consecrated in 1436?
21652.e: Filippo Brunelleschi built the dome without scaffolding as a double-shell structure with bricks in a herringbone pattern. It is considered the founding building of Renaissance architecture.
21652.m: Brunelleschi built the dome of Florence Cathedral without scaffolding.

21653.q: Which architect, born in La Chaux-de-Fonds, formulated the “Five Points of a New Architecture” in 1927?
21653.e: Le Corbusier, whose real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, called for pillars, a roof garden, a free plan, ribbon windows and a free façade. The Villa Savoye puts these points into practice.
21653.m: Le Corbusier summed up modern architecture in five points.

21654.q: Which features characterise the construction of a Gothic cathedral?
a: Pointed arches, rib vaults and flying buttresses
Round arches, thick walls and small windows
Dome, columned portico and triangular pediment
Oval rooms, stucco and ceiling frescoes
21654.e: The flying buttresses carry the forces of the vault outwards. This meant the walls could be opened up and filled with large stained-glass windows.
21654.m: Flying buttresses made the tall glass walls of Gothic possible.

21655.q: Which Ticino architect built the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1995) and the church on Monte Tamaro?
21655.e: Mario Botta is known for basic geometric shapes and façades of striped stone or brick. He belongs to the so-called Ticino School.
21655.m: Mario Botta builds with clear shapes and striped stone.

21656.q: Which Swiss architect won the Pritzker Prize in 2009 and built the thermal baths in Vals?
21656.e: The Therme Vals (1996) is built from layers of Vals quartzite. Peter Zumthor places great importance on material, light and atmosphere.
21656.m: Peter Zumthor builds spaces you experience with all your senses.

21657.q: Which Basel architecture firm designed the national stadium in Beijing, known as the “Bird's Nest”, for the 2008 Olympic Games?
21657.e: The stadium was created in collaboration with Ai Weiwei and got the nickname “Bird's Nest” because of its interwoven steel girders. The firm also converted Tate Modern in London.
21657.m: Herzog & de Meuron built the Bird's Nest in Beijing.

21658.q: Which principle of functionalism is attributed to the Chicago architect Louis Sullivan?
21658.e: In 1896 Louis Sullivan wrote, in essence, that the form of a building should follow from its function. He is regarded as one of the fathers of the skyscraper.
21658.m: In functionalism, form should follow from function.

21659.q: Which architectural style does the Grossmünster in Zurich, with its round arches, thick walls and heavy vaults, belong to?
21659.e: The Grossmünster was built from about 1100 to 1220. The Romanesque style was based on Roman building forms such as the round arch.
21659.m: The Romanesque built with round arches and thick walls.

21660.q: Which Basel historian published the work “The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy” in 1860?
21660.e: Jacob Burckhardt described the Renaissance as a time of the “discovery of the world and of man”. He is shown on the former 1000-franc note.
21660.m: Jacob Burckhardt shaped our picture of the Renaissance.

21661.q: What does the title “Homo Ludens” of Johan Huizinga's book about play as a factor in culture mean?
21661.e: In 1938 the Dutch historian Johan Huizinga showed that play is a foundation of culture. “Ludere” is Latin and means to play.
21661.m: Huizinga saw play as one of the roots of culture.

21662.q: Which era did Immanuel Kant describe as “man's emergence from his self-incurred immaturity”?
21662.e: In 1784 Kant answered the question “What is Enlightenment?” with this sentence. His motto was “Sapere aude”: have the courage to use your own understanding.
21662.m: The Enlightenment called on people to think for themselves.

21663.q: Which invention by Johannes Gutenberg around 1450 fundamentally changed the spread of knowledge?
21663.e: With movable metal type, texts could be printed quickly and in large numbers. Basel became an important printing centre in the 15th and 16th centuries.
21663.m: Printing made knowledge available to many more people.

21664.q: Which humanist published the first printed edition of the Greek New Testament in Basel in 1516?
21664.e: Erasmus had the work printed by Johann Froben in Basel. He lived in Basel for a long time and is buried in Basel Minster.
21664.m: Erasmus of Rotterdam was the prince of the humanists.

21665.q: Which reformer worked as people's priest at the Grossmünster in Zurich from 1519?
21665.e: Huldrych Zwingli preached at the Grossmünster and introduced the Reformation in Zurich. He fell in 1531 at the Battle of Kappel.
21665.m: Huldrych Zwingli brought the Reformation to Zurich.

21666.q: Which movement around 1770 emphasised feeling, nature and genius against pure reason?
21666.e: The name comes from a play by Friedrich Maximilian Klinger. Young writers such as Goethe and Schiller belonged to this movement.
21666.m: In Sturm und Drang, feeling counted for more than rules.

21667.q: What did the sociologist Norbert Elias study using old books of manners from the Middle Ages onwards?
a: How table manners and feelings of shame changed
21667.e: In “The Civilizing Process”, Norbert Elias showed how people controlled their feelings more and more, for example when eating with a fork or blowing their nose.
21667.m: Norbert Elias showed how behaviour changes over time.

21668.q: Which monastery in Switzerland is UNESCO World Heritage and has wall paintings from the Carolingian period around 800?
a: Monastery of St John in Müstair
21668.e: The monastery in the Val Müstair is said to go back to Charlemagne. The cycle of frescoes in the abbey church is considered one of the largest surviving from this period.
21668.m: The Müstair monastery preserves frescoes from the time of Charlemagne.

21669.q: What was the name of the Nazi propaganda exhibition of 1937 in Munich that ridiculed modern art?
21669.e: The exhibition showed confiscated works by artists such as Kirchner, Nolde or Klee with derogatory labels. At the same time, the regime showed the officially approved art nearby.
21669.m: The Nazis persecuted modern art as degenerate.

21670.q: In which Swiss city was modern art confiscated by the Nazis from German museums auctioned in 1939?
21670.e: At the Galerie Fischer auction in Lucerne in June 1939, works by van Gogh, Picasso and others were sold. The proceeds went to Nazi Germany, which is still critically discussed today.
21670.m: Switzerland too was involved in the trade in banned art.

21671.q: What is the research that clarifies the origin and ownership history of works of art, for example when Nazi-looted art is suspected, called?
21671.e: Provenance means origin. Museums use it to check whether works were unlawfully taken from their former owners, for example according to the Washington Principles of 1998.
21671.m: Provenance research clarifies where works of art come from.

21672.q: Which collection did the Kunstmuseum Bern inherit in 2014, sparking a wide debate about Nazi-looted art?
21672.e: Cornelius Gurlitt, son of an art dealer of the Nazi era, left his collection to the Kunstmuseum Bern. The museum accepted the inheritance and committed itself to provenance research.
21672.m: The Gurlitt bequest made looted art a big issue in Switzerland.

21673.q: Which controversial private collection has been on display in the extension of the Kunsthaus Zürich since 2021?
21673.e: Emil Bührle also made his fortune from arms sales in the Second World War, and the origin of some works is disputed. The new building by David Chipperfield opened in October 2021.
21673.m: The Bührle collection shows how closely art and history are linked.

21674.q: Which anonymous group of women artists has been protesting since 1985 in gorilla masks against the disadvantages women face in the art world?
21674.e: On posters, the Guerrilla Girls asked, for example, whether women have to be naked to get into the Metropolitan Museum. They back up their criticism with figures on exhibitions and collections.
21674.m: The Guerrilla Girls fight for equality with humour and figures.

21675.q: What does the term “patronage” (Mäzenatentum), named after the Roman Gaius Maecenas, refer to?
a: Private support for art and culture
State censorship of works of art
21675.e: Under Emperor Augustus, Maecenas supported poets such as Virgil and Horace. In the Renaissance, the Medici in Florence, for example, were important patrons.
21675.m: Patrons support art with private money.

21676.q: Which saying by Joseph Beuys belongs to his idea of “social sculpture”?
21676.e: Joseph Beuys saw shaping society itself as an artistic process. He put this idea into practice with the action “7000 Oaks” at documenta 7 (1982).
21676.m: For Beuys, everyone can help to shape society.

21677.q: Which painting did Pablo Picasso create in 1937 in response to the bombing of a Basque town in the Spanish Civil War?
21677.e: The large picture in black, white and grey was shown at the Paris World Exhibition in 1937. It is one of the best-known anti-war pictures and now hangs in the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid.
21677.m: Guernica is one of the best-known anti-war pictures.

21678.q: What do you call instruments that you hit with your hands or with sticks?
21678.e: Drums, xylophones and cymbals make a sound when you hit them. That is why they are called percussion instruments.
21678.m: You hit percussion instruments with your hands or with sticks.

21679.q: How do you make a wind instrument sound?
21679.e: In wind instruments, the air from your mouth makes the sound. Examples are the flute, trumpet and clarinet.
21679.m: Wind instruments sound because of the air you blow into them.

21680.q: Which very long wooden instrument is typical of the Swiss mountains?
21680.e: The alphorn is a long wind instrument made of wood. It is a well-known symbol of Swiss folk music.
21680.m: The alphorn is a long wooden instrument from the Swiss mountains.

21681.q: In which Swiss folk music instrument do you hit strings with small hammers?
21681.e: The hammered dulcimer is a box with lots of strings. You strike them with two small hammers, for example in Appenzell music.
21681.m: On the hammered dulcimer you hit strings with small hammers.

21682.q: What is the small accordion that is very popular in Swiss folk music called?
21682.e: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small button accordion. You pull and push the bellows while pressing buttons.
21682.m: The Schwyzerörgeli is a popular accordion in Swiss folk music.

21683.q: Which group of instruments does the harp belong to?
21683.e: The harp has lots of tight strings. You pluck them with your fingers.
21683.m: The harp is a string instrument you pluck with your fingers.

21684.q: Which small instrument do you hold to your mouth and blow and suck air through?
21684.e: The mouth organ is a small box with holes. Blowing in and breathing in make different notes.
21684.m: You play the mouth organ by breathing out and breathing in.

21685.q: What colours are the keys of a piano?
21685.e: A piano has wide white keys and narrow black keys. The black keys are in groups of two and three.
21685.m: The keys on a piano are black and white.

21686.q: How many keys does a normal piano have?
21686.e: A normal piano has 88 keys. 52 of them are white and 36 are black.

21687.q: What is inside a piano that makes the sound?
21687.e: Inside the piano there are lots of tight metal strings. When you press a key, you make a string sound.
21687.m: Tight metal strings sound inside a piano.

21688.q: What hits the strings inside a piano when you press a key?
21688.e: Each key moves a little hammer covered in felt. The hammer hits the string and bounces back.
21688.m: Inside a piano, little hammers hit the strings.

21689.q: What is the big piano with a long, lying-down case and a lid called?
21689.e: The grand piano is a big piano. Its strings lie flat and the lid can be opened.
21689.m: A grand piano is a big piano with strings lying flat.

21690.q: What do you press the pedals of a piano with?
21690.e: At the bottom of the piano there are pedals. You press them with your feet, for example to make the notes sound longer.
21690.m: You press the piano pedals with your feet.

21691.q: On which side of the piano keyboard are the low notes?
21691.e: On a piano, the low notes are on the left and the high notes on the right. The further right you go, the higher it sounds.
21691.m: On a piano, the low notes are on the left.

21692.q: What was the surname of the famous composer Wolfgang Amadeus, who played keyboard instruments as a small child?
21692.e: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart lived from 1756 to 1791. Even as a small child he performed as a child prodigy.
21692.m: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a famous musician even as a child.

21693.q: How many strings does a normal guitar have?
21693.e: A normal guitar has six strings. There are also special guitars with twelve strings.
21693.m: A normal guitar has six strings.

21694.q: How do you play the strings of a guitar?
21694.e: On a guitar, you pluck the strings with your fingers or strum them. With the other hand you press the strings onto the fingerboard.
21694.m: You pluck or strum guitar strings.

21695.q: What is the round hole in the middle of a classical guitar called?
21695.e: The sound comes out of the hollow body of the guitar through the sound hole. This makes it louder.
21695.m: The sound comes out of the guitar through the sound hole.

21696.q: What does an electric guitar need so that you can hear it loudly?
21696.e: An electric guitar usually has a solid body without a hollow space, so it sounds quiet. A cable takes the sound to an amplifier with a loudspeaker.
21696.m: An electric guitar needs an amplifier.

21697.q: What is the small flat piece you can use to strike guitar strings called?
21697.e: The plectrum is a small, flat piece, often made of plastic. You hold it between your thumb and index finger.
21697.m: You strike the strings with a plectrum.

21698.q: What is the small guitar with four strings known from Hawaii called?
21698.e: The ukulele is small and has four strings. It is especially popular in Hawaii.
21698.m: The ukulele is a small guitar with four strings.

21699.q: What is the body of a classical guitar usually made of?
21699.e: Classical guitars are made of wood. The wood helps to create a warm sound.
21699.m: A classical guitar is usually made of wood.

21700.q: What do you do if a guitar sounds out of tune?
21700.e: To tune it, you turn the tuning pegs at the head of the guitar. This makes the strings tighter or looser.
21700.m: A guitar that sounds out of tune needs tuning.

21701.q: What do you draw across the strings of a violin?
21701.e: The bow is a long wooden stick with lots of tight hairs. You draw it across the strings and the violin sounds.
21701.m: You play a violin with a bow.

21702.q: How many strings does a violin have?
21702.e: A violin has four strings. Each string sounds a different note.

21703.q: Where do you hold the violin while playing?
21703.e: The violin rests on the left shoulder and is held with the chin. That leaves the left hand free to press the strings.
21703.m: You hold the violin between your chin and shoulder.

21704.q: What is another word for violin?
21704.e: Fiddle is another, more informal word for violin. Both words mean the same instrument.
21704.m: A violin is also called a fiddle.

21705.q: Which instrument looks like a big violin and stands on the floor while being played?
21705.e: The cello is much bigger than the violin. You sit down and rest it on the floor on a spike.
21705.m: The cello is the violin's big sister.

21706.q: What do you rub onto the hairs of a violin bow so that it grips the strings well?
21706.e: You rub a solid resin onto the bow hairs. It is called rosin and makes the hairs grip.
21706.m: You rub resin onto a violin bow.

21707.q: What hair is a violin bow traditionally strung with?
21707.e: A violin bow is traditionally strung with hairs from horses' tails. One bow has over a hundred of these hairs.

21708.q: What do you call someone who plays the violin?
21708.e: Someone who plays the violin is a violinist. A pianist plays the piano.

21709.q: What do you often hit a drum with?
21709.e: Drumsticks are sticks made of wood. You can also play a drum with your hands.
21709.m: A drum is often played with drumsticks.

21710.q: What is the tight skin on a drum that you hit called?
21710.e: A drumhead is stretched over the drum. Today it is often made of plastic; in the past it was made of animal skin.
21710.m: A drum has a drumhead stretched over it.

21711.q: In which Swiss city do lots of people drum and play the piccolo at the famous carnival (Fasnacht)?
21711.e: At the Basel Fasnacht, lots of groups parade through the city drumming and playing piccolos. Since 2017 it has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
21711.m: The Basel Fasnacht is famous for drums and piccolos.

21712.q: What do you call several drums and cymbals together, as used in a band?
21712.e: A drum kit is made up of several drums and cymbals. One person plays them all together with hands and feet.
21712.m: A drum kit is made up of drums and cymbals.

21713.q: What is the big drum in a drum kit that you play with your foot called?
21713.e: The bass drum stands on the floor. A foot pedal hits a beater against the drumhead.
21713.m: You play the bass drum with your foot.

21714.q: What is the small hand drum with jingles around the edge called?
21714.e: The tambourine has a frame with small metal discs. When you shake or hit it, the jingles rattle.
21714.m: A tambourine has jingles around the edge.

21715.q: How does a big drum sound compared with a small one?
21715.e: Big drums have a big drumhead and a big body. That is why they sound lower than small drums.
21715.m: Big drums sound lower than small ones.

21716.q: What are the two small drums from Cuba that you play with your hands called?
21716.e: Bongos are two small drums joined together. You usually hold them between your legs and play with your fingers and hands.
21716.m: Bongos are two small hand drums from Cuba.

21717.q: Which flute do many children learn first at school?
21717.e: The recorder is easy to learn and not expensive. That is why many children play it at school.
21717.m: Many children learn the recorder first.

21718.q: How do you hold a flute (transverse flute) while playing?
21718.e: You hold the flute crossways, to the right side. You blow across a hole in the mouthpiece.
21718.m: You hold the flute sideways from your mouth.

21719.q: Which flute is made of several pipes lying side by side?
21719.e: Pan pipes have lots of pipes of different lengths. Each pipe makes a different note.
21719.m: Pan pipes have lots of pipes side by side.

21720.q: What are flutes usually made of today?
21720.e: Today flutes are usually made of metal, for example silver. In the past they were made of wood.
21720.m: Flutes today are usually made of metal.

21721.q: What is the small flute with very high notes called?
21721.e: The piccolo is about half as long as a normal flute. It sounds very high and bright.
21721.m: The piccolo is a small flute with very high notes.

21722.q: What do you do with your fingers on a recorder?
21722.e: The recorder has finger holes. Depending on which holes you cover, you get a different note.
21722.m: On a recorder, your fingers cover holes.

21723.q: What happens to the note of a recorder when you cover more holes?
21723.e: When more holes are covered, more air vibrates in the recorder. That is why the note sounds lower.
21723.m: Covering more holes makes the note lower.

21724.q: What is the small clay flute, often round like an egg, called?
21724.e: The ocarina is a vessel flute, often made of fired clay. It has several finger holes.
21724.m: The ocarina is a round flute made of clay.

21725.q: What material is a trumpet made of?
21725.e: A trumpet is made of metal, usually shiny brass. That is why it is called a brass instrument.
21725.m: A trumpet is made of metal.

21726.q: How many valves does a normal trumpet have?
21726.e: A trumpet has three valves. With them and your lips, you play different notes.
21726.m: A normal trumpet has three valves.

21727.q: Where do you blow into a trumpet?
21727.e: The mouthpiece is a small metal cup. You press your lips against it and blow.
21727.m: You blow into a trumpet through the mouthpiece.

21728.q: What is the wide, open end of the trumpet where the sound comes out called?
21728.e: At the end, the trumpet's tube widens like a funnel. That is where the sound comes out.
21728.m: The trumpet's sound comes out of the bell.

21729.q: What do your lips do when you play the trumpet?
21729.e: Your lips buzz and vibrate against the mouthpiece. This makes the sound that the trumpet makes louder.
21729.m: Your lips vibrate when you play the trumpet.

21730.q: Which brass instrument has a slide that you push back and forth?
21730.e: The trombone has a long slide. If you push it out, the note gets lower.
21730.m: The trombone has a slide that you push.

21731.q: Which is the biggest and lowest brass instrument in the orchestra?
21731.e: The tuba is very big and heavy. It plays the lowest notes of the brass section.
21731.m: The tuba is the lowest brass instrument.

21732.q: Which group does the trumpet belong to?
21732.e: The trumpet is made of metal and you blow into it. That is why it belongs to the brass instruments.
21732.m: The trumpet is a brass instrument.

21733.q: What is the person who stands in front of the orchestra and sets the beat called?
21733.e: The conductor shows with their arms the tempo and when each person plays. All the musicians watch the conductor.

21734.q: What does a conductor often hold in their hand while conducting?
21734.e: The baton is a thin stick, often white. It helps the musicians see the movements better.
21734.m: A conductor often conducts with a baton.

21735.q: Which instruments are there most of in an orchestra?
21735.e: Violins, violas, cellos and double basses are the biggest group in the orchestra. Often they make up more than half of the musicians.
21735.m: There are more string instruments than any other in an orchestra.

21736.q: What is a big orchestra with lots of musicians called?
21736.e: A symphony orchestra often has 60 to 100 members. It plays string, wind and percussion instruments.
21736.m: A symphony orchestra is a big orchestra.

21737.q: What are the big kettle drums in an orchestra called?
21737.e: Timpani look like big kettles with a drumhead. They can be tuned to particular notes.
21737.m: Timpani are big kettle drums in the orchestra.

21738.q: Where do the violins usually sit in an orchestra?
a: At the front near the conductor
21738.e: The violins usually sit at the front, to the left of the conductor. Loud instruments such as the timpani are further back.
21738.m: The violins usually sit at the front of the orchestra.

21739.q: Which famous orchestra is based in Zurich?
21739.e: The Tonhalle Orchestra plays in the Tonhalle in Zurich by the lake. It is one of the best-known orchestras in Switzerland.
21739.m: The Tonhalle Orchestra is a famous orchestra from Zurich.

21740.q: In many Swiss villages, what is the club where people mainly play wind instruments called?
21740.e: In the village band, people from the village play wind instruments and drums. It often performs at festivals, for example on 1 August.
21740.m: Many Swiss villages have a village band.

21741.q: What is a group that sings together called?
21741.e: A choir is a group of singers. Many schools have their own choir.
21741.m: A choir is a group that sings together.

21743.q: What in your throat vibrates when you sing and makes the sound?
21743.e: The vocal cords are in the voice box. The air from the lungs makes them vibrate.
21743.m: When you sing, the vocal cords in your throat vibrate.

21744.q: What do you call a piece of music that two people sing together?
21744.e: Duet comes from the word for two. In a quartet, four people sing.
21744.m: A duet is sung by two people.

21745.q: What is the highest voice of women and children in a choir called?
21745.e: The soprano sings the highest notes in the choir. The alto is the lower female voice.
21745.m: The soprano is the highest voice in the choir.

21746.q: What is the lowest male voice called?
21746.e: The bass sings the lowest notes. The tenor is the higher male voice.
21746.m: The bass is the lowest male voice.

21747.q: What is it called when one person sings or plays completely alone?
21747.e: Solo means alone. In a solo you hear only one single voice or one single instrument.
21747.m: In a solo, one person sings or plays alone.

21748.q: What do you call the steady beat in music that you can clap along to?
21748.e: The pulse is the basic beat of the music. It goes on evenly like the ticking of a clock.
21748.m: The pulse is the steady basic beat of music.

21749.q: Which device ticks steadily and helps you practise at the right tempo?
21749.e: A metronome ticks as fast as you set it. This helps you learn to play evenly.
21749.m: A metronome helps you practise at the right tempo.

21750.q: What do you call the speed of a piece of music?
21750.e: The tempo tells you how fast or slow the music is. A march, for example, has a brisk tempo.
21750.m: The tempo is the speed of the music.

21751.q: What is a place in music where you stop playing for a moment called?
21751.e: During a rest you are silent. Rests also have an exact length and are part of the rhythm.
21751.m: During a rest, you stop playing for a moment.

21752.q: Which note lasts longer, a minim (half note) or a quaver (eighth note)?
21752.e: A minim lasts as long as four quavers. So it sounds much longer.
21752.m: A minim lasts longer than a quaver.

21753.q: How many crotchets (quarter notes) together last as long as a semibreve (whole note)?
21753.e: A semibreve is divided into four quarters. So you need four crotchets.
21753.m: Four crotchets last as long as a semibreve.

21754.q: In which dance do you always count “one, two, three”?
21754.e: The waltz is in three-four time. So you always count to three and then start again.
21754.m: In a waltz you always count to three.

21755.q: Vertical lines divide the notes into sections of equal length. What are these sections called?
21755.e: The vertical lines are called bar lines. Between two bar lines there is one bar.
21755.m: Bar lines divide music into bars.

a: A series of notes one after another
21756.e: A melody is made of notes that sound one after another. You can sing or whistle it.
21756.m: A melody is a series of notes one after another.

21757.q: In Switzerland and other German-speaking countries, what is the note after A in the scale C, D, E, F, G, A called?
21757.e: In German-speaking countries, including Switzerland, the note after A is called “H”. In English it is called B.
21757.m: In Switzerland, the note after A is called “H”.

21758.q: How many lines does a musical stave have?
21758.e: Notes are written on five horizontal lines. You write them on the lines or in the spaces.

21759.q: What is the clef that looks like a curly G called?
21759.e: The treble clef is also called the G clef. It comes before notes for higher sounds, for example for the flute or violin.
21759.m: The treble clef looks like a curly G.

21760.q: What is a song where groups start one after another with the same melody called?
21760.e: In a round, one group starts and the next joins in later with the same melody. This way several voices sound together.
21760.m: In a round, groups sing the same melody at different times.

21761.q: What is the part of a song that keeps coming back with the same words called?
21761.e: The chorus comes after each verse with the same words and the same melody. The verses have different words.
21761.m: The chorus keeps coming back the same in a song.

21762.q: What is a series of notes that climbs step by step like a staircase called?
21762.e: A scale goes up or down note by note. It is like a ladder made of notes.
21762.m: A scale climbs note by note like a staircase.

21763.q: What do you call a person who invents and writes down melodies and whole pieces of music?
21763.e: A composer writes new music. Other musicians can then play it from the sheet music.
21763.m: A composer invents and writes music.

21764.q: Which instrument sounds lower, the double bass or the violin?
21764.e: The double bass is the biggest string instrument in the orchestra. It has long, thick strings and so sounds very low.
21764.m: The double bass sounds much lower than the violin.

21765.q: How does a short, thin string sound compared with a long, thick string?
21765.e: Short, thin strings vibrate faster. That is why they sound higher.

21766.q: Who usually has the lower voice?
21766.e: Grown men have bigger vocal cords. That is why their voices are usually lower.
21766.m: Grown men usually have lower voices.

21767.q: What happens to the sound when something vibrates faster?
21767.e: A sound is made by vibrations. The faster something vibrates, the higher the note.

21768.q: Where are high notes on the stave?
21768.e: In written music, higher notes are written higher up. Low notes are lower down.
21768.m: High notes are written higher up on the stave.

21769.q: You tap a glass of water. How does it sound if you pour in more water?
21769.e: The water slows down the glass's vibration, so it vibrates more slowly. That is why the note gets lower.
21769.m: More water in the glass makes the note lower.

21770.q: What is the metal device that always sounds exactly one note for tuning called?
21770.e: The tuning fork looks like a fork with two prongs. When you strike it, it always sounds at the same pitch.
21770.m: A tuning fork always gives the same note for tuning.

21771.e: Piano is Italian and means quiet. In sheet music it is often written as just p.

21772.e: Forte is Italian and means strong. In music it means loud, written as f for short.

21773.e: Crescendo means growing. The music gets louder step by step.
21773.m: In a crescendo, the music gets louder and louder.

21774.q: What protects your ears from very loud music?
21774.e: You put earplugs into your ears. They make loud music quieter and protect your hearing.
21774.m: Earplugs protect your ears from loud music.

21775.q: In which unit is loudness measured?
21775.e: Loudness is measured in decibels, dB for short. A whisper has only a few decibels, a concert a great many.

21776.q: Which sign in sheet music stands for “very quiet”?
21776.e: The sign pp stands for pianissimo and means very quiet. The sign ff means very loud.
21776.m: The sign pp means very quiet.

21777.q: What can happen if you often listen to very loud music?
21777.e: Very loud music can damage the tiny sensory cells in the ear. Then you hear less well, sometimes for ever.
21777.m: Music that is too loud can damage your hearing.

21778.q: How many crotchets (quarter notes) last as long as one semibreve (whole note)?
21778.e: A semibreve can be divided into two minims or four crotchets. So four crotchets fill one semibreve.
21778.m: Four crotchets together make one semibreve.

21779.q: Which sign raises a note by a semitone?
21779.e: A sharp in front of a note raises it by a semitone, so C becomes C sharp. The flat lowers a note by a semitone.
21779.m: A sharp makes a note a semitone higher.

21780.q: Which clef is also called the G clef?
21780.e: The treble clef shows that the note G is on the second line from the bottom. That is why it is also called the G clef.
21780.m: The treble clef shows where the note G is.

21781.q: What does a dot to the right of a note do?
a: The note becomes half as long again
The note becomes twice as long
The note becomes half as short
21781.e: The dot lengthens a note by half its value. So a dotted minim lasts three crotchets.
21781.m: A dot next to a note lengthens it by half its value.

21782.q: In German-speaking countries, what is the note called that is called “B” in English?
21782.e: In German, the notes are called C, D, E, F, G, A, H. The English “B” matches the German H; the German B is the note H lowered by a semitone, B flat.
21782.m: The English note B is called H in German.

21783.q: How many quavers (eighth notes) last as long as one minim (half note)?
21783.e: A minim lasts two crotchets, and each crotchet is made of two quavers. So 2 times 2 makes 4 quavers.
21783.m: A minim is as long as four quavers.

21784.q: How many different notes does a major scale have?
21784.e: A major scale has seven different degrees. The eighth note is the starting note again, an octave higher.
21784.m: A major scale has seven different notes.

21785.q: Which major scale has no sharps or flats at all?
21785.e: C major is made only of the natural notes C, D, E, F, G, A, B. On a piano you play it with only the white keys.
21785.m: C major needs neither sharps nor flats.

21786.q: Between which degrees of a major scale are the semitone steps?
21786.e: In major the steps go tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. So the semitones are between the 3rd and 4th and the 7th and 8th degrees.
21786.m: In major, the semitones are between the third and fourth and the seventh and eighth degrees.

21787.q: Which minor key is the relative minor of C major?
21787.e: The relative minor key starts a minor third below the major key's starting note. That is why A minor, like C major, has no sharps or flats.
21787.m: Every major key has a minor key with the same key signature.

21788.q: How many semitone steps are there in an octave?
21788.e: If you count all the white and black keys on a piano from C to the next C, you get twelve semitone steps.
21788.m: An octave is divided into twelve semitones.

21789.q: How many different notes does a pentatonic scale have?
21789.e: “Penta” means five in Greek. The pentatonic scale has no semitone steps and is common in folk music all over the world.
21789.m: The pentatonic scale is a scale of five notes.

21790.q: How many sharps are there in the key signature of G major?
21790.e: G major needs an F sharp so that the semitones are in the right place. That is why there is a sharp at the start of every line.
21790.m: G major has one sharp, F sharp.

21791.q: How many crotchet beats are there in a bar of 3/4 time?
21791.e: A bar of 3/4 time has three beats, and each one is a crotchet. You count “one, two, three”.
21791.m: A bar of 3/4 time has three crotchet beats.

21792.q: Which time signature is typical of the waltz?
21792.e: The waltz is a turning dance with an accent on the first of three beats. You count “one, two, three”.
21792.m: The waltz is in three-four time.

21793.q: What is an incomplete bar at the start of a piece of music called?
21793.e: If a piece begins before the first strong beat, it is called an upbeat. The missing beats are usually made up in the last bar.
21793.m: An upbeat is an incomplete bar at the start of a piece.

21794.q: Which time signature is often written with the sign “C”?
21794.e: The sign “C” stands for four-four time, also called common time. A C with a line through it, on the other hand, means cut time (alla breve).
21794.m: The sign C means four-four time.

21795.q: What is the vertical line in sheet music that separates the bars called?
21795.e: The bar line runs vertically through the whole stave. A double bar line marks the end of a section or piece.
21795.m: Bar lines divide music into bars.

21796.q: How many quavers (eighth notes) fit into a bar of 6/8 time?
21796.e: A bar of 6/8 time holds six quavers. You usually feel it as two groups of three quavers.
21796.m: A bar of 6/8 time has room for six quavers.

21797.q: What does the bottom number of a time signature tell you?
a: The note value of one beat
21797.e: The bottom number gives the note value that is counted, for example 4 for crotchets. The top number says how many of them fit in a bar.
21797.m: The bottom number of a time signature gives the note value counted.

21798.q: Which country does reggae music come from?
21798.e: Reggae began in Jamaica in the late 1960s. Bob Marley made it famous around the world.

21799.q: In which country did the tango mainly develop?
21799.e: The tango developed at the end of the 19th century on the Río de la Plata, mainly in Buenos Aires and also in Montevideo (Uruguay).
21799.m: The tango comes from Buenos Aires in Argentina.

21800.q: What is the often melancholy song style from Portugal called?
21800.e: Fado began in Lisbon in the 19th century. It is usually accompanied by guitars and is part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
21800.m: Fado is a sad song style from Portugal.

21801.q: Which country does the samba come from?
21801.e: The samba developed in Brazil, especially in Rio de Janeiro. It has African roots and shapes the carnival in Rio.

21802.q: Which instrument is typical of Swiss Ländler music?
21802.e: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small accordion and the most important instrument in Ländler music. The clarinet and double bass often play along.
21802.m: The Schwyzerörgeli belongs to Ländler music.

21803.q: What is the singing style in which you switch quickly between chest voice and head voice called?
21803.e: When yodelling, the voice jumps quickly back and forth between the low chest voice and the high head voice. Yodelling is especially common in Switzerland and Austria.
21803.m: When yodelling, you switch between chest voice and head voice.

21804.q: Which electronic dance music began in Chicago in the 1980s?
21804.e: House began in clubs in Chicago and is named after the club “Warehouse”. Techno began at about the same time in Detroit.

21805.q: Which three composers are regarded as the great Viennese classical composers?
21805.e: Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Ludwig van Beethoven all worked in Vienna. They shaped the music of the Classical period especially strongly.
21805.m: Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven are the three Viennese classical composers.

21806.q: Roughly when was the Viennese Classical period?
a: In the late 18th and early 19th century
In the second half of the 19th century
In the first half of the 20th century
21806.e: The heart of the Viennese Classical period lies roughly between 1780 and Beethoven's death in 1827. The Classical period as a whole is usually dated from about 1750 to the early 19th century.
21806.m: The Viennese Classical period flourished in the late 18th and early 19th century.

21807.q: Which composer is often called the “father of the symphony”?
21807.e: Joseph Haydn wrote over a hundred symphonies and developed the form decisively. He is also regarded as the father of the string quartet.
21807.m: Joseph Haydn is regarded as the father of the symphony.

21808.q: How many movements does a classical symphony usually have?
21808.e: A classical symphony usually has four movements: a fast first movement, a slow movement, a minuet and a fast finale.
21808.m: A classical symphony usually has four movements.

21809.q: Which instruments play in a string quartet?
a: Violin, viola, cello and double bass
21809.e: The classical string quartet is made up of a first and second violin, a viola and a cello.
21809.m: A string quartet has two violins, a viola and a cello.

21810.q: What do you call the separate, complete parts of a symphony?
21810.e: A symphony is made up of several movements, each with its own tempo and character. There is a short pause between the movements.
21810.m: A symphony is divided into movements.

21811.q: Which keyboard instrument increasingly replaced the harpsichord in the Classical period?
21811.e: In the fortepiano, little hammers strike the strings; in the harpsichord they are plucked. This lets you play loudly and quietly, hence the name pianoforte.
21811.m: On the fortepiano you can play loudly or quietly depending on your touch.

21812.q: In which city is jazz said to have begun?
21812.e: Jazz began around 1900 in New Orleans in the south of the USA. African American, European and Caribbean musical traditions mixed there.
21812.m: New Orleans is the birthplace of jazz.

21813.q: What do you call making up music on the spot while playing?
21813.e: When improvising, musicians make up the melody in the moment. Improvisation is at the heart of jazz.
21813.m: Improvisation means making up music on the spot while playing.

21814.q: Which jazz trumpeter had the nickname “Satchmo”?
21814.e: Louis Armstrong (1901 to 1971) came from New Orleans. He was famous for his trumpet playing and his gravelly voice.

21815.q: Which jazz style of the 1930s was played by large big bands?
21815.e: In the swing era, big bands such as those of Benny Goodman or Duke Ellington played dance music. Bebop only began in the 1940s.
21815.m: Swing is the jazz of the great big bands.

21816.q: Which musical form, usually with 12 bars, is an important root of jazz?
21816.e: The blues began among African Americans in the south of the USA. The typical blues pattern has twelve bars.
21816.m: The blues pattern usually has twelve bars.

21817.q: Which jazz singer was called the “First Lady of Song”?
21817.e: Ella Fitzgerald (1917 to 1996) was famous for her clear voice and her scat singing. She won several Grammys.
21817.m: Ella Fitzgerald was the First Lady of Song.

21818.q: Which famous music festival has taken place on Lake Geneva since 1967?
21818.e: The Montreux Jazz Festival was founded in 1967 by Claude Nobs. It is one of the best-known music festivals in the world.
21818.m: The Montreux Jazz Festival takes place on Lake Geneva.

21819.q: Which musician was called the “King of Rock and Roll”?
21819.e: Elvis Presley (1935 to 1977) became the biggest star of rock and roll in the 1950s.
21819.m: Elvis Presley was the King of Rock and Roll.

21820.q: Which city did the Beatles come from?
21820.e: The Beatles were formed in Liverpool in 1960. John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr are regarded as one of the most successful bands in history.

21821.q: Which instrument especially shapes the sound of rock music?
21821.e: The electric guitar is played through an amplifier and can sound loud and distorted. Together with bass and drums, it is the core of a rock band.
21821.m: The electric guitar is the typical instrument of rock music.

21822.q: In which decade did rock and roll begin?
21822.e: Rock and roll began in the USA in the early 1950s, growing out of rhythm and blues and country.
21822.m: Rock and roll began in the 1950s.

21823.q: Which Swiss hard rock band from Ticino is named after an Alpine pass?
21823.e: The band was formed in Ticino in the early 1990s and named itself after the Gotthard Pass. It had many number-one albums in Switzerland.
21823.m: The hard rock band Gotthard comes from Ticino.

21824.q: Which British band released the song “Bohemian Rhapsody” in 1975?
21824.e: “Bohemian Rhapsody” came out in 1975 on Queen's album “A Night at the Opera”. The singer was Freddie Mercury.
21824.m: Bohemian Rhapsody is a song by the band Queen.

21825.q: Which style of rock in the 1970s was known for short, fast and raw songs?
21825.e: Punk began in the mid-1970s in New York and London. Bands like the Ramones deliberately played simply, loudly and fast.
21825.m: Punk rock is short, fast and raw.

21826.q: Which singer was called the “King of Pop”?
21826.e: Michael Jackson (1958 to 2009) was one of the most successful musicians ever. His 1982 album “Thriller” is considered the best-selling album in the world.
21826.m: Michael Jackson was the King of Pop.

21827.q: Which word does the name “pop” come from?
21827.e: “Pop” comes from the English word “popular”, meaning well liked by many people. Pop music aims to appeal to a wide audience.

21828.q: In which Swiss city was the first Eurovision Song Contest held in 1956?
21828.e: The first Eurovision Song Contest took place in Lugano on 24 May 1956. It was won by the Swiss singer Lys Assia.
21828.m: The first Eurovision Song Contest took place in Ticino.

21829.q: Who won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 2024?
21829.e: Nemo from Biel won the contest in Malmö in 2024 with the song “The Code”. It was Switzerland's third win.
21829.m: Nemo won the Eurovision Song Contest for Switzerland in 2024.

21830.q: In which Swiss city was the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest held?
21830.e: Because Switzerland won in 2024, it hosted the contest in 2025. It took place in May 2025 in the St. Jakobshalle in Basel.
21830.m: The 2025 Eurovision Song Contest took place in Basel.

21831.q: What do you call the part of a song that comes back several times the same?
21831.e: The chorus is repeated between the verses with the same melody and usually the same words. That is why it sticks in your head.
21831.m: The chorus is the part of a song that keeps coming back.

21832.q: What is the best-known music award in the USA called?
21832.e: The Grammy has been awarded by the Recording Academy since 1959. The Oscar is a film award, the Emmy a television award and the Tony a theatre award.
21832.m: The Grammy is the best-known music award in the USA.

21833.q: In which city did hip-hop begin in the 1970s?
21833.e: Hip-hop began in the 1970s in the Bronx, a part of New York. Young people held block parties in the street there.
21833.m: Hip-hop began in the Bronx in New York.

21834.q: Which of these is NOT one of the classic elements of hip-hop?
21834.e: The classic elements of hip-hop are rap, DJing, breakdance and graffiti. Ballet is not one of them.
21834.m: Hip-hop includes rap, DJing, breakdance and graffiti.

21835.q: Which DJ is regarded as the founder of hip-hop because of a party in 1973?
21835.e: DJ Kool Herc played records at a party in the Bronx on 11 August 1973. He repeated the rhythm breaks of records so that people could dance for longer.
21835.m: DJ Kool Herc is regarded as the founder of hip-hop.

21836.q: What is a rapper in hip-hop also called?
21836.e: MC stands for “Master of Ceremonies”. Originally the MC got the crowd going; later the word came to mean rapper.

21837.q: What does a DJ do when “scratching”?
a: Moves the record back and forth
21837.e: When scratching, the DJ moves the record back and forth by hand. This makes a scratching sound.
21837.m: When scratching, a record is moved back and forth by hand.

21838.q: What do you call a section of someone else's recording that is used in a new song?
21838.e: A sample is a short piece of an existing recording, for example a drum rhythm. In hip-hop, samples are often used as the basis for new beats.
21838.m: A sample is a section of someone else's recording.

21839.q: What is the acrobatic hip-hop dance style with moves on the floor called?
21839.e: Breakdance began in the Bronx. Dancers spin on their backs, heads or hands. In Paris in 2024, breaking was part of the Summer Olympics for the first time.
21839.m: Breakdance is the dance of hip-hop.

21840.q: Which is the lowest string instrument in the orchestra?
21840.e: The double bass is the biggest and lowest string instrument. It is played standing or sitting on a high stool.
21840.m: The double bass is the lowest string instrument.

21841.q: Which group of instruments does the flute belong to?
21841.e: The flute is a woodwind instrument, even though it is usually made of metal today. What matters is how the sound is made, not the material.
21841.m: The flute belongs to the woodwind instruments.

21842.q: Which instrument usually gives the note A for tuning in an orchestra?
21842.e: The oboe has a clear, piercing sound that hardly changes in pitch. That is why the other instruments tune to its A.
21842.m: The oboe gives the orchestra its tuning note.

21843.q: What is the person who leads an orchestra called?
21843.e: The conductor uses the baton to show tempo, entries and volume. The leader heads the first violins.

21844.q: Which brass instrument changes pitch with a slide instead of valves?
21844.e: On the trombone you push the slide out or in. This makes the tube longer or shorter and the note lower or higher.
21844.m: The trombone has a slide instead of valves.

21845.q: Which percussion instrument in the orchestra can be tuned to a particular pitch?
21845.e: On the timpani, the drumhead can be tightened or loosened, often with a pedal. This makes a particular note sound.
21845.m: The timpani can be tuned to a note.

21846.q: How many strings does a violin have?
21846.e: The violin has four strings, tuned to G, D, A and E. It is the highest string instrument in the orchestra.

21847.q: In which city is the Orchestre de la Suisse Romande based?
21847.e: The Orchestre de la Suisse Romande was founded in 1918 by Ernest Ansermet. It plays mainly in the Victoria Hall in Geneva.
21847.m: The Orchestre de la Suisse Romande is based in Geneva.

21848.q: In which city was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart born?
21848.e: Mozart was born on 27 January 1756 in the Getreidegasse in Salzburg. The house where he was born is now a museum.

21849.q: How old was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart when he died?
21849.e: Mozart lived from January 1756 to December 1791 and died in Vienna aged only 35. Even so, he created over 600 works.
21849.m: Mozart died at the age of 35.

21850.q: In which Mozart opera does the bird-catcher Papageno appear?
21850.e: “The Magic Flute” was first performed in Vienna in 1791. Papageno is a funny bird-catcher in a costume of feathers.
21850.m: Papageno is a character from The Magic Flute.

21851.q: What was the name of Mozart's father, who taught him as a child?
21851.e: Leopold Mozart was a violinist and composer at the court in Salzburg. He travelled all over Europe with his children Wolfgang and Nannerl.
21851.m: Mozart's father Leopold was his first teacher.

21852.q: Which of Mozart's works was unfinished when he died?
21852.e: Mozart was working on a mass for the dead until his death. His pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed the work.

21853.q: What is the catalogue by which Mozart's works are numbered called?
21853.e: Ludwig Ritter von Köchel put Mozart's works in time order in 1862. That is why they have the abbreviation K (or KV) with a number.
21853.m: Mozart's works are numbered according to the Köchel catalogue.

21854.q: Roughly how old was Mozart when he composed his first little pieces?
21854.e: At about the age of five, Mozart was already writing his first little piano pieces, which his father wrote down. He was regarded as a child prodigy.
21854.m: Mozart was composing even as a small child.

21855.q: In which city was Ludwig van Beethoven born?
21855.e: Beethoven was born in Bonn on the Rhine. As a young man he moved to Vienna and stayed there until his death.

21856.q: In which year was Ludwig van Beethoven born?
21856.e: Beethoven was born in December 1770; the exact date is not known for certain. He was baptised on 17 December 1770.

21857.q: What condition did Beethoven suffer from from his late twenties onwards?
21857.e: Beethoven became more and more hard of hearing and in the end was almost deaf. Even so, he kept on composing, because he heard the music in his head.
21857.m: Beethoven kept composing even when he was almost deaf.

21858.q: How many symphonies did Beethoven complete?
21858.e: Beethoven completed nine symphonies. Especially well known are the 3rd (“Eroica”), the 5th and the 6th (“Pastoral”).

21859.q: Which poem by Friedrich Schiller did Beethoven set to music in the final movement of a symphony?
21859.e: In the last movement of his Symphony No. 9, Beethoven used a choir and solo singers, which was very unusual in a symphony at the time. It was first performed in Vienna in 1824.
21859.m: Beethoven set Schiller's poem Ode to Joy to music.

21860.q: Which official anthem is based on a melody by Beethoven?
21860.e: In 1972 the Council of Europe chose a melody from Beethoven’s 9th Symphony as its anthem. Since 1985 it has also been the anthem of the European Union.
21860.m: The European anthem comes from Beethoven.

21861.q: Which instrument did Beethoven write the famous piece “Für Elise” for?
21861.e: “Für Elise” is a short piano piece that many piano pupils learn. Beethoven was an excellent pianist himself.
21861.m: “Für Elise” is a piano piece by Beethoven.

21862.q: In which town was Johann Sebastian Bach born in 1685?
21862.e: Bach was born on 21 March 1685 in Eisenach in Thuringia. He came from a large family of musicians.

21863.q: In which city was Bach Thomaskantor (cantor of St Thomas) from 1723?
21863.e: From 1723 Bach, as Thomaskantor, directed the church music in Leipzig and the St Thomas Boys Choir. He stayed there until his death in 1750.

21864.q: Which instrument was Bach especially famous for playing during his lifetime?
21864.e: Bach was one of the best organists of his time and also tested new organs. He wrote many works for this instrument.

21865.q: Which period of music does Johann Sebastian Bach belong to?
21865.e: Bach is one of the most important composers of the Baroque. The year of his death, 1750, is often seen as the end of this period.

21866.q: What job did many members of Johann Sebastian Bach’s family have?
21866.e: Over generations the Bach family produced many organists, cantors and town musicians. Several of Johann Sebastian’s sons also became well-known composers.
21866.m: Bach came from a large family of musicians.

21867.q: What is a fugue, like the ones Bach often composed?
a: A piece in which a theme enters in several voices one after another
A song with only one voice
21867.e: In a fugue one voice introduces a theme, then the other voices take it up one after another. Bach was a master of this form.
21867.m: In a fugue a theme travels through several voices.

21868.q: Bach’s music is often polyphonic. What does that mean?
a: Several melodies sound at the same time
21868.e: In polyphonic music several independent melodies run at the same time and still fit together. Bach mastered this art like hardly anyone else.
21868.m: Polyphonic means several melodies sound at the same time.

21869.q: Which period of music followed the Baroque?
21869.e: The order of the great periods is Middle Ages, Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Romantic. The Classical period began around 1750 and lasted into the early 19th century.
21869.m: The Classical period followed the Baroque.

21870.q: What are the syllables do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti used for?
a: Singing the notes of a scale
21870.e: These syllables are used to sing the steps of a scale. The idea goes back to the monk Guido of Arezzo in the 11th century, who began with ut, re, mi.
21870.m: Do, re, mi are used to sing the scale.

21871.q: What is the single-line Latin church singing of the Middle Ages called?
21871.e: Gregorian chant is sung in a single melodic line without instruments. It is named after Pope Gregory the Great.
21871.m: Gregorian chant is church singing in a single melodic line.

21872.q: Which sound-recording device did Thomas Edison invent in 1877?
21872.e: Edison’s phonograph recorded sound on a cylinder covered with tinfoil. The gramophone with flat records only followed in 1887, from Emile Berliner.
21872.m: The phonograph was the first machine that could record sounds.

21873.q: Which period do Frédéric Chopin and Robert Schumann belong to?
21873.e: The Romantic period began in the early 19th century and shaped music until around 1900. Composers like Chopin and Schumann expressed strong feelings in their music.
21873.m: Chopin and Schumann are Romantic composers.

21874.q: Which 12th-century nun is one of the first female composers known by name?
21874.e: Hildegard of Bingen (1098 to 1179) was an abbess, scholar and composer. Many of her sacred songs have survived.
21874.m: Hildegard of Bingen was composing as early as the Middle Ages.

21875.q: Roughly when did the Baroque period in music begin?
21875.e: The Baroque lasted from about 1600 to 1750. The first operas were written then, for example by Claudio Monteverdi.
21875.m: The Baroque period in music began around 1600.

21877.q: How many semitones does a perfect fifth span?
21877.e: From C to G there are seven semitones. The perfect fourth has five, the tritone six.
21877.m: A perfect fifth consists of seven semitones.

21878.q: Which interval results from inverting a major third?
21878.e: When inverting, the intervals add up to an octave (3 plus 6 makes 9), and major becomes minor. So C to E becomes E to C, a minor sixth.
21878.m: Inverting turns a major interval into a minor one.

21879.q: Which major key has three sharps in its key signature?
21879.e: The sharps are added in the order F♯, C♯, G♯. Three sharps give A major.
21879.m: A major has the three sharps F♯, C♯ and G♯.

21880.q: Which minor key is the relative minor of E♭ major?
21880.e: The relative minor lies a minor third below the major key. Both share the three flats.
21880.m: Relative keys have the same key signature.

21881.q: Which interval is called the tritone?
21881.e: The tritone spans three whole tones, for example F to B. It divides the octave exactly in half.
21881.m: The tritone consists of three whole tones.

21882.q: Which church mode corresponds to a major scale with a minor seventh?
21882.e: Mixolydian starts on G and uses only natural notes, so F lies a minor seventh above G. This scale is common in rock and blues.
21882.m: Mixolydian sounds like major with a lowered seventh degree.

21883.q: What frequency ratio does a perfect octave have?
21883.e: A note an octave higher vibrates twice as fast. 3:2 is the fifth, 4:3 the fourth.

21884.q: At what frequency does the ISO 16 standard set concert pitch A (a¹)?
21884.e: ISO 16 sets the tuning note at 440 hertz. In practice many orchestras tune a little higher, baroque ensembles often lower.

21885.q: What do you call shifting the accent onto a beat that is normally unstressed?
21885.e: In syncopation a weak part of the bar is stressed, often by means of a tie. It is typical of jazz and ragtime.
21885.m: Syncopation shifts the accent onto weak beats.

21886.q: What function does the triad on the fifth degree of a major key have?
21886.e: In functional harmony the chord on degree V is called the dominant. It pulls strongly back to the tonic.
21886.m: The dominant is on the fifth degree.

21887.q: What do you call a cadence that ends on the dominant?
21887.e: The imperfect (half) cadence stays open on the dominant. It works like a comma, not a full stop.
21887.m: An imperfect cadence leaves the music open on the dominant.

21888.q: In an interrupted cadence in a major key, where does the dominant typically lead?
21888.e: Instead of the expected tonic, the dominant goes to degree VI, the relative minor of the tonic. The listener’s expectation is deceived.
21888.m: The interrupted cadence deceives the expectation of the tonic.

21889.q: Which chord progression forms a plagal cadence?
21889.e: The plagal cadence goes from degree IV to degree I. It is known from hymns as the “Amen cadence”.
21889.m: The plagal cadence goes from the subdominant to the tonic.

21890.q: Which part-writing counts as a mistake in classical four-part harmony?
21890.e: Two voices that move in parallel a perfect fifth apart lose their independence. That is why parallel fifths and octaves are forbidden.
21890.m: In strict harmony, parallel fifths are forbidden.

21891.q: By how many accidentals in the key signature do two neighbouring major keys on the circle of fifths differ?
21891.e: Each step on the circle of fifths adds a sharp or removes a flat. Neighbouring keys are therefore closely related.
21891.m: Neighbours on the circle of fifths differ by one accidental.

21892.q: On which root is the Neapolitan sixth chord built in C minor?
21892.e: The Neapolitan is the major triad on the flattened second degree, so in C minor D♭, F, A♭. It usually appears as a sixth chord with F in the bass.
21892.m: The Neapolitan is built on the flattened second degree.

21893.q: In harmony, what is meant by modulation?
21893.e: In a modulation a new tonal centre is established, often via a chord that belongs to both keys. This is called a pivot chord.
21893.m: A modulation leads into a new key.

21894.q: Which intervals make up a diminished triad?
21894.e: The diminished triad, for example B, D, F, consists of two minor thirds. There is a tritone between root and fifth.
21894.m: The diminished triad stacks two minor thirds.

21895.q: Which intervals make up an augmented triad?
21895.e: The augmented triad, for example C-E-G♯, consists of two major thirds. It divides the octave into three equal parts.
21895.m: The augmented triad stacks two major thirds.

21896.q: What is the inversion of a triad called in which the third is in the bass?
21896.e: If the third is at the bottom, the root on top forms a sixth with the bass. Hence the name sixth chord.
21896.m: With the third in the bass you get a first-inversion (sixth) chord.

21897.q: Which notes make up the dominant seventh chord in C major?
21897.e: The dominant of C major is G major, with the minor seventh F added. This chord typically resolves to C major.
21897.m: The dominant seventh chord in C major is G-B-D-F.

21898.q: Which notes make up the chord Cmaj7?
21898.e: Cmaj7 is a major triad with a major seventh. This lies a semitone below the root.
21898.m: A major seventh chord contains the major seventh.

21899.q: In a sus4 chord, what replaces the third?
21899.e: “sus” stands for suspended. The fourth replaces the third, which is why the chord is neither major nor minor.
21899.m: A sus4 chord has a fourth instead of a third.

21900.q: What does a power chord in rock music consist of?
21900.e: The power chord, written for example as C5, leaves out the third. With distortion it therefore sounds clearer than a full triad.
21900.m: A power chord consists of root and fifth without the third.

21901.q: How many different notes does a complete ninth chord contain?
21901.e: A ninth chord stacks root, third, fifth, seventh and ninth. That makes five different notes.
21901.m: A complete ninth chord has five notes.

21902.q: In sonata form, which section follows the exposition?
21902.e: After the themes are introduced, they are worked out and modulated in the development. Then the recapitulation returns.
21902.m: In the development the themes are worked out.

21903.q: What is the polyphonic form called in which a theme enters in each voice in turn and is skilfully worked out?
21903.e: In a fugue one voice introduces the theme, then the other voices enter one after another with the same theme. Johann Sebastian Bach is regarded as a great master of this form.
21903.m: In a fugue the theme enters in each voice in turn.

21904.q: Which baroque composer wrote “The Art of Fugue” and “The Well-Tempered Clavier”?
21904.e: In “The Well-Tempered Clavier” Bach wrote preludes and fugues in all 24 keys. “The Art of Fugue” shows how many ways a single theme can be worked out.
21904.m: Bach is regarded as the master of the fugue.

21905.q: In twelve-tone technique, what is the basic row read backwards called?
21905.e: Besides the basic row there are the retrograde (backwards), the inversion (mirrored intervals) and the retrograde inversion. All of them can be transposed to twelve levels.
21905.m: The retrograde is the row read backwards.

21906.q: What form scheme does a classical rondo typically have?
21906.e: In a rondo the refrain A keeps coming back, with changing episodes in between. The form is common in final movements.
21906.m: In a rondo the refrain keeps coming back.

21907.q: What do you learn in the subject of counterpoint?
a: how to combine several independent voices skilfully
how to play chords on the guitar
how to sing songs back by ear
21907.e: In counterpoint you learn to set melodies on top of each other so that each voice stays independent and all sound good together. Johann Joseph Fux wrote a famous textbook on it in 1725.
21907.m: Counterpoint is the art of combining several independent voices.

21908.q: What do you call a recurring motif that represents a person, an object or an idea?
21908.e: Leitmotifs link music with characters or ideas in the plot. Today they are also often used in film music.
21908.m: A leitmotif stands musically for a character or an idea.

21909.q: What is a constantly repeated musical figure, often in the bass, called?
21909.e: Ostinato comes from the Italian word for stubborn. A well-known example is the basso ostinato of the chaconne.
